entries.title: General-purpose registers
entries.definition:
Use x86-64 general-purpose registers such as RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RSP, RBP, and R8-R15.

Reference detail
The 64-bit RAX family overlaps: EAX is its low 32 bits, AX the low 16, AL the low 8. Writing EAX clears RAX bits 63:32; writing AX or AL preserves the rest. R8D/R8W/R8B behave analogously. RIP is the instruction pointer, not an ordinary MOV destination; RSP names the active stack. Register names carry width, not a permanent signed/unsigned type. Use ABI tables to decide which scratch registers survive a call.
entries.mental_model:
Registers are the CPU's tiny, ultra-fast scratchpad.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
After AX: RAX=0xffffffffffff1234. After EAX: RAX=7.
entries.return_value: MOV does not change arithmetic flags. RAX is the demonstrated destination.
entries.gotchas:
Some registers have ABI-defined roles across calls.

Do not expect a 32-bit write to preserve the upper half. AH/BH/CH/DH cannot be encoded with a REX prefix; prefer low byte registers in 64-bit examples.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: MOV; MOVZX; movsx; calling conventions.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Use x86-64 general-purpose registers such as RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RSP, RBP, and R8-R15.

entries.title: MOV
entries.definition:
Copy data between registers, memory, and immediates.

Reference detail
MOV copies an immediate, register or memory operand to a register or memory destination. Ordinary integer MOV permits at most one memory operand. Matching register widths often determine the memory width; an immediate-to-memory store needs byte/word/dword/qword when no register resolves it. A symbol without brackets denotes an address or immediate expression; brackets request a load/store. This example stores an eight-byte value in writable storage, then reloads it.
entries.mental_model:
MOV copies bits; it does not conceptually move ownership.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
value holds 123 as eight little-endian bytes; RAX=123.
entries.return_value: No arithmetic flags changed; destination memory and RAX change.
entries.gotchas:
Memory-to-memory MOV is generally not allowed.

A label is not a variable with an inferred element type. mov [rel value], 1 is ambiguous without a size. Never write into .rodata.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: Memory addressing; Sections; LEA.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Copy data between registers, memory, and immediates.

entries.title: LEA
entries.definition:
Compute an effective address without dereferencing it.

Reference detail
LEA performs address arithmetic and writes the computed integer without reading that address. The permitted form combines base + index*scale + displacement; scale is 1,2,4,8. It can implement a small multiplication/addition without changing flags. LEA does not validate whether an address is mapped. A 32-bit destination still zero-extends into its 64-bit register.
entries.mental_model:
Treat LEA as integer/address arithmetic using addressing syntax.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=3+3*4+8=23; no memory at address 23 is read.
entries.return_value: LEA preserves arithmetic flags. RAX is written, RCX is only read.
entries.gotchas: Do not confuse lea rax,[rcx] with mov rax,[rcx]. RIP-relative addressing cannot include an index; load a relative base first.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: Memory addressing; Position-independent addresses.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Compute an effective address without dereferencing it.

entries.title: MOVZX
entries.definition:
Copy a smaller unsigned value into a larger register and zero-extend it.

Reference detail
MOVZX reads an 8- or 16-bit source and fills the added high bits with zeros in a larger destination. Use it for unsigned bytes such as masks or raw octets. There is no movzx rax,eax encoding: mov eax,eax already clears RAX high bits. The source can be memory or an appropriately sized register.
entries.mental_model:
Promote a small unsigned integer without preserving garbage in upper bits.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
AL starts with 0xff; EAX and RAX become 255.
entries.return_value: Arithmetic flags unchanged. Source bits preserved, high destination bits cleared.
entries.gotchas: Zero extension changes width, not the source bits. For a signed byte -1 use MOVSX instead.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: movsx; General-purpose registers.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Copy a smaller unsigned value into a larger register and zero-extend it.

entries.title: ADD and SUB
entries.signature: add dst, src / sub dst, src
entries.definition:
Perform integer addition and subtraction.

Reference detail
ADD and SUB compute modulo 2^width. The same result bits can represent signed or unsigned integers; CF reports unsigned carry/borrow while OF reports signed overflow. SF mirrors the high result bit, ZF tests zero, PF tests even parity of the low byte, and AF reports carry/borrow across bit 3. Use these flags immediately or save the condition before another flag-writing instruction.
entries.mental_model:
Mutate the destination register in place.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
ADD wraps to 0; SUB wraps back to 0xffffffff (RAX=4294967295).
entries.return_value: ADD/SUB define CF,OF,SF,ZF,AF,PF from their result. Final SUB has CF=1,ZF=0,SF=1,OF=0.
entries.gotchas: Overflow does not automatically throw an exception. A 32-bit destination zero-extends even when its signed interpretation is negative.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: CMP; Signed versus unsigned branches; ADC and SBB.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Perform integer addition and subtraction.

entries.title: IMUL
entries.definition:
Perform signed integer multiplication.

Reference detail
Two-operand IMUL multiplies signed operands and stores the low destination-width bits. Three-operand IMUL takes a register/memory source and immediate multiplier. One-operand IMUL instead uses implicit accumulator registers and produces a double-width result. In the two/three-operand forms CF and OF indicate that the signed product did not fit in the destination width.
entries.mental_model:
Signed multiplication with convenient two-operand forms.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
EAX=0xffffffd6 (signed -42); RAX=4294967254 because EAX write clears high bits.
entries.return_value: CF=OF=0 here. SF,ZF,AF,PF are undefined after IMUL; do not branch on them.
entries.gotchas: For signed 64-bit -42 use mov rax,-7 / imul rax,rax,6. Low product bits alone do not show whether a signed product overflowed.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: idiv; Width and signedness.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Perform signed integer multiplication.

entries.title: CMP
entries.definition:
Compare two operands by setting CPU flags as if subtraction occurred.

Reference detail
CMP subtracts source from destination only to set flags; neither operand is modified. After cmp a,b, signed less-than uses SF != OF; unsigned below uses CF=1. Equality uses ZF=1 for either interpretation. Operands must have compatible width and cannot both be memory. Arrange the branch or SETcc before instructions that overwrite these flags.
entries.mental_model:
CMP prepares flags for a later conditional instruction.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
Comparison sees 0xffffffff-1; signed SETL produces AL=1 and final RAX=1.
entries.return_value: CMP defines CF,OF,SF,ZF,AF,PF like SUB, but discards the result. SETL and MOVZX preserve them.
entries.gotchas: CMP ordering matters: cmp a,b means a-b, not b-a. Signedness belongs to the chosen condition, not CMP itself.

entries.title: TEST
entries.definition:
Perform a bitwise AND for flags without storing the result.

Reference detail
TEST computes a bitwise AND solely for flags. test reg,reg asks whether a value is zero; test reg,mask asks whether any selected bit is set. It does not compare numerical ordering and does not store the AND result. For every selected bit to be set, AND a copy then CMP against the mask.
entries.mental_model:
Use TEST when you care about flags, not the AND result.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
0x12 AND 0x10 is nonzero: ZF=0, DL=0, final RAX=0.
entries.return_value: TEST clears CF/OF; SF,ZF,PF reflect the AND result; AF undefined. Operands unchanged.
entries.gotchas: jz after TEST means the intersection is empty, not that every original bit was zero unless the mask covered them.

entries.title: Bitwise operations
entries.definition:
Manipulate bits with AND, OR, XOR, NOT, SHL, and SHR.

Reference detail
AND clears unselected bits, OR sets selected bits, XOR toggles selected bits; XORing a register with itself makes zero. NOT flips every bit at the operand width. SHL shifts left, SHR shifts right inserting zero; SAR replicates the sign bit. Shift counts are masked (5 bits for 32-bit operands, 6 for 64-bit). A zero effective count preserves the destination and flags.
entries.mental_model:
Think masks, flags, packing, and powers of two.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
0x12 -> 2 -> 0x82 -> 0x80; NOT AL makes low byte 0x7f, final RAX=127.
entries.return_value: AND/OR/XOR clear CF/OF, set SF/ZF/PF, leave AF undefined. NOT changes no flags. Shift flag rules are covered separately.
entries.gotchas: Do not group all bit operations under one flag rule; NOT differs. SHR is not signed division of negative values.

entries.title: JMP
entries.definition:
Perform an unconditional branch.

Reference detail
A direct JMP changes instruction flow to a label and creates no return address. A conditional branch chooses a path; JMP can skip the other path when it rejoins. An indirect JMP takes its destination from a register or memory, so only use a valid code address. Keep data out of the execution path.
entries.mental_model:
Replace fall-through execution with an explicit destination.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
The second MOV is skipped, so RAX=4.
entries.return_value: JMP does not modify arithmetic flags; RIP changes. RET later uses the caller return address.
entries.gotchas: Falling through into another function is possible: labels do not create blocks or implicit returns.

entries.title: Conditional jumps
entries.definition:
Branch based on CPU flags using JE, JNE, JL, JG, JB, JA, and related instructions.

Reference detail
JE/JZ tests ZF; JNE/JNZ tests !ZF. After CMP, signed JL/JGE test SF versus OF; JLE/JG also consider ZF. Unsigned JB/JAE test CF; JBE/JA also consider ZF. Choose the family from the intended interpretation. Branch instructions preserve the tested flags, so several branches may test one CMP if nothing between changes flags.
entries.mental_model:
CMP/TEST sets flags; Jcc consumes them.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
Signed -1 is less than 1, so the function returns 1. Changing JL to JB would return 0.
entries.return_value: Jcc reads relevant flags; does not write them. CMP defines the flags.
entries.gotchas: Equality makes strict JL/JB false. An intervening ADD or TEST would replace the comparison condition.

entries.title: CALL and RET
entries.definition:
Call a function and return using the stack-stored return address.

Reference detail
A near CALL in 64-bit mode pushes the next instruction address (8 bytes) and transfers control. RET pops that address into RIP. The callee must restore its stack to the state expected at return and preserve ABI-designated registers. This pair is control flow, not a complete calling convention: argument registers, alignment and ownership come from the ABI.
entries.mental_model:
CALL is controlled stack bookkeeping plus a jump.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
At System V function entry RSP%16=8. SUB makes it 0 before CALL; .two sees 8 again. RAX=2 and original RSP restored.
entries.return_value: CALL/RET themselves preserve arithmetic flags. SUB/ADD adjust flags as arithmetic instructions.
entries.gotchas: The old compact CALL fragment is illustrative: a real caller needs a defined entry/exit path and must not fall through into its callee.

entries.title: PUSH and POP
entries.definition:
Save and restore stack values.

Reference detail
In 64-bit code a normal register PUSH subtracts 8 from RSP then stores 8 bytes; POP reads 8 bytes then adds 8. Save/restore in reverse order. This preserves a callee-saved register while letting the function use it. Stack alignment depends on the total pushes/local allocation and the ABI at each call site.
entries.mental_model:
RSP moves as values are pushed and popped.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=99; RBX restored to caller value; RSP restored before RET.
entries.return_value: PUSH/POP do not change arithmetic flags. Memory and RSP change; POP writes its destination.
entries.gotchas:
Maintain ABI-required stack alignment before external calls.

Do not pop into the wrong register or forget a saved slot. A 16-bit push is possible but changes RSP by 2 and usually breaks ABI assumptions.

entries.title: System V AMD64 calling convention
entries.signature: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9
entries.definition:
Pass integer/pointer arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, and R9 on Linux/macOS System V x86-64.

Reference detail
For ordinary System V AMD64 integer/pointer arguments, the first six use RDI,RSI,RDX,RCX,R8,R9; integer return values usually use RAX. Preserve RBX,RBP,R12–R15 and restore RSP. Caller-saved registers may be overwritten. Before an ordinary CALL the caller aligns RSP to 16 bytes; the pushed return address makes entry RSP%16=8. Aggregate/vector/variadic rules need the full ABI, not this integer summary.
entries.mental_model:
Registers are agreed-upon mail slots between caller and callee.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
For demo(20,22), RAX=42. No stack storage or callee-saved register is used.
entries.return_value: ADD defines arithmetic flags; ABI callers must not assume these flags survive an ordinary call.
entries.gotchas:
Windows x64 uses a different convention.

Linux syscall argument 4 uses R10, unlike function argument 4 RCX. The 128-byte red zone is a System V user-space facility, not a universal stack rule or a Windows feature.

entries.title: Memory addressing
entries.definition:
Address memory with base, index, scale, and displacement expressions.

Reference detail
An x86-64 memory operand can use base + index*scale + signed displacement. Scale is bytes per element only when you choose it to match your data: dwords use 4, qwords use 8. The brackets describe an address; the instruction/register determines the transferred width. Bounds are your responsibility: a valid CPU address can still be outside your logical array.
entries.mental_model:
Effective addresses are arithmetic expressions evaluated by the CPU.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
Index 2 selects the third dword, so RAX=30.
entries.return_value: MOV/LEA preserve flags. RCX is the element index; RDI is the base pointer.
entries.gotchas: [rel values+rcx*4] cannot encode RIP+index. Compute the RIP-relative base into a register first. An index is not automatically scaled by its conceptual type.

entries.title: Sections
entries.definition:
Organize code and data into sections such as .text, .data, .rodata, and .bss.

Reference detail
Sections describe parts of an object file; the linker arranges them into loadable segments and permissions. Conventional .text holds instructions, .rodata read-only constants, .data initialized writable storage, .bss zero-filled static storage in typical ELF executables. NASM switches the current section with SECTION. This is not a runtime instruction and changing it does not change CPU mode.
entries.mental_model:
Sections tell the linker what kind of bytes you are defining.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=42 loaded from .rodata; no output is printed.
entries.return_value: Assembler directives do not execute and have no CPU flag effects. MOV preserves flags.
entries.gotchas: Section names and defaults depend on the output format. Do not assume ELF .rodata conventions are identical in Windows COFF.

entries.title: Labels
entries.definition:
Name instruction or data addresses.

Reference detail
A label names the current location; it allocates no storage and emits no instruction itself. NASM dot-local labels belong to the preceding nonlocal label, so routine.done and other.done can coexist. Reusing a nonlocal name is an error. Explicitly guard zero counts before a decrement loop, otherwise zero wraps and a supposedly empty operation can run many iterations.
entries.mental_model:
A label is a symbolic address resolved by the assembler/linker.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
ECX:3->2->1->0; EAX:0->2->4->6; final RAX=6.
entries.return_value: DEC sets OF,SF,ZF,AF,PF but preserves CF. JNZ reads ZF.
entries.gotchas: This fixed nonzero trace is not a general array loop. For external counts, test before the loop and validate the memory range.

entries.title: DB, DW, DD, DQ
entries.definition:
Define byte, word, doubleword, and quadword data.

Reference detail
DB/DW/DD/DQ emit initialized units of 1/2/4/8 bytes. On x86 a multibyte integer uses little-endian order, so its least significant byte appears first. Strings emit their bytes, not an automatic terminator; add 0 when a C-style terminator is needed. $ is the current assembly position, so $-label is a byte count within the section.
entries.mental_model:
Directives emit raw bytes into the object file.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
number dd 0x12345678 occupies bytes 78 56 34 12; first byte loaded is 0x78 (120).
entries.return_value: Data directives have no runtime flag effect; MOVZX preserves flags.
entries.gotchas: dd 1 reserves four initialized bytes, not four elements. UTF-8 character count may differ from byte count; syscall write uses bytes.

entries.title: EQU
entries.definition:
Define an assembly-time constant.

Reference detail
EQU binds a name to an assembly-time constant/expression; it does not allocate a memory cell. Use it for byte lengths and fixed offsets. A label difference must be meaningful to the assembler, commonly two positions in the same section. Runtime data still needs DB/DW/DD/DQ or reserved storage and a load/store instruction.
entries.mental_model:
EQU is textual/assembly-time meaning, not runtime memory.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
msg contains three bytes H i newline; msg_len=3, returned in RAX.
entries.return_value: No runtime flags from EQU; MOV preserves flags.
entries.gotchas: mov eax,msg_len loads the constant. mov eax,[msg_len] would read memory at address 3 here.

entries.title: GLOBAL and EXTERN
entries.definition:
Export symbols and reference symbols provided by other object files.

Reference detail
GLOBAL makes a defined symbol visible to other object files; EXTERN declares a symbol supplied elsewhere. Neither calls a function nor allocates a runtime object. The linker resolves references and reports missing definitions. Visibility does not guarantee ABI compatibility: caller and callee must agree on argument order, widths, return registers and saved state.
entries.mental_model:
GLOBAL opens a door outward; EXTERN declares a door expected elsewhere.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
The object exports demo; a compatible C harness can call it and receive 42.
entries.return_value: Directives have no runtime effects. MOV and RET preserve arithmetic flags.
entries.gotchas: A declaration is not a definition. Platform symbol naming and relocation rules differ; do not mix ELF64 and COFF objects.

entries.title: syscall instruction
entries.definition:
Enter the Linux kernel using the x86-64 syscall ABI.

Reference detail
Linux x86-64 raw syscalls place the service number in RAX, then arguments in RDI,RSI,RDX,R10,R8,R9. SYSCALL transfers to the kernel and normally resumes at the next instruction. RCX receives the user return address and R11 the saved flags as part of the hardware transition; regard both as clobbered. Raw Linux errors are negative errno values in RAX, not C library errno handling.
entries.mental_model:
Place the syscall number and arguments in ABI-defined registers, then cross into the kernel.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
Linux getpid returns a positive process ID in RAX; the exact value varies.
entries.return_value: RAX is return value; RCX/R11 clobbered. Do not carry a condition in flags across a system service.
entries.gotchas:
Syscall numbers and conventions are OS/architecture specific.

These numbers and registers apply to Linux x86-64, not i386, Windows, ARM or RISC-V. _start exits through a service; it has no caller return address for RET.

entries.title: write syscall
entries.definition:
Write bytes to a file descriptor directly through Linux.

Reference detail
Linux write(fd,buffer,count) attempts to transfer count bytes. It can return a smaller positive count, zero, or a negative raw errno result. A correct write-all loop advances both pointer and remaining count; retries must distinguish EINTR and avoid an endless loop on zero progress. The buffer must remain readable for the full requested range. write does not require a terminating NUL.
entries.mental_model:
A minimal path from your process to the kernel without libc.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
On an ordinary writable stdout, prints Hi plus newline and returns 3. Other return values must be handled by a caller.
entries.return_value: RAX is byte count/error; RCX/R11 clobbered. Syscall arguments are caller supplied registers.
entries.gotchas: A short-write-capable API is not an all-or-nothing print. The single-call demonstration deliberately leaves error/retry policy to its caller.

entries.title: Facts

entries.title: Capability selection

entries.mental_model: Describe constraints, then query for satisfying choices.
entries.summary: Select tools or actions by declaring required and provided capabilities.

entries.title: Constraint-style validation
entries.definition: Represent configuration rules as predicates that succeed only when a state is valid.
entries.mental_model: Validation becomes provability.
entries.summary: Represent configuration rules as predicates that succeed only when a state is valid.

entries.title: Variables and assignment
entries.definition: Bind names to Python objects.
entries.mental_model: Names point at objects rather than containing fixed storage types.
entries.summary: Bind names to Python objects.

entries.title: if / elif / else
entries.definition: Select code paths based on truthy conditions.
entries.mental_model: Evaluate conditions from top to bottom until one matches.
entries.summary: Select code paths based on truthy conditions.

entries.title: for loops
entries.definition: Iterate over items from any iterable.
entries.mental_model: for asks an iterable for successive values.
entries.summary: Iterate over items from any iterable.

entries.title: Functions
entries.definition: Package reusable behavior behind a callable name.
entries.mental_model: A function is a named transformation with its own local scope.
entries.summary: Package reusable behavior behind a callable name.

entries.title: Comprehensions
entries.definition: Build collections concisely from iterables.
entries.mental_model: Map/filter syntax compressed into an expression.
entries.summary: Build collections concisely from iterables.

entries.title: Pattern matching
entries.definition: Match structured values using match/case.
entries.mental_model: Think structural switch with destructuring.
entries.summary: Match structured values using match/case.

entries.title: Lists
entries.definition: Store ordered mutable sequences.
entries.mental_model: A resizable ordered container.
entries.summary: Store ordered mutable sequences.

entries.title: Dictionaries
entries.definition: Map hashable keys to values.
entries.mental_model: A fast key-value index.
entries.summary: Map hashable keys to values.

entries.title: Sets
entries.definition: Store unique hashable values.
entries.mental_model: A membership-focused bag of unique values.
entries.summary: Store unique hashable values.

entries.title: Tuples
entries.definition: Store fixed ordered sequences, often for lightweight records or multiple returns.
entries.mental_model: An immutable positional record.
entries.summary: Store fixed ordered sequences, often for lightweight records or multiple returns.

entries.title: dataclasses
entries.definition: Generate boilerplate for data-centric classes.
entries.mental_model: Describe fields and let Python generate initialization and representation helpers.
entries.summary: Generate boilerplate for data-centric classes.

entries.title: Path
entries.definition: Represent filesystem paths as objects.
entries.mental_model: Paths become composable objects instead of string glue.
entries.summary: Represent filesystem paths as objects.

entries.title: read_text()
entries.definition: Read a text file using a chosen encoding.
entries.mental_model: One method combines open/read/close for small text files.
entries.summary: Read a text file using a chosen encoding.

entries.title: loads()
entries.definition: Parse JSON text into Python objects.
entries.mental_model: Convert wire-format text into Python dictionaries/lists/scalars.
entries.summary: Parse JSON text into Python objects.

entries.title: dumps()
entries.definition: Serialize Python values into JSON text.
entries.mental_model: Turn in-memory values into portable text.
entries.summary: Serialize Python values into JSON text.

entries.title: run()
entries.definition: Run a child process and optionally capture/check its result.
entries.mental_model: Treat an external command as a function call with explicit inputs and outputs.
entries.summary: Run a child process and optionally capture/check its result.

entries.title: Type hints
entries.definition: Annotate parameters, returns, and variables for tooling and static analysis.
entries.mental_model: Type hints are contracts for humans and tools.
entries.summary: Annotate parameters, returns, and variables for tooling and static analysis.

entries.title: Virtual environments
entries.definition: Isolate project dependencies from system Python.
entries.mental_model: Give each project its own dependency sandbox.
entries.summary: Isolate project dependencies from system Python.

entries.title: pyproject.toml
entries.definition: Central project metadata and build/dependency configuration file.
entries.mental_model: Python packaging configuration gathered under one standardized roof.
entries.summary: Central project metadata and build/dependency configuration file.

entries.title: argparse
entries.definition: Parse command-line flags and arguments using the standard library.
entries.mental_model: Describe a CLI grammar, then let argparse validate input.
entries.summary: Parse command-line flags and arguments using the standard library.

entries.title: Event queue
entries.definition: Poll and process queued input and window events every frame.
entries.mental_model: Think of Event queue as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Poll and process queued input and window events every frame.

entries.title: Surface
entries.definition: Represent an image or drawable pixel buffer.
entries.mental_model: Think of Surface as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Represent an image or drawable pixel buffer.

entries.title: blit()
entries.definition: Copy one Surface onto another.
entries.mental_model: Think of Surface.blit() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Copy one Surface onto another.

entries.title: Rect
entries.definition: Store and manipulate integer rectangular areas for positioning and collision.
entries.mental_model: Think of Rect as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Store and manipulate integer rectangular areas for positioning and collision.

entries.title: Sprite
entries.definition: Build reusable game objects with image and rect conventions.
entries.mental_model: Think of Sprite as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Build reusable game objects with image and rect conventions.

entries.title: Group
entries.definition: Store, update, and draw collections of Sprites.
entries.mental_model: Think of Group as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Store, update, and draw collections of Sprites.

entries.title: spritecollide()
entries.definition: Test a Sprite against Sprites in a Group.
entries.mental_model: Think of spritecollide() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Test a Sprite against Sprites in a Group.

entries.title: Keyboard state
entries.definition: Read held keyboard keys each frame.
entries.mental_model: Think of Keyboard state as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Read held keyboard keys each frame.

entries.title: Drawing primitives
entries.definition: Draw shapes directly onto Surfaces.
entries.mental_model: Think of Drawing primitives as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Draw shapes directly onto Surfaces.

entries.title: Font rendering
entries.definition: Render text into a Surface.
entries.mental_model: Think of Font rendering as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Render text into a Surface.

entries.title: Sound effects
entries.definition: Load and play short sound effects with pygame.mixer.Sound.
entries.mental_model: Think of Sound effects as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Load and play short sound effects with pygame.mixer.Sound.

entries.title: Custom timers
entries.definition: Post repeated events to the event queue on a timer.
entries.mental_model: Think of Custom timers as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Post repeated events to the event queue on a timer.

entries.title: init()
entries.definition: Initialize imported Pygame modules.
entries.mental_model: Think of pygame.init() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Initialize imported Pygame modules.

entries.title: set_mode()
entries.definition: Create the main display Surface.
entries.mental_model: Think of display.set_mode() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Create the main display Surface.

entries.title: tick()
entries.definition: Cap frame rate and measure elapsed frame time.
entries.mental_model: Think of Clock.tick() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Cap frame rate and measure elapsed frame time.

entries.title: load()
entries.definition: Load an image file into a Surface.
entries.mental_model: Think of image.load() as one of the core tools behind this concept.
entries.summary: Load an image file into a Surface.

entries.title: var declarations
entries.definition: Create mutable local variables.
entries.mental_model: A named slot whose value can change.
entries.summary: Create mutable local variables.

entries.title: if / else
entries.definition: Choose between branches based on a boolean condition.
entries.mental_model: Wren conditions are explicit boolean decisions.
entries.summary: Choose between branches based on a boolean condition.

entries.title: while
entries.definition: Repeat a block while a condition remains true.
entries.mental_model: Loop until the guard turns false.
entries.summary: Repeat a block while a condition remains true.

entries.title: for
entries.definition: Iterate over any object implementing Wren iteration protocol.
entries.mental_model: Iteration is protocol-driven rather than limited to built-in lists.
entries.summary: Iterate over any object implementing Wren iteration protocol.

entries.title: Functions
entries.definition: Create callable function objects with Fn.new.
entries.mental_model: Functions are first-class objects.
entries.summary: Create callable function objects with Fn.new.

entries.title: Classes
entries.definition: Define reusable object types.
entries.mental_model: A class groups state, constructors, and methods.
entries.summary: Define reusable object types.

entries.title: Constructors
entries.definition: Initialize new instances using construct methods.
entries.mental_model: Constructors are specially marked instance methods.
entries.summary: Initialize new instances using construct methods.

entries.title: Fields
entries.definition: Store per-instance state in names beginning with underscore.
entries.mental_model: Underscore-prefixed names are instance fields.
entries.summary: Store per-instance state in names beginning with underscore.

entries.title: Static methods
entries.definition: Attach behavior to the class object itself.
entries.mental_model: Useful for constructors, factories, and namespaces.
entries.summary: Attach behavior to the class object itself.

entries.title: Inheritance
entries.definition: Create a subclass that inherits behavior from a superclass.
entries.mental_model: Subclass lookup falls back to the parent class.
entries.summary: Create a subclass that inherits behavior from a superclass.

entries.title: Lists
entries.definition: Store ordered mutable collections.
entries.mental_model: A growable indexed sequence.
entries.summary: Store ordered mutable collections.

entries.title: Maps
entries.definition: Map keys to values.
entries.mental_model: A hash-based dictionary.
entries.summary: Map keys to values.

entries.title: Ranges
entries.definition: Represent integer ranges for iteration and slicing-like operations.
entries.mental_model: Ranges are lightweight iterable interval objects.
entries.summary: Represent integer ranges for iteration and slicing-like operations.

entries.title: import
entries.definition: Load names from another Wren module.
entries.mental_model: Modules are the unit of code loading and namespace separation.
entries.summary: Load names from another Wren module.

entries.title: Foreign methods
entries.definition: Declare methods implemented by the embedding host application.
entries.mental_model: Wren names the API; your host language supplies the implementation.
entries.gotchas: Requires embedding API support from the host.
entries.summary: Declare methods implemented by the embedding host application.

entries.title: new()
entries.definition: Create a cooperatively scheduled fiber around a function.
entries.mental_model: A fiber is a resumable stack managed cooperatively.
entries.summary: Create a cooperatively scheduled fiber around a function.

entries.title: yield()
entries.definition: Yield control from the current fiber back to its caller.
entries.mental_model: Think suspendable function execution.
entries.summary: Yield control from the current fiber back to its caller.

entries.title: Primitive types
entries.definition: Use fixed primitive value types such as int, long, double, boolean, char, byte, short, and float.
entries.mental_model: Primitives are direct values, distinct from object references.
entries.summary: Use fixed primitive value types such as int, long, double, boolean, char, byte, short, and float.

entries.title: Classes
entries.definition:
Define object types containing fields, constructors, and methods.

new Type(arguments) calls a constructor to create an instance. An instance method is called on an object, and its declared return type determines the type of the next value.
entries.mental_model: A class is a blueprint for state plus behavior.
entries.notes: Read a chained expression from left to right. Expanding it into explicitly typed intermediate variables makes each constructor call, receiver, and return value visible.
entries.summary: Define object types containing fields, constructors, and methods.

entries.title: Interfaces
entries.definition: Define behavioral contracts that classes can implement.
entries.mental_model: Program to capabilities instead of concrete classes.
entries.summary: Define behavioral contracts that classes can implement.

entries.title: Records
entries.definition:
Define concise immutable data carriers.

A record component automatically has an accessor method with the same name and no arguments. For a component named payload, call packet.payload(), not packet.getPayload().
entries.mental_model: Records are purpose-built transparent data holders.
entries.gotchas: Record components cannot be reassigned, but a byte[] component still refers to a mutable array. A generated accessor returns that array reference, not a defensive copy.
entries.notes: Lumen's Packet accessors are payload(), sequenceNumber(), and totalPackets(). Each accessor's return type is the corresponding component's declared type.
entries.summary: Define concise immutable data carriers.

entries.title: Enums
entries.definition: Represent a closed set of named constants, optionally with behavior.
entries.mental_model: A finite type-safe set of values.
entries.summary: Represent a closed set of named constants, optionally with behavior.

entries.title: switch expressions
entries.definition: Select a value with expression-style switch syntax.
entries.mental_model: Switch can be an expression, not only a statement.
entries.summary: Select a value with expression-style switch syntax.

entries.title: System
entries.definition: java.lang.System is a utility class exposing standard streams and process/runtime helpers through static members.
entries.mental_model: Treat System as the JVM application's doorway to process-level facilities such as stdout, stderr, stdin, environment variables, and exit status.
entries.gotchas: System cannot be instantiated. System.out and System.err are PrintStream fields; print() and println() are methods on those stream objects.
entries.summary: Access standard input/output streams, environment information, and JVM process controls.

entries.title: out
entries.definition: A PrintStream connected to the process's standard output destination.
entries.mental_model: The normal stream for program output that should appear on stdout.
entries.notes: Methods shown beneath out are convenience navigation to commonly used PrintStream operations.
entries.summary: The standard output stream.

entries.title: print()
entries.definition: Writes the supplied value through the standard output PrintStream.
entries.mental_model: Write now, keep the cursor on the same line.
entries.summary: Write a value to standard output without automatically terminating the line.

entries.title: println()
entries.definition: Writes the supplied value through the standard output PrintStream and then terminates the line.
entries.mental_model: Print a value, then move output to the next line.
entries.summary: Write a value followed by a line terminator to standard output.

entries.title: err
entries.definition: A PrintStream connected to the process's standard error destination.
entries.mental_model: Use stderr for diagnostics and errors that should remain distinct from normal program output.
entries.notes: Methods shown beneath err are convenience navigation to commonly used PrintStream operations.
entries.summary: The standard error stream.

entries.title: print()
entries.definition: Writes the supplied value through the standard error PrintStream.
entries.mental_model: Diagnostic output that stays on the current stderr line.
entries.summary: Write diagnostic text to standard error without automatically terminating the line.

entries.title: println()
entries.definition: Writes the supplied value through the standard error PrintStream and terminates the line.
entries.mental_model: The stderr counterpart to System.out.println().
entries.summary: Write diagnostic text followed by a line terminator to standard error.

entries.title: in
entries.definition: An InputStream connected to the process's standard input source.
entries.mental_model: Raw bytes arriving from stdin, commonly wrapped by Scanner or BufferedReader for convenient text input.
entries.gotchas: InputStream works with bytes; text-oriented code often wraps System.in in a reader or Scanner.
entries.summary: The standard input stream.

entries.title: getenv()
entries.definition: Returns the value of an environment variable, or null when the named variable is not defined.
entries.mental_model: Ask the operating-system process environment for configuration inherited by the JVM.
entries.gotchas: Environment variable names and case sensitivity are platform-dependent.
entries.summary: Read environment variables visible to the Java process.

entries.title: exit()
entries.definition: Terminates the currently running Java Virtual Machine with the supplied status code.
entries.mental_model: Immediately hand an exit status back to the operating system.
entries.gotchas: This terminates the JVM, so normal control flow does not continue afterward.
entries.summary: Terminate the current JVM process with a status code.

entries.title: Generics
entries.definition: Parameterize types and methods while preserving compile-time type safety.
entries.mental_model: A type-level placeholder filled by the caller.
entries.summary: Parameterize types and methods while preserving compile-time type safety.

entries.title: List
entries.definition: Store ordered collections with duplicates.
entries.mental_model: An indexed ordered sequence abstraction.
entries.summary: Store ordered collections with duplicates.

entries.title: Map
entries.definition: Associate keys with values.
entries.mental_model: Key-value lookup abstraction.
entries.summary: Associate keys with values.

entries.title: Streams
entries.definition: Transform and aggregate collection-like data declaratively.
entries.mental_model: A lazy-ish transformation pipeline over elements.
entries.summary: Transform and aggregate collection-like data declaratively.

entries.title: Lambdas
entries.definition: Create anonymous function values for functional interfaces.
entries.mental_model: Compact behavior passed as data.
entries.summary: Create anonymous function values for functional interfaces.

entries.title: Exceptions
entries.definition:
Represent and propagate exceptional failures.

IOException is a checked exception used for I/O failures. A method that lets it escape declares throws IOException; its caller must catch it or also declare it.
entries.mental_model:
Exceptions unwind the call stack until a matching handler appears.

throws declares a possible exit from a method; throw actually takes that exit.
entries.gotchas: throws IOException does not handle the failure. throw new IOException("message") creates and raises an exception, so normal execution does not continue past that throw.
entries.notes: Lumen: a false result from ImageIO.write or a null result from ImageIO.read can be turned into an IOException explicitly; these return values are separate from exceptions the APIs may throw.
entries.summary: Represent and propagate exceptional failures.

entries.title: try-with-resources
entries.definition: Automatically close AutoCloseable resources.
entries.mental_model: Resource lifetime is tied to the lexical block.
entries.summary: Automatically close AutoCloseable resources.

entries.title: Path and Files
entries.definition: Use java.nio.file for platform-aware filesystem operations.
entries.mental_model: Path models location; Files performs operations.
entries.summary: Use java.nio.file for platform-aware filesystem operations.

entries.title: ProcessBuilder
entries.definition: Launch external programs with explicit arguments and I/O behavior.
entries.mental_model: Build a child-process configuration, then start it.
entries.summary: Launch external programs with explicit arguments and I/O behavior.

entries.title: ExecutorService
entries.definition: Run tasks using managed thread pools.
entries.mental_model: Separate task submission from thread management.
entries.summary: Run tasks using managed thread pools.

entries.title: CompletableFuture
entries.definition: Compose asynchronous operations and continuations.
entries.mental_model: A future plus a graph of dependent stages.
entries.summary: Compose asynchronous operations and continuations.

entries.title: JAR files
entries.definition: Package compiled classes and resources into Java archives.
entries.mental_model: A ZIP-based application/library bundle understood by the JVM ecosystem.
entries.summary: Package compiled classes and resources into Java archives.

entries.title: JVM bytecode
entries.definition: Java source compiles to class-file bytecode executed or JIT-compiled by the JVM.
entries.mental_model: Portable intermediate instructions sit between source and machine code.
entries.summary: Java source compiles to class-file bytecode executed or JIT-compiled by the JVM.

entries.title: val and var
entries.signature: val name = value / var name = value
entries.definition: Declare immutable values with val and mutable variables with var.
entries.mental_model: Prefer val; reach for var only when mutation is truly useful.
entries.notes: Write val name: String = "Europa" for an explicit type, or val name = "Europa" to let the compiler infer String. Inferred types are still static. val prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not make a referenced mutable object immutable. The existing var/+= example shows deliberate reassignment.
entries.summary: Declare immutable values with val and mutable variables with var.

entries.title: Expression-oriented blocks
entries.definition: Blocks evaluate to their final expression and can directly produce values.
entries.mental_model: Many Scala constructs produce values instead of only causing effects.
entries.notes: A method body also takes its result from its final expression. A final val declaration or println does not provide the Int/String result you intended. Unit means no useful result, and () is its value.
entries.summary: Blocks evaluate to their final expression and can directly produce values.

entries.title: Functions
entries.definition: Define methods with def and anonymous functions with => syntax.
entries.mental_model: Functions are first-class while methods belong to objects/classes.
entries.notes: A lambda can name its parameter type: (n: Int) => n * 2. When a function is expected, a compatible method can be passed directly, as in values.map(twice). Placeholder syntax _.length abbreviates a one-parameter lambda; this underscore is different from a wildcard pattern in case clauses. The existing def example already covers typed parameters, return annotations, and a final-expression result.
entries.summary: Define methods with def and anonymous functions with => syntax.

entries.title: Pattern matching
entries.definition: Deconstruct values and choose branches with match/case.
entries.mental_model: Pattern matching combines branching with destructuring.
entries.notes: A case guard follows if and must be true for that case to match. Some(_) matches a present value while ignoring its content; case _ is a catch-all. Use | between alternative patterns such as None | Some(""); do not introduce different variable bindings in the alternatives.
entries.summary: Deconstruct values and choose branches with match/case.

entries.title: for comprehensions
entries.definition: Compose map/flatMap/filter-style operations with readable syntax.
entries.mental_model: Syntactic sugar for functional collection/monadic composition.
entries.summary: Compose map/flatMap/filter-style operations with readable syntax.

entries.title: Case classes
entries.definition: Define concise immutable data models with structural equality and pattern matching support.
entries.mental_model: Product types with generated ergonomic machinery.
entries.notes: Case classes supply companion apply construction, so Song(...) needs no new. Read a field with song.title. Named arguments use parameterName = value and can make construction clearer. Named arguments are general call syntax, not limited to case classes.
entries.summary: Define concise immutable data models with structural equality and pattern matching support.

entries.title: Enums
entries.definition: Define closed families of values and algebraic data types.
entries.mental_model: A finite set of alternatives that pattern matching can exhaust.
entries.summary: Define closed families of values and algebraic data types.

entries.title: Traits
entries.definition: Define reusable interfaces and behavior that classes/objects can extend.
entries.mental_model: Traits are composable capabilities with optional implementation.
entries.summary: Define reusable interfaces and behavior that classes/objects can extend.

entries.title: Option
entries.definition: Represent a value that may be present or absent without null.
entries.mental_model: Absence is an explicit branch in the type.
entries.notes: Option(possiblyNull) converts a Java null reference to None; a non-null value becomes Some(value). Some(null) stays present and is not a null-safe conversion. Arguments are evaluated before either wrapper is called: Some(failingExpression) cannot catch a failure from that expression.
entries.summary: Represent a value that may be present or absent without null.

entries.title: Either
entries.definition: Represent a computation that yields one of two typed outcomes, commonly error or success.
entries.mental_model: Two-track computation with explicit alternatives.
entries.summary: Represent a computation that yields one of two typed outcomes, commonly error or success.

entries.title: given / using
entries.definition: Provide and consume contextual values in Scala 3.
entries.mental_model: The compiler can thread ambient capabilities explicitly through types.
entries.summary: Provide and consume contextual values in Scala 3.

entries.title: Extension methods
entries.definition: Add callable syntax to existing types without modifying them.
entries.mental_model: Static helper behavior with instance-like call syntax.
entries.summary: Add callable syntax to existing types without modifying them.

entries.title: List
entries.definition: Immutable linked sequence with functional transformation APIs.
entries.mental_model: Immutable sequence nodes shared safely across transformations.
entries.notes: map transforms every element; filter keeps elements whose predicate is true; foreach performs side effects and returns Unit. These operations can be chained while keeping explicitly typed intermediate collections.
entries.summary: Immutable linked sequence with functional transformation APIs.

entries.title: Map collection
entries.definition: Immutable key-value mapping by default.
entries.mental_model: Lookup naturally integrates with Option.
entries.notes: params(key) directly retrieves a value and can throw when the key is absent; params.get(key) returns Option. Map.empty[K, V] creates a typed empty map. A sequence of key/value tuples can use .toMap. Duplicate keys collapse during conversion, so reject duplicates before .toMap when ambiguity is an error.
entries.summary: Immutable key-value mapping by default.

entries.title: Future
entries.definition: Represent an asynchronously computed value.
entries.mental_model: A placeholder completed later by concurrent execution.
entries.summary: Represent an asynchronously computed value.

entries.title: Java interoperability
entries.definition: Call Java classes directly and expose Scala code to JVM ecosystems.
entries.mental_model: Scala and Java share the JVM type/runtime world.
entries.summary: Call Java classes directly and expose Scala code to JVM ecosystems.

entries.title: sbt basics
entries.definition: Use sbt to compile, test, run, and manage dependencies.
entries.mental_model: sbt maintains an incremental build graph for Scala/JVM projects.
entries.summary: Use sbt to compile, test, run, and manage dependencies.

entries.title: Variables
entries.definition: Assign and expand shell variables.
entries.mental_model: Shell variables are strings unless arithmetic/context gives them another interpretation.
entries.summary: Assign and expand shell variables.

entries.title: Quoting
entries.definition: Control shell expansion with single quotes, double quotes, and escaping.
entries.mental_model: Quoting determines which characters the shell interprets before launching commands.
entries.summary: Control shell expansion with single quotes, double quotes, and escaping.

entries.title: Command substitution
entries.definition: Capture command output into another command or variable.
entries.mental_model: Run a subcommand and splice its stdout into the surrounding command.
entries.summary: Capture command output into another command or variable.

entries.title: Arrays
entries.definition: Store indexed shell values.
entries.mental_model: Bash arrays preserve element boundaries better than space-separated strings.
entries.summary: Store indexed shell values.

entries.title: Parameter expansion
entries.definition: Transform or provide defaults for variables during expansion.
entries.mental_model: Small string/default operators built into expansion syntax.
entries.summary: Transform or provide defaults for variables during expansion.

entries.title: if
entries.definition: Branch based on command success or test expressions.
entries.mental_model: In shell, conditions are commands whose exit status matters.
entries.summary: Branch based on command success or test expressions.

entries.title: case
entries.definition: Match a value against shell patterns.
entries.mental_model: Pattern-oriented multi-way branch.
entries.summary: Match a value against shell patterns.

entries.title: for
entries.definition: Iterate over a list of words/items.
entries.mental_model: Each iteration assigns the next item to the loop variable.
entries.summary: Iterate over a list of words/items.

entries.title: while
entries.definition: Repeat while a command succeeds.
entries.mental_model: The guard is reevaluated as a command/expression each iteration.
entries.summary: Repeat while a command succeeds.

entries.title: Functions
entries.definition: Group shell commands under a reusable function name.
entries.mental_model: A shell function executes in the current shell context unless explicitly isolated.
entries.summary: Group shell commands under a reusable function name.

entries.title: Exit status
entries.definition: Use 0 for success and nonzero values for failure/conditions.
entries.mental_model: Exit codes are Bash's primary success/failure data channel.
entries.summary: Use 0 for success and nonzero values for failure/conditions.

entries.title: Pipelines
entries.definition: Connect stdout of one command to stdin of the next.
entries.mental_model: Commands become stages in a byte stream pipeline.
entries.summary: Connect stdout of one command to stdin of the next.

entries.title: Redirection
entries.definition: Send stdin/stdout/stderr to files or other descriptors.
entries.mental_model: File descriptors are rewired before the command starts.
entries.summary: Send stdin/stdout/stderr to files or other descriptors.

entries.title: Background jobs
entries.definition: Run commands asynchronously in the shell with & and manage them with jobs/wait.
entries.mental_model: The shell launches the child without blocking immediately.
entries.summary: Run commands asynchronously in the shell with & and manage them with jobs/wait.

entries.title: trap
entries.definition: Run cleanup or signal handlers when the script exits or receives signals.
entries.mental_model: Register callbacks for shell lifecycle events.
entries.summary: Run cleanup or signal handlers when the script exits or receives signals.

entries.title: test / [[ ]]
entries.definition: Evaluate file, string, and numeric conditions.
entries.mental_model: [[ ]] is Bash's safer expressive conditional syntax.
entries.summary: Evaluate file, string, and numeric conditions.

entries.title: find
entries.definition: Walk directory trees and filter filesystem entries.
entries.mental_model: Declarative filesystem query engine.
entries.summary: Walk directory trees and filter filesystem entries.

entries.title: grep
entries.definition: Search text using fixed strings or regular expressions.
entries.mental_model: Stream/file filter that emits matching lines.

entries.title: push
entries.definition:
Decrement the stack pointer and store a value on the stack.

Reference detail
Instruction detail: PUSH r64 first makes room by subtracting eight from RSP, then writes the source. Ordinary long-mode PUSH has 64-bit or overridden 16-bit operand size, not a 32-bit register form. Immediate encodings are sign-extended to the stack operand width. Flags are separate; PUSHFQ is a different instruction.
entries.mental_model:
Decrement the stack pointer and store a value on the stack.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
The stored eight bytes are ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff; RAX becomes 0xffffffffffffffff; RSP restored.
entries.return_value: PUSH/POP preserve arithmetic flags; RSP and the stack slot change.
entries.gotchas: push 0xffffffff is not a general way to push unsigned 4294967295: its encoded immediate is sign-extended. Load a register first for arbitrary 64-bit values.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Debugger exercise: assemble with nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf demo.asm -o demo.o. Link only with a compatible harness; break at demo and use stepi, info registers and x/8gx $rsp. Inspect the stated result before RET; compare the relevant flags, not undefined bits.

Related: PUSH and POP; Stack frames.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Decrement the stack pointer and store a value on the stack.

entries.title: pop
entries.definition:
Load the top stack value and advance the stack pointer.

Reference detail
Instruction detail: POP r64 reads at the current RSP, then advances the stack by eight. The destination receives bits without conversion. It does not erase the old bytes; it only changes which stack locations are active. Special cases such as POP RSP or a memory destination with RSP addressing need the full instruction rules; use ordinary registers while learning.
entries.mental_model:
Load the top stack value and advance the stack pointer.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX restored to 12; RSP restored before RET. The old slot contents may remain in memory.
entries.return_value: POP preserves flags; XOR in the setup defines its own logical flags.
entries.gotchas: POP cannot restore a register that was never pushed on this path. Every branch into a common epilogue must agree on stack depth.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html

entries.title: call
entries.definition:
Push a return address and branch to a procedure.

Reference detail
Instruction detail: near CALL records its continuation on the current stack. A call target may be a relative label or an indirect register/memory code pointer. No argument validation or callee-saved register saving happens automatically. In this leaf-callee example the caller adjusts alignment, calls, then undoes only its own allocation.

Push a return address and branch to a procedure.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=8; entry, callee and caller stack depths differ by the explicit allocation plus return-address pushes.
entries.return_value: CALL preserves arithmetic flags; RSP and RIP change. SUB/ADD flags are separate.
entries.gotchas: Never jump into the middle of a function expecting a CALL return address. Windows needs shadow space in addition to alignment.
entries.notes:
Scope: linux-x64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

entries.title: ret
entries.definition:
Pop a return address and transfer control to it.

Reference detail
Instruction detail: near RET loads the next instruction pointer from the stack. It does not know how many local slots or saved registers your function used: restore them before RET. A normal System V or Windows x64 function uses plain RET; ret immediate additionally discards argument bytes and belongs to specific conventions, not a universal epilogue.

Pop a return address and transfer control to it.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
Returns 17 while restoring RBX and the caller stack.
entries.return_value: RET preserves arithmetic flags; RIP/RSP change. POP restores RBX.
entries.gotchas: RET at Linux process entry is invalid because _start was not called. A missing POP makes RET treat saved data as an address.

entries.title: syscall
entries.definition:
Enter the operating-system kernel using the x86-64 syscall mechanism.

Reference detail
Instruction detail versus operating-system contract: SYSCALL is a CPU transition instruction, while RAX service numbers and Linux argument registers are an OS ABI. Hardware consumes configured syscall entry state and saves continuation information; user code cannot use one operating system’s syscall table on another. This local example chooses Linux getpid, which has no external arguments.

A raw syscall is not the same as calling libc’s syscall wrapper. Do not assume Windows internal syscall numbers are a stable public API.

entries.title: idiv
entries.definition:
Perform signed division using an implicit wide dividend.

Reference detail
IDIV r/m64 divides signed RDX:RAX by its explicit operand. CQO sign-extends RAX into RDX:RAX before a normal signed 64-bit divide; CDQ does the EDX:EAX equivalent for 32 bits. Quotient truncates toward zero into RAX, remainder goes to RDX and has the dividend sign when nonzero. Divide-by-zero or quotient overflow faults rather than setting an overflow flag.
entries.mental_model:
Perform signed division using an implicit wide dividend.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RDX:RAX is sign-extended -17; quotient RAX=-3, remainder RDX=-2; -17=(-3)*5+(-2).
entries.return_value: IDIV leaves CF,OF,SF,ZF,AF,PF undefined. CQO preserves flags. RDX/RAX are implicit inputs and outputs.
entries.gotchas:
On x86-64 the dividend uses RDX:RAX; prepare/sign-extend it correctly before division.

XOR EDX,EDX is correct zero-extension for unsigned DIV, not for negative signed IDIV. INT64_MIN / -1 also faults.

entries.title: section .bss
entries.definition:
Declare uninitialized static storage.

Reference detail
In a normal ELF executable, .bss contributes a memory size without storing a file byte for every zero-filled element. The loader provides initially zero bytes. This is static process storage, not a stack allocation and not automatically per-call or thread-local. Reserve space with RES directives and choose alignment for the objects you place there.
entries.mental_model:
Declare uninitialized static storage.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
On the first call in a fresh ELF process: initial counter=0, stored/returned counter=1. Later calls increment shared state.
entries.return_value: Section/RES directives have no CPU flags; ADD sets arithmetic flags.
entries.gotchas: This example is not thread-safe. Bare-metal startup must arrange memory initialization itself; do not assume an ELF user-space loader there.

entries.title: resb / resw / resd / resq
entries.definition:
Reserve uninitialized storage units in BSS.

Reference detail
RESB/RESW/RESD/RESQ reserve count units of 1/2/4/8 bytes, normally in .bss. The expression is an element count, so resq 3 needs 24 bytes. entries.title: extern
entries.definition:
Declare a symbol that will be resolved by another object or library.

Directive detail: EXTERN describes a symbol owned by another module. An unused declaration need not create a relocation; a reference does. entries.title: cmovz
entries.definition:
Conditionally move when the zero flag is set without branching.

Reference detail
CMOVZ copies its source into a register only when ZF=1. Its condition comes from an earlier instruction such as CMP or TEST; there is no immediate-source form or 8-bit destination form. The memory-source form can read/fault even when the condition is false, so it is not a safe guard around an invalid pointer.
entries.mental_model:
Use cmovz as the focused tool for this job instead of rebuilding the behavior manually.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
ZF=1 after CMP, so EAX/RAX becomes 42.
entries.return_value: CMOVZ reads ZF and preserves arithmetic flags. The 32-bit destination has x86-64 zero-extension semantics.
entries.gotchas: Do not treat CMOV as short-circuit memory access. Branch around a potentially invalid load.

Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html

entries.title: movsx
entries.definition:
Move a smaller signed value into a larger register with sign extension.

Reference detail
MOVSX copies a signed 8- or 16-bit source into a wider register and repeats its sign bit. MOVSXD handles signed 32-to-64 extension. Destination width matters: movsx eax,al gives signed 32-bit -1 but the EAX write clears RAX’s upper half; movsx rax,al gives signed 64-bit -1.
entries.mental_model:
Use movsx as the focused tool for this job instead of rebuilding the behavior manually.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=0xffffffffffffffff, interpreted as signed 64-bit -1.
entries.return_value: MOVSX/MOVSXD preserve arithmetic flags. Source is read; destination overwritten.
entries.gotchas: Use MOVZX for an unsigned byte 255. For widening a signed int32 in EDI use movsxd rax,edi, not mov eax,edi.
entries.notes:
Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.

Related: MOVZX; General-purpose registers.
Official references: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html
https://www.nasm.us/doc/nasm03.html
entries.summary: Move a smaller signed value into a larger register with sign extension.

entries.title: bswap
entries.definition:
Reverse the byte order inside a register.

Reference detail
BSWAP reverses byte order within a 32- or 64-bit register; it does not reverse bits within each byte. It is useful when converting between byte sequences with opposite endianness. The 32-bit form also clears the upper 32 bits of its corresponding 64-bit register. There is no defined 16-bit BSWAP form for ordinary use.
entries.mental_model:
Use BSWAP when converting register-sized integers between opposite byte orders.

Trace the operand width, then the destination, then flags.
RAX=0x78563412. A second BSWAP EAX would restore 0x12345678.
entries.return_value: BSWAP changes no arithmetic flags. Only destination byte order changes.
entries.gotchas: Memory is unchanged until a store. Reversing a whole integer is not the same as converting each element in an array.

Scope: x86-64. NASM Intel operand order is destination, source. Existing short examples above remain illustrative fragments; the annotated example adds its own context.
