entries.title: AArch64: X/W registers and zero register
entries.definition: AArch64 uses 64-bit X0–X30 registers; W0–W30 name their low 32-bit views. Writing Wn clears the high half of Xn. XZR/WZR reads as zero and discards writes. Encoding register number 31 denotes SP or ZR depending on the instruction, so SP is not interchangeable with an ordinary X register. AAPCS64 integer arguments generally use X0–X7 and an integer result X0.
entries.mental_model: The W view changes both arithmetic width and what remains in the X register.
entries.return_value: These MOV aliases and RET preserve NZCV. X0 is written; X30 is read as return address.
entries.gotchas: Cortex-M4 does not have X registers or A64 instructions. Platform ABIs may reserve X18; avoid treating it as portable scratch.
entries.notes:
Scope: aarch64.
Assemble: llvm-mc -triple=aarch64-linux-gnu -filetype=obj demo.s -o demo.o. This ELF function assumes a compatible caller, not a Linux process entry point.
Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: AArch64: stack frames and nested calls.
Official references: https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst
entries.summary: AArch64 uses 64-bit X0–X30 registers; W0–W30 name their low 32-bit views.

entries.title: AArch64: scaled loads, sign extension and writeback
entries.definition: A64 is a load/store architecture: arithmetic normally operates on registers. LDR Wn loads 32 bits and clears the high Xn half; LDRSW sign-extends 32 bits into an X register. LDR Xn loads 64 bits. Address encodings have different offset ranges/scaling; pre/post-index forms update the base. This example uses an X-register index scaled by four for a signed 32-bit element.
entries.mental_model: Address calculation and extension determine which integer your arithmetic receives.
entries.return_value: LDRSW and RET preserve NZCV. The original base in X0 is overwritten by the result.
entries.gotchas: A load is not a bounds check. If you need the base afterward, load into a different register. A W-register load would return 4294967293 for the same negative 32-bit bits.
entries.notes:
Scope: aarch64.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: AArch64: X/W registers and zero register.
Official references: https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst
entries.summary: A64 is a load/store architecture: arithmetic normally operates on registers.

entries.title: AArch64: CMP, CSET and zero branches
entries.definition: CMP is an alias of flag-setting subtraction with a discarded destination. CSET writes a 0/1 integer based on NZCV; signed LT uses N!=V, unsigned LO uses C=0 after subtraction. CBZ/CBNZ test a register directly without changing NZCV. Ordinary ADD/SUB omit flag updates; ADDS/SUBS request them.
entries.mental_model: Choose between a register test and an arithmetic condition; do not assume every arithmetic instruction refreshes flags.
entries.return_value: CMP defines NZCV. CSET/RET preserve them; the W0 write zero-extends the boolean.
entries.gotchas: Arm C=1 after subtraction means no borrow. Importing x86 CF rules gives wrong unsigned branches.
entries.notes:
Scope: aarch64.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: Cortex-M4: comparisons, branches and APSR; SETcc produces a byte boolean.
Official references: https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst
entries.summary: CMP is an alias of flag-setting subtraction with a discarded destination.

entries.title: AArch64: stack frames and nested calls
entries.definition: BL writes return address X30/LR, so a nonleaf function must retain its caller’s return address across another BL. AAPCS64 requires 16-byte stack alignment; X19–X29 are callee-saved. STP/LDP can save/restore register pairs while adjusting SP. X29 commonly serves as frame pointer, but unwind/frame requirements still depend on the platform and toolchain.
entries.mental_model: A nested call replaces LR; save that continuation before making the call.
entries.return_value: STP/LDP, MOV, non-S ADD, BL and RET preserve NZCV. X0 is the return value.
entries.gotchas: This instructional ELF function does not claim production unwind metadata, pointer authentication or platform hardening. Do not substitute an 8-byte SP adjustment.
entries.notes:
Scope: aarch64.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: AArch64: X/W registers and zero register.
Official references: https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst
entries.summary: BL writes return address X30/LR, so a nonleaf function must retain its caller’s return address across another BL.

entries.title: RV32I: registers, loads and integer widths
entries.definition: RV32I has 32-bit integer registers x0–x31. x0 always reads as zero; writes to it are discarded. ABI aliases name roles: a0–a7 arguments, a0 result, ra return address, sp stack pointer, t registers scratch and s registers saved. LB sign-extends a byte while LBU zero-extends it. A load/store address is base plus a signed immediate; arithmetic does not directly take a memory operand.
entries.mental_model: RV32 means XLEN=32; the register file is not a set of x86-sized overlapping subregisters.
entries.return_value: RV32I has no x86-style condition-code flags. LBU writes only its destination; RET is a JALR pseudoinstruction using RA.
entries.gotchas: The caller must provide readable memory. Naturally aligned word data avoids environment-dependent misaligned-access behavior.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv32.
Assemble: llvm-mc -triple=riscv32-unknown-elf -mattr=+i -filetype=obj demo.s -o demo.o. Integer-only ILP32 ABI, no optional compressed/multiply/float instructions assumed.
Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: RISC-V: branches and pseudoinstructions.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv32.html
https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/
entries.summary: RV32I has 32-bit integer registers x0–x31.

entries.title: RV32I: bounded word-array sum
entries.definition: This ILP32 integer function takes a word-array pointer in A0 and an unsigned element count in A1. It checks the empty case before loading, uses T0 for a wrapping 32-bit sum, advances the pointer by four bytes and decrements the remaining count. A0 receives the result. The caller supplies count readable aligned words.
entries.mental_model: No global condition flags exist: each branch compares registers or uses a zero-test pseudoinstruction.
entries.return_value: Integer add/load/branch instructions do not update a condition-code register. A0,A1,T0,T1 are caller-saved.
entries.gotchas: The sum wraps modulo 2^32. A bogus length is not safe merely because the loop is bounded. RV64 word data uses different extension considerations.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv32.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: Bounded array sum with an empty-input path.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv32.html
https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/
entries.summary: This ILP32 integer function takes a word-array pointer in A0 and an unsigned element count in A1.

entries.title: RV32I: stack alignment and preserving RA
entries.definition: JAL writes a return address, usually to RA; RET returns through RA. A function that makes another call must preserve its own return address. The standard integer ILP32 ABI uses a 16-byte-aligned stack and callee-saved S0–S11; T and A registers are caller-saved. This example allocates 16 bytes, saves one 32-bit RA value, and restores it before returning.
entries.mental_model: The stack allocation obeys the ABI even when the saved value itself is only four bytes.
entries.return_value: No integer arithmetic condition flags. SP,RA and A0 change during the call; final SP/RA restored.
entries.gotchas: RV32E/ILP32E is a different reduced-register ABI and is not assumed here. GP and TP are reserved platform/thread roles, not ordinary scratch.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv32.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: RISC-V: branches and pseudoinstructions.
Official references: https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/
https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv32.html
entries.summary: JAL writes a return address, usually to RA; RET returns through RA.

entries.title: RV64I: 64-bit registers and sign-extended words
entries.definition: RV64I uses XLEN=64 but retains 32-bit word operations. LW sign-extends a 32-bit memory value; LWU zero-extends it. ADDIW computes a 32-bit result then sign-extends it into the full 64-bit register. This differs from x86 EAX or AArch64 W-register writes, which zero-extend. LD/SD transfer full 64-bit values.
entries.mental_model: A word operation’s extension rule is part of the ISA; do not transfer assumptions between architectures.
entries.return_value: No x86-style arithmetic flags. ADDIW writes a sign-extended 32-bit result.
entries.gotchas: Do not use LW when you require an unsigned 32-bit quantity in a 64-bit register; choose LWU. Pointers in the ordinary LP64 ABI are 64-bit.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv64.
Assemble: llvm-mc -triple=riscv64-unknown-elf -mattr=+i -filetype=obj demo.s -o demo.o. This page uses integer LP64, not a floating-point ABI.
Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: RV32I: registers, loads and integer widths.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv64.html
https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/
entries.summary: RV64I uses XLEN=64 but retains 32-bit word operations.

entries.title: RV64I: LP64 stack frame and nested call
entries.definition: The ordinary LP64 integer ABI passes arguments in A0–A7 and results in A0 (and A1 when needed by the type). A nested call replaces RA, which is 64-bit here, so save it with SD and restore with LD. The stack remains 16-byte aligned. S0–S11 are callee-saved; A/T registers are scratch. Function calls and operating-system requests are separate contracts.
entries.mental_model: Width changes the save/load instruction and slot size, while stack alignment remains an ABI requirement.
entries.return_value: No integer condition flags. ADD computes a wrapping XLEN-wide result.
entries.gotchas: Using SW/LW for a 64-bit return address can truncate it. This instructional function has no unwind directives and does not claim production exception unwinding.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv64.

Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: RV32I: stack alignment and preserving RA.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv64.html
https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/
entries.summary: The ordinary LP64 integer ABI passes arguments in A0–A7 and results in A0 (and A1 when needed by the type).

entries.title: RISC-V: branches and pseudoinstructions
entries.definition: BEQ/BNE compare registers directly. BLT/BGE use signed interpretation; BLTU/BGEU use unsigned interpretation. SLT writes a numeric 0/1 result. Pseudoinstructions such as MV,LI,RET and BEQZ are assembler conveniences that expand to real encodings; LI may need multiple instructions for a large constant. Inspect disassembly to distinguish aliases from the base ISA.
entries.mental_model: Conditions are explicit register comparisons, not state left by an earlier ADD.
entries.return_value: SLT writes its destination; no condition flags are produced. RET expands to a JALR using RA.
entries.gotchas: An integer add does not set a hidden zero flag for a later branch. Recheck the correct registers after modifications.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv32, rv64.
The same source is assembled for both RV32I and RV64I in validation. The target object still must match its caller.
Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: RV32I: bounded word-array sum.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv32.html
https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv64.html
entries.summary: BEQ/BNE compare registers directly.

entries.title: RISC-V: extensions, ECALL and execution environment
entries.definition: RV32I/RV64I describe base integer instruction sets; M adds multiply/divide and C adds compressed encodings. Select extensions explicitly and match the hardware/runtime. ECALL requests service from the execution environment; Linux, an SBI interface, a simulator and bare metal can assign different meanings. There is no universal RISC-V print syscall. This no-service leaf works with the base integer ISA only.
entries.mental_model: ISA instructions tell you what the CPU can decode; an environment contract tells you what a service request means.
entries.return_value: No integer condition flags. Only A0 changes before RET.
entries.gotchas: Do not paste simulator syscall numbers into Linux or firmware. MUL is not guaranteed by a base I target. Object compatibility and ABI extensions must agree across modules.
entries.notes:
Scope: rv32, rv64.
Exercise: cross-assemble with only the base ISA and inspect the architecture attributes. Adding MUL should require the M extension; do not execute privileged/hardware exercises. Both widths are assembled during validation.
Validation scope: cross-assembly/disassembly only. Expected execution state is a reasoned trace, not a hardware/emulator observation. No peripheral access or firmware flashing.
Related: BITS, object format, and CPU mode.
Official references: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv32.html
https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/rv64.html
https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/

entries.title: A simple thank-you
entries.definition: Learn this response as a whole. Say it in a short practice exchange after someone helps you or compliments your work. Its immediate purpose is easy to remember, and there is no need to invent a word-by-word English expansion.
entries.mental_model: A short expression can be learned before its history.
entries.gotchas: This entry provides the complete formula, not a productive suffix rule.
entries.notes:
https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/4/text/?lang=eng — mini dialogue 10.

Example source locations:
Thanks — Lecture 4, mini dialogue 10. [Lecture 4: Practice and repetition]
entries.summary: An attested response expressing thanks.
entries.formality: Ordinary courtesy formula; the lesson gives no formal/informal contrast.

entries.title: Ask and give a name
entries.definition: Learn this exchange as a pair. The question asks how the listener is named; the answer identifies the speaker as Tika. Notice the change from the question ending to the first-person statement ending. Naming uses a verb whose literal idea is having a name.
entries.mental_model: Recognize the complete exchange, then find the person endings.
entries.gotchas: The name itself appears as Tikamik here; do not assume every name keeps the same shape.
entries.notes:
https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/4/text/?lang=eng — dialogue 1; https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/5.1/text/?lang=eng — name construction; https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/5x/?lang=eng — interrogative endings.

Example source locations:
Ask — Lecture 4, mini dialogue 1; Lecture 5.1, naming stem; chapter 5 X-tra, interrogative endings. [Lecture 4: Practice and repetition; Lecture 5.1: Words and lexicons in lesson one; Introduction to chapter 5 X-tra]
Answer — Lecture 4, mini dialogue 1; Lecture 5.1, name construction and first-person ending. [Lecture 4: Practice and repetition; Lecture 5.1: Words and lexicons in lesson one]
entries.summary: The naming verb carries person information.
entries.formality: Conversational introduction; no special honorific distinction given.

entries.title: A verb can be a whole clause
entries.definition: The shared stem means work. Different endings identify who works, allowing each word to stand as a clause.
entries.mental_model: Read the stem and ending together.
entries.gotchas: Third-person meaning can be he, she or it in general; the work example naturally refers to a person.
entries.notes:
https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/5.1/text/?lang=eng — first sound rules, suli examples.

Example source locations:
Person contrast — Lecture 5.1, sound-rules section, explicitly contrasts both forms. Capitalization and punctuation added. [Lecture 5.1: Words and lexicons in lesson one]
entries.summary: The ending distinguishes the speaker from a third person.
entries.formality: Grammatical illustration; source does not assign a special register.

entries.title: Recognize “in Nuuk”
entries.definition: The locative suffix expresses location. In this attested combination, the meeting of k and m surfaces as mm. Learn both the independent place name and its location form; the written change is part of the combination, not a misspelling.
entries.mental_model: Store the base and its attested location form together.
entries.gotchas: This entry does not predict the location form of every place name.
entries.notes:
https://oqa.dk/assets/aitwg2ED.pdf — definition 3.9 (p. 52), locative discussion (pp. 138–139), and §10.6 (p. 203).

Example source locations:
Location phrase — Lybech definition 3.9 verifies assimilation; locative section verifies the ending; §10.6, printed p. 203, attests the location form in a sentence. [An Introduction to West Greenlandic, second edition v2.3]
entries.summary: A location ending appears inside the place-name word.
entries.formality: Grammatical illustration; source does not assign a special register.

entries.title: “I’m fine” contains a negative
entries.definition: The source analyzes this familiar answer with a stem meaning bad and a negative suffix. The natural English response is “I’m fine.” Keep the polite conversational meaning and the literal analysis separate; both help you remember the form.
entries.mental_model: A natural translation need not mirror the internal pieces.
entries.gotchas: Negative verbs use special endings here; attaching an ordinary indicative ending mechanically gives the wrong form.
entries.notes:
https://learngreenlandic.com/online/lg1/5x/?lang=eng — special mood marker after NNGIT.

Example source locations:
Not bad — Chapter 5 X-tra, negative mood-marker section, explicitly supplies the analysis and wellbeing interpretation. [Introduction to chapter 5 X-tra]
entries.summary: Ajunngilanga expresses being well through “not bad.”
entries.formality: Conversational wellbeing response; grammatical analysis applies to this attested form.
entries.related_concepts: negative suffix; surface form; conversational meaning

entries.title: Read Hangul in syllable blocks
entries.definition: A block is assembled from letters; it is not a single indivisible picture. The vowel shape helps determine the arrangement, and a final consonant occupies the bottom. Start by finding the vowel and then reading the consonants around it.
entries.mental_model: First identify each block, then the letters inside it.
entries.gotchas: A block boundary is not a word boundary. This is a spelling exercise, not a rule that every written consonant has one unchanging sound.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 2, Writing Syllables, pp. 46–47. https://publish.illinois.edu/iaslibrary/2017/01/05/learning-korean-is-as-easy-as-a-b-cs/ — block composition.

Example source locations:
Two blocks — p. 47 example (1) supplies the spelling and meaning; p. 46 supplies block arrangement. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: Hangul letters combine inside syllable-sized blocks.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Choose a greeting speech level
entries.definition: 안녕하세요? is the everyday polite greeting taught for people who are not close friends. 안녕하십니까? belongs to a more formal style. Learn each as a complete social expression rather than assembling it from an English greeting.
entries.mental_model: The ending helps establish how you address the listener.
entries.gotchas: The question mark in this conventional greeting does not require a detailed health report. The casual 안녕? should not replace the polite form indiscriminately.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 1, Greetings, pp. 5–6.

Example source locations:
Everyday polite greeting — p. 5 gives the exact form, meaning and honorific label. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
Formal greeting — p. 5 gives the formal/honorific form and translation. The English output labels the register instead of reproducing the textbook’s English greeting. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: The greeting changes with the relationship and setting.
entries.formality: 안녕하세요?: polite, honorific greeting; 안녕하십니까?: formal, honorific greeting.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Introduce yourself with 는 and 이에요
entries.definition: 은/는 marks the topic. The identifying noun takes 이에요 after a consonant and 예요 after a vowel. That choice follows the noun’s final sound, not the person of the subject. The two particles are attached to their preceding words.
entries.mental_model: The topic opens the frame; the noun and ending supply the identification.
entries.gotchas: This noun pattern is not a universal translation of English “be” before adjectives. Use 는 after a vowel and 은 after a consonant.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 1 p. 9; Unit 4 p. 108. https://krdict.korean.go.kr/eng/dicSearch/SearchView?ParaWordNo=86232&nation=eng&nationCode=6 — relevant headword/rule in source ledger. https://krdict.korean.go.kr/eng/dicSearch/SearchView?ParaWordNo=86111&nation=eng&nationCode=6 — relevant headword/rule in source ledger. https://www.korean.go.kr/front/onlineQna/onlineQnaView.do?mn_id=27&pageIndex=1&qna_seq=332192 — relevant headword/rule in source ledger.

Example source locations:
A name ending in a consonant — p. 9 gives this complete sentence and translation; p. 108 checks the topic-particle distribution. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: A topic-marked person can be identified by a noun plus the polite copula.
entries.formality: Polite conversational style; 저 is the humble first-person pronoun.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Put the destination before the predicate
entries.definition: In this beginner pattern, the destination comes before 가요. The particle 에 follows the place noun and marks where the person is going. Keep the predicate at the end while you learn to recognize the preceding particles.
entries.mental_model: Read the noun plus particle as one functional phrase.
entries.gotchas: 에 has other uses; the destination interpretation here comes from the verb “go.” Do not transfer English preposition order to Korean.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 3 pp. 80–81; Unit 4 p. 108, example (4). https://krdict.korean.go.kr/m/eng/searchResultView?ParaWordNo=86572&nation=eng&nationCode=6 — sense 3, destination. https://krdict.korean.go.kr/eng/dicSearch/SearchView?ParaWordNo=86111&nation=eng&nationCode=6 — sense 2, topic.

Example source locations:
Going to a bookshop — p. 108 explicitly pairs this sentence with its English translation. English output is a fresh nonpast rendering; the source also permits ongoing English aspect. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: Particles identify a phrase’s role before the clause-final predicate.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Ask what something is
entries.definition: Use this question about an already indicated thing. The question word stays where the identifying noun would occur; there is no English-style inversion. Context identifies the thing being discussed.
entries.mental_model: Ask for the missing identity, then keep the polite ending.
entries.gotchas: 그거 is conversational. The example does not establish a complete system of demonstratives or question intonation.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 9 p. 270; Unit 3 p. 82 on contextual omission in questions. https://krdict.korean.go.kr/m/eng/searchResultView?ParaSenseSeq=&ParaWordNo=84991&fileNo=&imgCount=&multiMediaSeq=&nation=eng&searchKind=&searchKindValue=&shortenUrl=&studySeq= — question-word meaning / polite ending. https://www.korean.go.kr/front/onlineQna/onlineQnaView.do?mn_id=27&pageIndex=1&qna_seq=332192 — question-word meaning / polite ending.

Example source locations:
An indicated thing — p. 270 prints the complete question and English translation. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: 뭐 occupies the identity slot in a polite noun question.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Deny an identity with 아니에요
entries.definition: Use 아니에요 when correcting what something is. Unlike 이에요/예요 attached to a noun, 아니에요 is written separately. The short conversational example leaves the noun’s particle unexpressed; learn that exact form before expanding it.
entries.mental_model: An identification and its denial use different predicates.
entries.gotchas: 아니요 is the response “no”; 아니에요 is a predicate. Do not simply attach the negative form to the noun as if it were 이에요.
entries.notes:
https://talkingtokoreans.com/downloads/my-korean-1-3rd.pdf — Unit 9 pp. 270–271, 아니에요; 아니야. https://krdict.korean.go.kr/m/eng/searchResultView?ParaWordNo=26878&currentPage=1&exaType=&font_size=12&mainSearchWord=%EC%95%84%EB%8B%88&nation=eng&nationCode=6&proverbType=&searchType=W&sort=W&viewType=A&wordMatchFlag=N — negative predicate / spelling. https://www.korean.go.kr/front/onlineQna/onlineQnaView.do?mn_id=27&pageIndex=1&qna_seq=332192 — negative predicate / spelling.

Example source locations:
Correcting ownership — p. 271 prints the complete sentence, translation and spacing rule. [My Korean 1, third edition (2015)]
entries.summary: 아니에요 is a separate word used to deny a noun identification.
entries.formality: Polite conversational style; particle omission in the attested example.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard South Korean; textbook conversational usage.

entries.title: Recognize kana and kanji together
entries.signature: kanji + hiragana; katakana for many loanwords
entries.definition: Kanji carries much lexical content; hiragana writes many particles and endings. Katakana commonly writes loanwords and foreign names. Learn each word’s reading.
entries.mental_model: Read the word, not an isolated character.
entries.gotchas: Furigana gives the kanji reading; do not read it twice.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L03.pdf — Japanese characters, L3 p. 18. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/grammar/writing — roles of kana and kanji.

Example source locations:
One character, two readings — L3 p. 18 explicitly gives this word, reading and meaning. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 3]
entries.summary: Japanese combines kanji with hiragana and katakana.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.

entries.title: Greet someone in the morning
entries.signature: おはようございます。 / おはよう。
entries.definition: おはようございます is the polite morning greeting; おはよう is its casual alternative. Choose according to the relationship.
entries.mental_model: The longer greeting adds politeness.
entries.gotchas: Keep the time of day and the relationship in view.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L01.pdf — L1 pp. 1–3, activity 1 and morning greetings.

Example source locations:
Polite morning greeting — L1 p. 2 contrasts politeness; p. 3 identifies both as morning greetings. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 1]
Casual alternative — L1 pp. 2–3 supply the contrast. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 1]
entries.summary: The longer morning greeting is the more polite choice.
entries.formality: おはようございます: polite; おはよう: casual.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.

entries.title: Name the topic, then identify it
entries.definition: は introduces the topic; noun + です gives a polite identification. An obvious topic can remain unspoken.
entries.mental_model: Topic first, identification afterward.
entries.gotchas: Particle は is read わ. Avoid さん on your own name.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L03.pdf — grammar note 1, L3 p. 14; さん note, p. 16. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/complete/topic_particles — は topic particle. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/grammar/polite — polite noun predicate.

Example source locations:
Self-introduction — L3 p. 14 supplies the sentence, translation and particle explanation. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 3]
entries.summary: は marks the topic; a noun followed by です supplies the identification.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.

entries.title: Mark an object with を
entries.definition: を follows the object. The verb completes the clause. Here the polite nonpast describes a breakfast habit.
entries.mental_model: Object and particle belong together.
entries.gotchas: Read を as お here. “I” is understood from context.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L05.pdf — grammar note 4, L5 p. 26. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/grammar/verbparticles — direct object を. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/grammar/polite — verb stem and ます.

Example source locations:
A breakfast habit — L5 p. 26 gives the exact sentence and translation, the object function and habitual interpretation. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 5]
entries.summary: The object phrase comes before the polite verb.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.

entries.title: Make a polite question with か
entries.definition: Add か after the polite ending to ask about the statement; no English-style inversion is needed.
entries.mental_model: Final か asks about the preceding proposition.
entries.gotchas: Casual questions differ; mechanical か can sound rough. The question mark is optional.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L03.pdf — grammar note 4, L3 p. 16. https://guidetojapanese.org/learn/grammar/question — Questions in polite form and casual-speech caution.

Example source locations:
Checking a relationship — L3 p. 16 gives the exact sentence, translation and statement/question contrast. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 3]
entries.summary: か can turn a polite statement into a question.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.
entries.related_concepts: question particle; clause endings; contextual omission

entries.title: Negate a noun predicate
entries.definition: Use じゃないです to deny a noun identification. Another polite negative is じゃありません; uncontracted では is more formal.
entries.mental_model: Learn the noun-negative ending together.
entries.gotchas: Do not extend this pattern to every adjective or verb. “From” is contextual.
entries.notes:
https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X_L03.pdf — grammar note 6, L3 p. 17. https://md.jpf.go.jp/userfiles/file/2018/Lengua%20Japonesa/Gramatica/A2-B1-JP_rev.pdf — printed pp. 12–13, section 5, noun-negative alternatives.

Example source locations:
Correcting an assumed origin — L3 p. 17 gives this precise contextual English translation. [Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan, Starter, Lesson 3]
entries.summary: じゃないです is a conversational polite negative of a noun predicate.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Japanese; everyday teaching register.
entries.related_concepts: noun predicates; では; negative endings

entries.title: Keep Georgian consonant letters distinct
entries.signature: თ / ტ; ფ / პ; ქ / კ
entries.definition: Mkhedruli has 33 letters, written left to right. თ and ტ distinguish aspirated and ejective consonants; copy them distinctly.
entries.mental_model: Similar-looking letters can represent distinct consonants.
entries.gotchas: Written comparison cannot replace listening and articulation practice.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — Lesson 1, alphabet and consonants, pp. 21–22. https://fsi-languages.yojik.eu/languages/PeaceCorps/Georgian/Georgian%20Audio%20Language%20Files/GE_Georgian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lesson 1, alphabet count.

Example source locations:
Two distinct letters — pp. 21–22 list and contrast these letters; p. 21 visually inspected. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013)]
entries.summary: Mkhedruli has separate letters for consonants that beginners may confuse.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Greet and choose respectful address
entries.definition: გამარჯობა is a greeting. ხართ is second-person plural, also used respectfully to one listener.
entries.mental_model: Respectful address uses a plural person form.
entries.gotchas: Familiar singular ხარ does not preserve the same address choice.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — p. 29 greeting, p. 35 question. https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/Caucasian/georgian_a_learners_grammar.pdf — Lesson 1, Formality, p. 18. https://fsi-languages.yojik.eu/languages/PeaceCorps/Georgian/Georgian%20Audio%20Language%20Files/GE_Georgian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 3–4, familiar and formal address.

Example source locations:
Greeting — p. 29 vocabulary explicitly pairs spelling and meaning. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013)]
Respectful or plural inquiry — Makharoblidze p. 35 gives the plural question; Hewitt p. 18 establishes respectful plural address. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013); Georgian: A Learner’s Grammar, second edition (2005)]
entries.summary: The greeting can be followed by a question using respectful or plural address.
entries.formality: Greeting plus respectful singular or plural address.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Learn copula forms with their person
entries.signature: მე ვარ; შენ ხარ; ის არის
entries.definition: The copula distinguishes person. Pronouns can be omitted, while the verb retains its form. არის is third person.
entries.mental_model: Person is built into the verb.
entries.gotchas: These are paradigm fragments. ის does not distinguish masculine and feminine.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — Lesson 3, p. 30. https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/Caucasian/georgian_a_learners_grammar.pdf — Lesson 1, pp. 17–19. https://fsi-languages.yojik.eu/languages/PeaceCorps/Georgian/Georgian%20Audio%20Language%20Files/GE_Georgian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lesson 2, pronoun/copula table.

Example source locations:
First person — Makharoblidze p. 30 paradigm visually inspected; Hewitt p. 18 corroborates person. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013); Georgian: A Learner’s Grammar, second edition (2005)]
Second person — Same paradigms; formality corroborated in Hewitt p. 18. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013); Georgian: A Learner’s Grammar, second edition (2005)]
entries.summary: The present copula changes with the person being referred to.
entries.formality: Neutral grammar; შენ addresses one person familiarly.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Recognize two orders of a location clause
entries.definition: The source gives both orders for this location statement. The person and location forms preserve the same basic meaning.
entries.mental_model: Recognize the forms across both orders.
entries.gotchas: This pair does not make every order equally natural or establish transitive-clause rules.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — Lesson 3, p. 31, grammar point 5.

Example source locations:
Copula before location — p. 31 explicitly gives and translates this order; page visually inspected. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013)]
Copula after location — p. 31 explicitly gives the second order. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013)]
entries.summary: A simple Georgian clause can retain its meaning with more than one order.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Compare a noun with its in-location form
entries.definition: ოთახში attaches -ში to ოთახ-. The consonant-stem noun’s nominative -ი is absent before this postposition.
entries.mental_model: Find the stem before adding the postposition.
entries.gotchas: Some nouns have vowel-final stems: do not strip every final ი.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — Lesson 2 pp. 25–26. https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/Caucasian/georgian_a_learners_grammar.pdf — Citation form and Locative expressions, p. 16.

Example source locations:
Room and in the room — Makharoblidze p. 25 gives ოთახი; p. 26 explicitly gives ოთახში and the deletion of nominative -ი. Hewitt p. 16 corroborates the restricted rule. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013); Georgian: A Learner’s Grammar, second edition (2005)]
entries.summary: The dictionary form and a form with -ში need not keep the same ending.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Ask what this is
entries.definition: რა asks “what” before არის; ეს indicates “this.” Listen for the identifying noun in the reply.
entries.mental_model: Ask for the indicated thing’s identity.
entries.gotchas: ვინ asks “who.” English question inversion does not determine Georgian person forms.
entries.notes:
https://eprints.iliauni.edu.ge/3035/1/Basic-Georgian%202%20bolo%20versia.pdf — Lesson 2 vocabulary and text, pp. 25–26. https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/Caucasian/georgian_a_learners_grammar.pdf — Asking questions, p. 17.

Example source locations:
An identification question — Exact question in Makharoblidze p. 26; lexical components in pp. 25–26. Hewitt p. 17 checks question-word placement. [Basic Georgian, second edition (2013); Georgian: A Learner’s Grammar, second edition (2005)]
entries.summary: რა asks for an identification in a short copular question.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Georgian, written in Mkhedruli.

entries.title: Recognize click letters as consonants
entries.definition: These letters are part of the ordinary writing system, not punctuation or optional sound effects. Their combinations with other letters can mark further consonant distinctions. Start by recognizing which base click letter a word contains.
entries.mental_model: Read the click letter as part of the word itself.
entries.gotchas: English letter names do not supply the sounds. This note does not replace listening or teach the complete click inventory.
entries.notes:
https://emandulo.apc.uct.ac.za/collection/FHYA%20Depot/Mncube_F_S_M_Xhosa_Manual.pdf — Phonetic Structure, pp. 9–11. https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/African/Niger-Congo/Bantu/Xhosa%2C%20Teach%20Yourself.pdf — Introduction, The clicks.

Example source locations:

entries.summary: c, q and x identify distinct click families in Xhosa spelling.
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.

entries.title: Greet one person or several
entries.definition: Molo addresses one person; Molweni addresses several. UNISA also documents respectful plural greetings to one person.
entries.mental_model: Address reflects number and relationship.
entries.gotchas: A plural greeting to one person can express respect.
entries.notes:
https://www.unisa.ac.za/static/corporate_web/Content/UnisaOpen/freeOnlineCourse/PDF/Xhosa/Learn%20online%20Xhosa%20-%20Theme%201.pdf — p. 1, Greetings and Comments.

Example source locations:

More than one person — p. 1 explicitly labels this greeting plural and discusses respectful singular use. [Learn online Xhosa: Theme 1, Greetings and Courtesies]
entries.summary: Molo and Molweni distinguish the ordinary singular and plural greeting.
entries.formality: Ordinary social greetings; plural forms can express respect.
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.
entries.related_concepts: greeting etiquette; singular and plural address

entries.title: An emphatic pronoun does not replace agreement
entries.definition: The independent pronoun mna adds emphasis or contrast. It can accompany a verb that already marks its subject with ndi-. Keep that subject marking: the independent word does not take its place.
entries.mental_model: The separate pronoun highlights a participant already represented in the verb.
entries.gotchas: This entry covers the first-person example only, not every independent pronoun or every verb form.
entries.notes:
https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/African/Niger-Congo/Bantu/Xhosa%2C%20Teach%20Yourself.pdf — Unit 3, Emphatic pronouns, p. 50. https://emandulo.apc.uct.ac.za/collection/FHYA%20Depot/Mncube_F_S_M_Xhosa_Manual.pdf — p. 13, agreement retained with a noun or pronoun.

Example source locations:

entries.summary: mna can emphasize the speaker while the verb keeps its subject marker.
entries.formality: Neutral declarative speech with emphasis on the speaker.
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.

entries.title: Find the subject at the start of the verb
entries.definition: The beginning of the verb changes with the speaker group. In this affirmative present pair, ndi- refers to the speaker and si- includes the speaker in a plural group. The remainder is shared.
entries.mental_model: Look at the front of the verb for person and number.
entries.gotchas: -ya- is not an independent word meaning “am” or “are,” and it is not used in every present-tense environment.
entries.notes:
https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/African/Niger-Congo/Bantu/Xhosa%2C%20Teach%20Yourself.pdf — Unit 2, The present tense – positive, p. 37. https://aclanthology.org/W09-0714.pdf — morphology overview. https://emandulo.apc.uct.ac.za/collection/FHYA%20Depot/Mncube_F_S_M_Xhosa_Manual.pdf — p. 16, ndi- and si- person concords.

Example source locations:
First-person singular — Printed p. 37 visually checked: exact form, translation and segmentation rule. [Teach Yourself Xhosa (1999)]
First-person plural — Same p. 37 paradigm, visually checked. [Teach Yourself Xhosa (1999)]
entries.summary: A short subject prefix distinguishes “I” from “we.”
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.
entries.related_concepts: subject concords; present tense; word boundaries

entries.title: Learn a noun together with its class
entries.signature: um-ntu ↔ aba-ntu; class 1 u- ↔ class 2 ba-
entries.definition: The source groups umntu in class 1 and abantu in class 2. Their associated subject concords are u- and ba-. Keep this small noun pair and its agreement pair together when learning the vocabulary.
entries.mental_model: A noun belongs to an agreement group; the prefix is a useful clue.
entries.gotchas: Not every noun naming a person belongs to these two classes. The class number is a grammatical label, not a number pronounced in the sentence.
entries.notes:
https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/African/Niger-Congo/Bantu/Xhosa%2C%20Teach%20Yourself.pdf — Unit 3, Noun groups, pp. 48–49. https://aclanthology.org/W09-0714.pdf — morphology overview and Table 2.

Example source locations:
A person and people — Teach Yourself p. 48 table visually checked; Table 2 of Pretorius/Bosch independently shows Xhosa um-ntu. [Teach Yourself Xhosa (1999); Exploiting Cross-linguistic Similarities in Zulu and Xhosa Computational Morphology (2009)]
entries.summary: The noun’s class selects agreement forms as well as helping express number.
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.
entries.related_concepts: noun classes; singular/plural pairing; subject concords

entries.title: Say that you do not know or understand
entries.definition: Andazi reports not knowing; Andiqondi reports not understanding. Learn these as complete negative predicates.
entries.mental_model: Knowing and understanding are distinct.
entries.gotchas: These words do not establish a general rule for forming negatives.
entries.notes:
https://www.unisa.ac.za/static/corporate_web/Content/UnisaOpen/freeOnlineCourse/PDF/Xhosa/Learn%20online%20Xhosa%20-%20Theme%201.pdf — p. 1, Courtesies.

Example source locations:

Lacking understanding — p. 1 explicitly pairs Andiqondi with this meaning. [Learn online Xhosa: Theme 1, Greetings and Courtesies]
entries.summary: Two short negative predicates help repair a conversation.
entries.formality: Ordinary neutral conversational statements; a courteous tone and context matter.
entries.dialect: Standard South African isiXhosa; the teaching sources use ordinary contemporary spelling for these forms.

entries.title: Length changes words; vowels choose suffix variants
entries.definition: Finnish writes short and long vowels differently, and also distinguishes short and long consonants. Treat doubled letters as meaningful rather than decorative. Vowel harmony is a separate pattern: a, o and u belong to the back group; ä, ö and y belong to the front group. The vowels e and i can accompany either group. A simple word containing only e and i normally takes a front-vowel suffix. Thus the two spellings of the same suffix fit different stems.
entries.mental_model: First preserve each word's length; then choose the suffix's vowel partner.
entries.return_value: More accurate reading and a first guide to suffix selection.
entries.gotchas: This is a starter rule for simple words; compounds and loanwords require further attention. Length and harmony are different phenomena.
entries.notes:
Aalto: Vowels, Summary (https://openlearning.aalto.fi/mod/page/view.php?id=3383); Consonants, Summary (https://openlearning.aalto.fi/mod/page/view.php?id=3386); Vowel Harmony (https://openlearning.aalto.fi/mod/page/view.php?id=3385).

Example source locations:

The same suffix in two forms — Vowel Harmony: baari+ssa and työ+ssä with English glosses. [Vowel Combinations and Vowel Harmony]
entries.summary: Single versus double letters matter, and Finnish suffix vowels often follow the stem's vowel group.
entries.related_concepts: Vowel harmony; consonant quantity; vowel quantity; inessive.

entries.title: Choose a greeting for the situation
entries.definition: For a relaxed greeting, Moi is a useful short choice. Aalto's beginner course places it with informal greetings between acquaintances. Hyvää päivää belongs to its more formal greeting group and literally corresponds to wishing a good day. Learn the full expression as a fixed phrase rather than trying to replace its endings with dictionary forms. Register is part of the phrase's meaning: choosing a longer greeting can change the social tone even when the basic function remains hello.
entries.mental_model: Choose the greeting as a whole expression, including its social tone.
entries.gotchas: The course's categories are guidance, not a claim that every speaker always uses one greeting in one setting.
entries.notes:
Aalto, How to greet in Finnish, sections Greeting informally and Greeting formally: https://openlearning.aalto.fi/mod/page/view.php?id=3390.

Example source locations:
Relaxed hello — Greeting informally: Moi with English Hi. [How to greet in Finnish]
More formal daytime greeting — Greeting formally: Hyvää päivää with the daytime greeting translation. [How to greet in Finnish]
entries.summary: Moi is an informal hello, while Hyvää päivää is a more formal daytime greeting.
entries.formality: Moi: informal. Hyvää päivää: more formal daytime greeting.
entries.dialect: Finnish as taught in Finland; broadly standard expressions.

entries.title: Introduce yourself with minä olen
entries.definition: Minä means I, sinä addresses one person, and hän can mean either he or she. Aalto also lists me, te and he for we, plural you and they. The verb olla has an irregular present paradigm: first-person singular uses olen, second-person singular olet, and third-person singular on; the corresponding plural forms are olemme, olette and ovat. Start with a name introduction to connect the subject to the right verb form. These are standard forms; conversational Finnish can use different pronoun and verb shapes.
entries.mental_model: Choose the person, then choose the matching form of be.
entries.gotchas: Do not use the infinitive olla as the present verb. Hän does not encode the English he/she distinction.
entries.notes:
Pronouns: Aalto, https://openlearning.aalto.fi/mod/page/view.php?id=3403. Olla forms: Uusi kielemme, Perfect Tense §2, https://uusikielemme.fi/finnish-grammar/verbs/verb-tenses-and-moods/the-perfect-tense-perfekti. Introduction: Beginner Finnish Topics dialogue. Register contrast: Spoken-language verbs §4.1 (source ledger).

Sources:
Beginner Finnish Topics — Level A1 — https://uusikielemme.fi/language-levels/beginner-finnish-topics-level-a1-a1-1-to-a1-3 (Basic introductory dialogue: Minä olen Anna)
Verbs in Finnish Spoken Language — https://uusikielemme.fi/spoken-language/spoken-language-grammar/verbs-in-finnish-spoken-language (§4.1 Olla)

Example source locations:

entries.summary: Finnish olla means be, and its present form changes with the subject.
entries.formality: Standard written forms, also usable in speech; colloquial paradigms are not substituted here.
entries.dialect: Standard Finnish; conversational forms explicitly distinguished.

entries.title: Read the person in a present-tense ending
entries.definition: For the type-1 verb istua, remove the final infinitive a to obtain istu-. The endings -n and -mme then produce the first-person singular and plural forms. The subject pronoun and verb ending point to the same participant: changing I to we requires changing the verb too. This is a useful small model of Finnish agreement, not a universal instruction to remove the last letter from every verb.
entries.mental_model: The stem names the action; the ending tells you who performs it.
entries.return_value: A basic present statement about one speaker or a group including the speaker.
entries.gotchas: Other verb types build stems differently, and some type-1 stems undergo consonant gradation. Learn the verb's class as well as its infinitive.
entries.notes:
Uusi kielemme, Verbtype 1 Conjugation, §2 Present Tense and §3 Consonant Gradation: https://uusikielemme.fi/finnish-grammar/verbs/verbtypes/verbtype-1-conjugation-all-tenses-and-moods.

Example source locations:
One speaker — §2 table: minä istun and its segmentation/translation. [Verbtype 1 Conjugation — All Tenses and Moods]
A group including the speaker — §2 table: me istumme and its segmentation/translation. [Verbtype 1 Conjugation — All Tenses and Moods]
entries.summary: In a regular type-1 example, the verb stem stays recognizable while the ending identifies the subject.
entries.related_concepts: Verb types; present tense; person agreement; consonant gradation.

entries.title: Ask a yes/no question with -ko or -kö
entries.definition: The question suffix attaches to an already conjugated word. In the ordinary verb-first pattern, keep the verb's person ending, add the appropriate harmony variant, and place the subject after it. Use -ko with back-vowel words and -kö with front-vowel or neutral-only words. The suffix can also attach to another constituent to focus the question on that constituent, so its position is meaningful.
entries.mental_model: Conjugate first; attach the question marker; put that marked word up front.
entries.return_value: A question inviting confirmation or denial.
entries.gotchas: Do not add English-style do. First- and second-person pronouns can be omitted in the basic pattern, but the displayed example keeps the subject visible.
entries.notes:
Uusi kielemme, Kysymyslause, §§2.1–2.3: https://uusikielemme.fi/finnish-grammar/syntax/sentence-types/kysymyslause-making-questions-in-finnish-lausetyypit.

Example source locations:
Question about the statement — §2.3 bilingual focus contrast; §§2.1–2.2 suffix and word order. [Kysymyslause — Making Questions in Finnish]
entries.summary: A neutral yes/no question usually puts the finite verb first and attaches -ko/-kö to it.
entries.related_concepts: Vowel harmony; focus; verb agreement; subject omission.

entries.title: Let the negative verb carry the person ending
entries.definition: Finnish does not form these negatives by simply adding an unchanging word to the positive verb. The negative verb marks person: en, et, ei, emme, ette and eivät correspond to the six persons. With puhua, the following lexical verb is puhu throughout this present-tense pattern. That separates two jobs: the first word carries negation and person; the second identifies the action.
entries.mental_model: In the negative, person marking moves to the negative verb.
entries.return_value: A present-tense denial of an action.
entries.gotchas: Do not retain a positive personal ending on puhu. Past, perfect and other negative constructions need additional forms; this entry covers present indicative only.
entries.notes:
Uusi kielemme, Making Verbs Negative, §1 Negative Present Tense: https://uusikielemme.fi/finnish-grammar/verbs/verb-tenses-and-moods/making-verbs-negative-in-finnish-dont-havent-hadnt-shouldnt.

Example source locations:
Negative with I — §1 puhua table: minä en puhu and English translation. [Making Verbs Negative in Finnish]
Negative with we — §1 puhua table: me emme puhu and English translation. [Making Verbs Negative in Finnish]
entries.summary: In present negation, the negative verb changes for person while the lexical verb uses its negative form.
entries.related_concepts: Negative verb; connegative; agreement; present tense.

entries.title: Preserve the letters; learn length in context
entries.signature: koma ↔ komma; preserve þ, ð, æ, ö and accented vowels
entries.definition: Preserve þ, ð and vowel accents. An accented vowel has its own sound value: á is not simply a longer a. In stressed syllables, a vowel is generally short before a long consonant or consonant cluster, and long before a short consonant. Some clusters are exceptions. The pair below demonstrates this relationship.
entries.mental_model: Read the whole syllable, not just the vowel letter.
entries.return_value: A reliable first distinction between spelling, vowel quality and duration.
entries.gotchas: This is a starter guide; regional variants and exceptional clusters require a pronunciation reference.
entries.notes:
Rögnvaldsson, Sound System overview, §2.6 Length (printed p. 7) and vowel spellings (pp. 19–21): https://eirikur.hi.is/ipv.pdf.

Example source locations:
One spelling change alters the syllable — §2.6, printed p. 7: bilingual length-contrast table. [A Short Overview of the Icelandic Sound System, Pronunciation Variants and Phonetic Transcription — IPA Version]
entries.summary: Icelandic vowel length depends on its sound environment, and an acute accent is not simply a length mark.
entries.dialect: Modern standard Icelandic, with regional pronunciation variation acknowledged.
entries.related_concepts: Vowel quantity; consonant length; letter identity.

entries.title: Say hæ and takk
entries.definition: Use these as complete turns: the first opens contact, and the second acknowledges help. No subject or verb is required.
entries.mental_model: One word can perform a social action.
entries.gotchas: These two expressions do not cover formal greetings.
entries.notes:
Hall, A very short Icelandic grammar, Useful words and phrases: https://alarichall.org.uk/teaching/icelandic_grammar.php.

Example source locations:
Greeting — Useful words and phrases: hæ, English hi. [A very short Icelandic grammar]
Gratitude — Useful words and phrases: takk, English thanks. [A very short Icelandic grammar]
entries.summary: Hæ greets; takk thanks.

entries.title: Match vera to its subject
entries.definition: Ég means I; við means we. Present vera uses er with the first and erum with the second. Learn the pronoun and its matching verb form together.
entries.mental_model: The verb agrees with the participant.
entries.gotchas: These are fragments; add the needed complement.
entries.notes:
Hall, magic sheet, PDF p. 1: Pronouns and Verbs/Present; p. 2: first-person pronoun meanings. https://www.alarichall.org.uk/teaching/Alaric%27s_modern_icelandic_magic_sheet.pdf.

Example source locations:
Singular and plural openings — p. 1 first-person nominative pronouns and vera present rows; p. 2 first-person English pronoun column. [Alaric’s modern Icelandic magic sheet, version 2.4]
entries.summary: Vera changes for person and number.

entries.title: Keep the finite verb second when another phrase comes first
entries.definition: A statement can put an object first as its topic. The finite verb then comes before the subject. Second means the second constituent, not necessarily the second written word. Case forms still identify grammatical roles.
entries.mental_model: The opening slot can change occupants; the finite verb follows it.
entries.return_value: A statement that highlights a topic without losing the subject–object distinction.
entries.gotchas: This covers ordinary main clauses, not every question or embedded clause.
entries.notes:
Arnbjörnsdóttir, Thráinsson and Nowenstein (2018), p. 379, example (ii): https://uni.hi.is/hoski/files/2018/11/HoskBirnaIris_V2V3NAmIcel_JLC_011_03.pdf.

Example source locations:
Put the person talked about first — p. 379, example (ii): original sentence, accusative gloss, English translation and V2 explanation. [V2 and V3 Orders in North-American Icelandic]
entries.summary: A standard Icelandic statement can begin with an object, but the finite verb still follows the first constituent.
entries.formality: Neutral standard syntax; fronting adds discourse focus.
entries.dialect: Standard Icelandic baseline; heritage North-American variants in the cited paper are outside scope.

entries.title: Recognize fisk as a form of fiskur
entries.definition: The nominative singular headword fiskur has accusative singular fisk. In this sentence the latter is the object of eating. Connect the sentence form to its paradigm for lookup.
entries.mental_model: One noun has several case forms.
entries.gotchas: Removing -ur is not a universal rule; learn each paradigm.
entries.notes:
Hall, magic sheet, PDF p. 1 Nouns and p. 2 What is case?: https://www.alarichall.org.uk/teaching/Alaric%27s_modern_icelandic_magic_sheet.pdf.

Example source locations:
An accusative object — p. 2 nominative/accusative teaching examples; p. 1 fiskur/fisk paradigm. [Alaric’s modern Icelandic magic sheet, version 2.4]
entries.summary: The sentence form can differ from the dictionary form.

entries.title: Ask with er; negate with ekki
entries.definition: Put the finite verb before its subject to ask the displayed yes/no question. In the matching negative statement, ekki follows the verb.
entries.mental_model: Order asks; a negative word denies.
entries.gotchas: These patterns cover simple main clauses.
entries.notes:
Hall, A very short Icelandic grammar, Questions and ekki: https://alarichall.org.uk/teaching/icelandic_grammar.php.

Example source locations:
Ask about location — Questions: er ég hér with the English equivalent. [A very short Icelandic grammar]
Deny the location — Ekki: ég er ekki hér with the English equivalent. [A very short Icelandic grammar]
entries.summary: Verb-first order asks; ekki negates.

entries.title: Notice å, ä, ö and the length contrast
entries.definition: Preserve å, ä and ö as distinct letters. A stressed long vowel commonly pairs with a short following consonant; a short vowel pairs with a long consonant. Doubling is a useful cue below. Swedish word-accent melodies vary by region, so spelling is not a complete pronunciation guide.
entries.mental_model: The vowel and following consonant share the timing of the stressed syllable.
entries.return_value: Recognize a useful spelling contrast without substituting an English reading.
entries.gotchas: Length cues have exceptions. Learn sound quality and accent from audio for your chosen variety.
entries.notes:
Hinchliffe and Holmes, Basic Swedish, Unit 1, Pronunciation, pp. 1–2: https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781351169677_A34228448/preview-9781351169677_A34228448.pdf.

Example source locations:
A written consonant contrast — Printed p. 1, long/short a examples and English glosses. [Basic Swedish: A Grammar and Workbook]
entries.summary: Swedish has three additional vowel letters, and stressed vowel length can distinguish words.
entries.dialect: Standard Swedish orthography; pronunciation and pitch accent vary regionally.
entries.related_concepts: Vowel quantity; consonant quantity; pitch accent.

entries.title: Use hej, and keep du lowercase
entries.definition: Hej starts contact and Tack expresses gratitude. For written address, the Swedish Language Council recommends lowercase du, including in customer letters. Capitalizing it does not reliably make the message more respectful; some readers may instead find that distancing. Sentence-initial capitalization still applies normally. Keep the choice of greeting and the spelling of an address pronoun separate: politeness depends on the interaction and wording as a whole.
entries.mental_model: Choose a clear greeting; do not use an unusual capital as a politeness shortcut.
entries.return_value: Basic social phrases and a dependable address-spelling convention.
entries.gotchas: This entry does not present ni as a universal polite substitute for du.
entries.notes:
Uppsala, Sentences in Swedish, p. 1: https://www.uu.se/download/18.2f8c577918d548f1b011774d/1707137252525/glossary.pdf. Språkrådet, customer-letter answer: https://frageladan.isof.se/faqs/21774.

Example source locations:
Greeting and gratitude — PDF p. 1: Hej/Hello and Tack/Thank you. [Sentences in Swedish]
entries.summary: Hej is a useful hello; ordinary du is written lowercase inside a sentence.
entries.formality: Hej and Tack: ordinary everyday expressions. Lowercase du is recommended in both informal and professional writing.
entries.dialect: Contemporary standard Swedish usage in Sweden.

entries.title: Keep är when the subject changes
entries.definition: Useful subject pronouns include jag for I, du for singular you and vi for we. The verb vara means be; its present form is är. Unlike English am/is/are, this form does not switch when the subject's person or number changes. Keep the subject in the ordinary statement and let it identify who or what is being described.
entries.mental_model: The subject changes; the present verb form stays.
entries.gotchas: Vara is the infinitive, not the present form. This entry introduces a few pronouns rather than an exhaustive modern pronoun inventory.
entries.notes:
Pronoun meanings: https://swedishgrammar.com/pronouns.html, Subject Pronouns. Vara/är: https://swedishgrammar.com/verbs.html, Group 4. Person invariance: Hinchliffe/Holmes p. 4, Simple verb forms. Complete phrase: Uppsala p. 1 (source ledger).

Sentences in Swedish — https://www.uu.se/download/18.2f8c577918d548f1b011774d/1707137252525/glossary.pdf (PDF p. 1: greetings, thanks, Det är bra, Jag förstår inte)

Example source locations:
A short evaluation — Uppsala p. 1 Det är bra; SwedishGrammar.com Verbs, Group 4, vara/är. [Sentences in Swedish; Verbs]
entries.summary: The present of vara is är, and modern Swedish verbs do not change their form for each person.
entries.related_concepts: Subject pronouns; copula; finite versus infinitive.

entries.title: Put the verb second after a time phrase
entries.definition: When a time phrase starts a statement, place the finite verb next and the subject after it. Count whole constituents, not individual words: a multiword opening phrase still fills one slot.
entries.mental_model: Opening phrase, then finite verb.
entries.gotchas: This is a main-clause pattern.
entries.notes:
Word-order example and formula: https://swedishgrammar.com/word_order.html, Main Clause Formula. Inversion corroboration: Stensson, Syntax, https://www.lysator.liu.se/language/Languages/Swedish/Grammar.html. Gå/går and jag: separate verb/pronoun tables in source ledger. Lexical meanings: Cambridge nu (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/swedish-english/nu) and go, movement sense (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-swedish/go).

Pronouns — https://swedishgrammar.com/pronouns.html (Subject Pronouns: parallel Swedish/English tables)

entries.summary: A fronted time phrase comes before the verb and subject.

entries.title: Learn a noun with en or ett
entries.signature: en flaska → flaskan; ett brev → brevet
entries.definition: Swedish nouns have common or neuter gender. Store the article en or ett with each noun. In these bare singular phrases, the indefinite article is separate and the definite marking attaches to the noun: -n after flaska and -et after brev.
entries.mental_model: Store article and noun together; recognize the noun's definite form as part of the same family.
entries.return_value: A/an and the versions of two basic noun phrases.
entries.gotchas: Learn gender with the word. Definite phrases containing adjectives need additional rules.
entries.notes:
Stensson, Nouns, singular paradigm and English gloss row: https://www.lysator.liu.se/language/Languages/Swedish/Grammar.html. Article/gender explanation: https://swedishgrammar.com/nouns.html.

Neuter gender — Stensson Nouns: brev/brevet, letter (mail); noun reference: neuter ett. [Swedish Grammar; Nouns]
entries.summary: Noun gender determines the indefinite article and helps you recognize the attached definite ending.
entries.related_concepts: Common gender; neuter; definiteness; noun endings.

entries.title: Ask with verb-first order; negate with inte
entries.definition: Put the finite verb before the subject for a neutral yes/no question. In the displayed negative main clause, inte follows the finite verb.
entries.mental_model: Order asks; inte denies.
entries.return_value: A basic question or negative statement.
entries.gotchas: Subordinate clauses need a separate word-order rule.
entries.notes:
SwedishGrammar.com, Word order, Peter kommer contrast and Main Clause Formula: https://swedishgrammar.com/word_order.html. Negative phrase: Uppsala Sentences in Swedish, p. 1 (source ledger).

Sources:
Sentences in Swedish — https://www.uu.se/download/18.2f8c577918d548f1b011774d/1707137252525/glossary.pdf (PDF p. 1: greetings, thanks, Det är bra, Jag förstår inte)

Say you do not understand — Uppsala p. 1: Jag förstår inte; main-clause formula corroborates inte placement. [Sentences in Swedish; Word order]
entries.summary: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, while inte follows it in a simple negative main clause.
entries.related_concepts: Inversion; negation; finite verb; main versus subordinate clause.

entries.title: Keep æ, ø and å; learn the sound separately
entries.definition: Danish uses æ, ø and å in addition to the familiar basic Latin letters. Preserve them when copying words or looking them up. The official language reference explains that Danish has more vowel sounds than vowel letters and that consonant letters also have different realizations in different contexts. A useful first habit is therefore to learn a word's spelling, meaning and recorded sound together. Recognizing the letters is a starting point, not the end of pronunciation study.
entries.mental_model: Spelling identifies the word; listening teaches how the written word is realized.
entries.return_value: Accurate written forms and realistic expectations about reading aloud.
entries.gotchas: Do not replace unfamiliar letters with English sound spellings. This entry deliberately supplies no approximate pronunciation.
entries.notes:
Official alphabet overview: https://denmark.dk/people-and-culture/danish-language/. Sproget.dk, Bogstaver og lyde, vowel/consonant sections: https://sproget.dk/sprogviden/sprogtemaer/udtale/bogstaver-og-lyde/. Lexical example: SpeakDanish Noun gender.

Sources:

Example source locations:

entries.summary: Danish spelling distinguishes æ, ø and å, but a letter is not a dependable one-to-one pronunciation instruction.
entries.dialect: Standard written Danish; no regional pronunciation model selected.

entries.title: Greet with hej and write address pronouns carefully
entries.definition: Hej is a short way to open an interaction. When writing to someone, use the ordinary lowercase spelling du inside a sentence; it is not capitalized simply to sound respectful. Danish spelling does require capitals in the address forms I, De, Dem and Deres. Keep that orthographic distinction separate from deciding which form of address suits the situation.
entries.mental_model: A greeting opens contact; an address pronoun follows its own spelling rule.
entries.return_value: A usable greeting and fewer capitalization mistakes.
entries.gotchas: Ordinary sentence-initial capitalization still applies. The capitalized forms listed here are spelling examples, not a recommendation to replace everyday du with De.
entries.notes:
