Example source locations:
Say hello — English/Danish phrase book: Hello! / Hej!. [The Danish language: A story of history and identity]
entries.summary: Hej is an everyday hello, while Danish has specific capitalization conventions for address pronouns.
entries.formality: Hej: everyday greeting. Capitalization rule applies across registers.

entries.title: Use er for the present of være
entries.definition: Jeg means I, du addresses one person, and vi means we. The infinitive være means be, but its present form is the irregular er. Danish present verbs keep the same form across persons, so a change of subject does not create separate am/is/are forms. Learn er directly rather than trying to make it by adding the usual present -r to være.
entries.mental_model: The subject identifies the person; one present form does the work of am/is/are.
entries.return_value: The opening of an identity, description or location statement.
entries.gotchas: The example is a subject–verb fragment for learning the form; add a suitable complement when introducing or describing someone.
entries.notes:
SpeakDanish, Present tense, Irregular forms and all-person table: https://speakdanish.dk/course/grammar/present-tense/.

Example source locations:
Recognize the irregular present — Irregular forms table: at være → Jeg er, translated I am. [Present tense]
entries.summary: Danish er means am, is or are according to the subject; its form does not change for person.
entries.related_concepts: Subject pronouns; infinitive; irregular present; person invariance.

entries.title: Put the finite verb second
entries.definition: After an opening time phrase, place the finite verb before the subject. Second position counts constituents, so a whole phrase can occupy the first slot.
entries.mental_model: Opening phrase, then verb.
entries.gotchas: This covers ordinary main clauses.
entries.notes:
SpeakDanish, Introduction to Danish Grammar, Word order (V2) and Continuous meaning: https://speakdanish.dk/course/grammar/introduction-to-danish-grammar/.

Example source locations:
Start with now — V2 examples: Jeg spiser nu / Nu spiser jeg; Continuous meaning: Jeg spiser = I am eating. [Introduction to Danish Grammar]
entries.summary: A time-first statement puts the verb before the subject.

entries.title: Learn en/et with the noun
entries.signature: en stol → stolen; et hus → huset
entries.definition: Record new count nouns with their article: en marks common gender and et marks neuter. In the two bare singular phrases shown here, the definite meaning is carried by an ending on the noun. That gives you a practical three-part memory unit: article, basic noun, definite form.
entries.mental_model: Keep a small noun family together instead of learning an isolated word.
entries.return_value: Indefinite and definite forms for two everyday nouns.
entries.gotchas: Do not guess gender from the object's meaning or assume the endings of these two examples cover every noun. Phrases containing adjectives need further rules.
entries.notes:
SpeakDanish, Noun gender, Common/neuter examples and Definite form endings: https://speakdanish.dk/course/grammar/danish-noun-gender/.

Example source locations:
Common gender — Common examples: en stol; definite table: stolen, with English glosses. [Danish noun gender]
Neuter gender — Neuter examples: et hus; definite table: huset, with English glosses. [Danish noun gender]
entries.summary: Danish noun gender controls en or et, and these simple definite noun phrases attach an ending to the noun.

entries.title: Ask with the verb first; deny with ikke
entries.definition: Put the finite verb before the subject for a neutral yes/no question. In the displayed negative statement, ikke follows the verb. Danish does not insert English-style do.
entries.mental_model: Order asks; ikke denies.
entries.return_value: A practical language question or negative statement.
entries.gotchas: These are main-clause patterns.
entries.notes:
Denmark.dk phrase book supplies both examples: https://denmark.dk/people-and-culture/danish-language/. Rules: SpeakDanish Introduction, Questions and Negation, https://speakdanish.dk/course/grammar/introduction-to-danish-grammar/.

Example source locations:
Ask about English — Official English/Danish phrase book: Taler du engelsk and English equivalent; syntax corroborated by the entry's grammar source. [The Danish language: A story of history and identity]
Say you do not speak Danish — Official English/Danish phrase book: Jeg taler ikke dansk and English equivalent; syntax corroborated by the entry's grammar source. [The Danish language: A story of history and identity]
entries.summary: A basic yes/no question places the verb before the subject, while ikke negates the displayed main clause.
entries.related_concepts: Inversion; negation; finite verb; language names.

entries.title: Hard and soft consonants matter
entries.signature: [paired consonant] + ь; [paired consonant] + а/я, у/ю, о/ё, э/е, ы/и
entries.definition: Russian consonants often come in hard and palatalized (soft) pairs. Softness changes the consonant itself; it is not a separate extra syllable. The soft sign ь has no independent sound. Following vowel letters can also signal the contrast. Learn each new word with its stress because an unstressed vowel may sound different from its written letter.
entries.mental_model: Read the consonant together with the next letter, rather than sounding out each letter independently.
entries.gotchas: Not every consonant has a hard/soft partner. These examples isolate a contrast; they are not a complete pronunciation guide.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Introduction/IntrUnit6/IntrUnit6.htm — §6.1 Hard and Soft Consonants; https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Introduction/IntrUnit3/IntrUnit3.htm — Stress and vowel reduction

Example source locations:
Soft sign contrast — §6.1 explicitly pairs the two words and meanings. [Russian for Everyone: Introductory Lesson 6]
Vowel-letter contrast — §6.1 comparison immediately after the soft-sign example. [Russian for Everyone: Introductory Lesson 6]
entries.summary: Consonant softness can distinguish words; spelling and stress guide pronunciation.

entries.title: Greetings and ты / вы
entries.definition: Здравствуйте is a broadly usable greeting. Привет is informal and suits people you know well. The pronoun ты addresses one person informally; вы addresses more than one person or one person politely. Choose the relationship first, then use the corresponding pronoun and verb forms.
entries.mental_model: English “you” leaves a distinction unstated that Russian usually makes explicit.
entries.gotchas: A familiar greeting does not itself grant permission to use ты with an unfamiliar adult. Capital Вы is used in polite correspondence to one addressee.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Phrasebook/Topic1_Greetings/Topic1.htm — §1.1 Saying Hello; https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit3/GramUnit3_1.htm — §1 Personal pronouns; §2 Pronouns ты and вы

Example source locations:
Broadly usable greeting — §1.1 gives the expression and English meaning. [Russian for Everyone: Greetings and Goodbyes]
Informal greeting — §1.1 labels this greeting informal. [Russian for Everyone: Greetings and Goodbyes]
entries.summary: Greeting choices and forms of “you” reflect the relationship between speakers.

entries.title: Present identity sentences without “is”
entries.definition: In basic present-tense identity sentences, Russian normally has no separate word corresponding to English am, is or are. It also has no articles corresponding to a and the. The identity noun stays in the nominative. The pronouns он, она and оно can also refer to inanimate nouns according to grammatical gender.
entries.mental_model: A complete Russian sentence can directly connect a person and their role.
entries.gotchas: This is a present identity pattern, not a claim that Russian lacks a verb “to be”; existence, possession and other tenses use different constructions.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit1/GramUnit1_1.htm — §§1.2–1.4: pronouns, articles, present-tense to be; https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit3/GramUnit3_1.htm — §1 Personal pronouns; §2 Pronouns ты and вы

Example source locations:
Masculine role noun — §1.2 example 1 and §1.4 present copula discussion. [Russian for Everyone: Grammar Lesson 1]
Feminine role noun — Lesson 1 §§1.2/1.4 and Lesson 4 §1, examples 5–6. [Russian for Everyone: Grammar Lesson 1; Russian for Everyone: Personal Pronouns]
entries.summary: A present identity sentence normally links its parts without an overt form of “to be.”

entries.title: Why книга becomes книгу
entries.definition: In the example, the book is what is being read, so it takes the accusative form книгу instead of the dictionary form книга. For this feminine noun, -а changes to -у. Recognizing the ending helps you track the noun’s role without assuming that its position alone explains the sentence.
entries.mental_model: The ending labels what participates as the direct object.
entries.gotchas: This -а → -у pattern does not cover all nouns. Some accusative forms look unchanged, and animate masculine nouns require a different rule.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit9/GramUnit9_1.htm — §1 Transitive verbs; §2 Accusative singular

Example source locations:
A book as direct object — §2 gives книга → книгу and the complete translated sentence. [Russian for Everyone: The Accusative Case]
entries.summary: The accusative marks the direct object of a verb such as “read.”

entries.title: Questions can keep statement word order
entries.definition: Russian can signal a yes/no question through intonation without inserting English-style do or does. In writing, the question mark signals the change. For identifying something, Что это? asks what it is.
entries.mental_model: Change what you ask the listener to supply: confirmation, or the identity of a thing.
entries.gotchas: Written punctuation cannot teach the full intonation contour; use the source audio. Что asks about things, while кто asks who.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit8/GramUnit8_3.htm — §1 possession and question intonation; §2 У меня нет + genitive; https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit4/GramUnit4_1.htm — §1 Asking What and Who

Example source locations:
Yes/no question — §1 compares У них есть дом. with the question. [Russian for Everyone: Having and Not Having Something]
Ask what something is — §1, dialogue 1. [Russian for Everyone: Asking What, Who and Where]
entries.summary: A yes/no question can keep the same words as a statement; question words request specific information.

entries.title: Not having something: нет + genitive
entries.signature: У [possessor in genitive] нет [missing item in genitive]
entries.definition: У меня identifies the possessor. Нет says the item is absent. The missing textbook appears as учебника, not the nominative учебник. This is a useful complete pattern for “I do not have …”.
entries.mental_model: Think “with me, no textbook exists.”
entries.gotchas: Нет can also be a standalone “no.” Do not assume every English “not” should become нет.
entries.notes:
https://russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit8/GramUnit8_3.htm — §1 possession and question intonation; §2 У меня нет + genitive

Example source locations:
Missing textbook — §2, example 1 and its explanation of both genitives. [Russian for Everyone: Having and Not Having Something]
entries.summary: Нет expresses absence and places the missing item in the genitive.

entries.title: Cyrillic letters and unpredictable stress
entries.definition: Bulgarian uses Cyrillic: ъ is a vowel, while щ represents a consonant sequence. Stress must be learned with each word; it has no fixed position.
entries.mental_model: Letters have language-specific values.
entries.gotchas: Bulgarian ъ is a vowel. Learn stress from the course audio.
entries.notes:
http://www.seelrc.org:8080/grammar/pdf/stand_alone_bulgarian.pdf — Chapter 1 pp. 7–8; Chapter 2 p. 19, Stress Alternation; Chapter 3 pp. 33–35, articles; Chapter 6 pp. 50–51, pronouns; https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/bulgaria/BG_Bulgarian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 1–7, printed pp. 2–5

Example source locations:
The vowel letter ъ — Lesson 3, p. 3, country names; letter value checked in Lesson 1 and Leafgren Chapter 1. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
entries.summary: Learn each letter’s value and each word’s stress.

entries.title: Здравей and Здравейте
entries.definition: Здравей addresses one person informally; Здравейте is plural or polite. The lesson also contrasts А ти? with А вие? for “And you?” Match the greeting to your relationship with the listener.
entries.mental_model: Choose a relationship and number of listeners, then keep that choice consistent.
entries.gotchas: A polite form may address a single person; it does not necessarily signal several listeners.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/bulgaria/BG_Bulgarian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 1–7, printed pp. 2–5

Example source locations:
One familiar person — Lesson 4, p. 4, Greetings/Wishes. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
Polite or plural greeting — Lesson 4, p. 4, matching greeting explicitly marked plural/formal. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
entries.summary: The greeting changes for one familiar addressee versus polite or plural address.
entries.formality: Здравей: informal singular; Здравейте: polite singular or plural.

entries.title: Keep the present form of съм
entries.definition: Аз is the subject pronoun “I”; съм expresses “am.” Third-person singular е expresses “is.” Start by learning these as complete sentence patterns. They let you identify yourself or something nearby without importing the zero-copula pattern of some other Slavic languages.
entries.mental_model: The linking verb is a small but meaningful part of the sentence.
entries.gotchas: This starter introduces only съм and е, not the complete conjugation. Bulgarian has no separate indefinite article corresponding exactly to English “a” in the hotel example.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/bulgaria/BG_Bulgarian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 1–7, printed pp. 2–5

Example source locations:
Introduce your origin — Lesson 3, p. 3, introduction model. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
Identify a building — Lesson 7, p. 5, translated identification example; Cyrillic х normalized from the PDF’s Latin-looking x glyph. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
entries.summary: Bulgarian uses present forms of “be” in these simple identity and location sentences.

entries.title: The verb can identify the speaker
entries.definition: The verb and context can identify the subject. Аз makes the speaker explicit.
entries.mental_model: The subject can be understood.
entries.gotchas: Use the correct verb ending.
entries.notes:
http://www.seelrc.org:8080/grammar/pdf/stand_alone_bulgarian.pdf — Chapter 1 pp. 7–8; Chapter 2 p. 19, Stress Alternation; Chapter 3 pp. 33–35, articles; Chapter 6 pp. 50–51, pronouns; https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/bulgaria/BG_Bulgarian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 1–7, printed pp. 2–5

Example source locations:
Subject stated — Chapter 6, printed p. 50, Nominative Personal Pronouns, first example. [A Concise Bulgarian Grammar]
Subject understood — Peace Corps Lesson 5, p. 4, translated phrase. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
entries.summary: Verb forms often identify an unstated subject.

entries.title: The definite article attaches to the phrase
entries.definition: Книга takes -та. With an adjective first, the article appears there.
entries.mental_model: Mark the noun phrase.
entries.gotchas: Article forms vary; masculine singular has full and short written forms.
entries.notes:
http://www.seelrc.org:8080/grammar/pdf/stand_alone_bulgarian.pdf — Chapter 1 pp. 7–8; Chapter 2 p. 19, Stress Alternation; Chapter 3 pp. 33–35, articles; Chapter 6 pp. 50–51, pronouns

Example source locations:
Article on the noun — Chapter 3, printed p. 33, Indefinite and Definite Noun Phrases. [A Concise Bulgarian Grammar]
Article on the adjective — Same table, second row. [A Concise Bulgarian Grammar]
entries.summary: A definite article attaches to the first eligible word.
entries.formality: Neutral; written standard for article rules.

entries.title: ли asks; не negates
entries.definition: The particle ли turns the illustrated verb phrase into a yes/no question. It follows the verb in this beginner pattern. Не comes before the verb to negate it. The source’s polite/plural question form is useful with an unfamiliar listener.
entries.mental_model: Ли requests confirmation; не rejects the action or state.
entries.gotchas: Ли can follow other focused elements, so “always after the verb” would be too broad. The reply’s verb has first-person form.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/bulgaria/BG_Bulgarian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lessons 1–7, printed pp. 2–5

Example source locations:
A useful question — Lesson 5, p. 4, paired understanding expressions. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
A negative reply — Lesson 5, p. 4, translated negative reply. [An Introductory Guide to the Bulgarian Language]
entries.summary: Use ли in a first yes/no question and не before a verb in a negative reply.
entries.formality: Question: polite singular or plural; reply: neutral.

entries.title: Keep ă, â, î, ș and ț
entries.definition: Â and î represent the same vowel; ă represents another. Modern ș and ț have a comma below.
entries.mental_model: The mark belongs to the letter.
entries.gotchas: The circumflex does not mark stress. Older digital sources may show cedilla glyphs ş/ţ.
entries.notes:
http://www.seelrc.org:8080/grammar/pdf/stand_alone_romanian.pdf — §§1.2.1.1–1.2.2.1 p. 16; §3.2.1.1 p. 42; §3.4.1.1 p. 55; https://dexonline.ro/text/diacritice — SEMN, DTL (Dicționar de termeni lingvistici), semn diacritic; ALFABET, DGSSL (1997)

Example source locations:

entries.summary: Keep Romanian’s distinctive letter marks.

entries.title: Greetings and polite address
entries.signature: Bună ziua!; Ce mai faceți? / Ce mai faci?
entries.definition: Bună ziua is a polite daytime greeting; Salut is informal. The course pairs formal Ce mai faceți? with informal Ce mai faci? for “How are you?” The different verb forms help maintain the chosen relationship throughout an exchange.
entries.mental_model: Politeness is heard in the form of the question as well as the greeting.
entries.gotchas: Learn the whole formal or informal question; do not mix their verb forms.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/romania/RO_Romanian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lesson 1 p. 3; Lesson 2 p. 4; Lesson 3 p. 5; Lesson 9 p. 11; Lesson 10 p. 12

Example source locations:
Daytime greeting — Lesson 2, p. 4, formal greetings. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
Polite question — Lesson 10, p. 12, formal set contrasted with Ce mai faci? in the informal set. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
entries.summary: Greetings and question forms distinguish informal from formal address.
entries.formality: Bună ziua and Ce mai faceți?: formal/polite; Salut and Ce mai faci?: informal.

entries.title: First forms of a fi
entries.signature: eu sunt; tu ești; el/ea este; noi suntem; voi sunteți; ei/ele sunt
entries.definition: The infinitive a fi names the verb “to be.” Its present forms are irregular: the person is not obtained by adding one predictable ending to fi. Eu, tu, el and ea identify singular participants; noi, voi, ei and ele identify plural ones. Sunt is shared by first-person singular and third-person plural.
entries.mental_model: Learn the pronoun and verb as a pair before using them inside longer sentences.
entries.gotchas: Sunt is shared by “I am” and “they are”; context identifies which meaning is intended.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/romania/RO_Romanian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lesson 1 p. 3; Lesson 2 p. 4; Lesson 3 p. 5; Lesson 9 p. 11; Lesson 10 p. 12

Example source locations:
Identify yourself — Lesson 3, p. 5, a fi paradigm and Maria’s dialogue line. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
Identify a profession — Lesson 3, p. 5, Maria’s profession statement, extracted from its following question. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
entries.summary: The verb a fi changes with person, so learn “be” as a small set of forms.

entries.title: A sentence does not always need eu
entries.definition: Sunt din America is complete without eu. Romanian often leaves the pronoun unstated when the verb and context identify its subject.
entries.mental_model: An unspoken subject is still understood.
entries.gotchas: Sunt serves both “I am” and “they are”; context must distinguish them.
entries.notes:

Example source locations:
Origin without an overt pronoun — Lesson 3, p. 5, John’s reply; omission explained in Cojocaru §3.4.1.1. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
entries.summary: The verb and context can identify an unstated subject.

entries.title: An article before the noun or attached to it
entries.definition: Un/o are separate. Studentul attaches -ul; studenta replaces studentă’s final ă with a.
entries.mental_model: Check before and after the noun.
entries.gotchas: Un also accompanies neuter nouns. Other nouns use other definite endings.
entries.notes:
http://www.seelrc.org:8080/grammar/pdf/stand_alone_romanian.pdf — §§1.2.1.1–1.2.2.1 p. 16; §3.2.1.1 p. 42; §3.4.1.1 p. 55

Example source locations:
Masculine example — §3.2.1.1.1–2, p. 42, masculine article examples. [Romanian Grammar]
entries.summary: Indefinite articles precede nouns; definite articles can attach.

entries.title: Ask where; say you do not understand
entries.definition: Unde requests a location. Este is the third-person singular form of a fi. For a basic negative statement, nu precedes the verb, as in Nu înțeleg. Learn that whole reply early: it lets you signal a communication problem while you are still building vocabulary.
entries.mental_model: A question leaves one piece of information open; nu changes a statement to its negative.
entries.gotchas: The bathroom form baia includes the definite article. More complex sentences may place short pronouns between nu and the verb; this entry gives the basic pattern.
entries.notes:
https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/romania/RO_Romanian_Language_Lessons.pdf — Lesson 1 p. 3; Lesson 2 p. 4; Lesson 3 p. 5; Lesson 9 p. 11; Lesson 10 p. 12

Find a room — Lesson 9, p. 11, exact question and translation. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
Request understanding through a negative reply — Lesson 10, p. 12, exact phrase and translation; punctuation added. [Survival Romanian Language Lessons]
entries.summary: Unde asks about location, while nu negates a first verb sentence.

entries.title: Recognize ў as its own letter
entries.signature: У у / Ў ў; хлеў → у хляве
entries.definition: Keep the breve in ў. The source calls it “short у.” Related forms can alternate ў and в, as in the example; copy the attested forms carefully.
entries.mental_model: Inflection can change a stem’s spelling.
entries.gotchas: The example also changes a vowel and an ending; it is not a minimal sound pair.

entries.title: A first greeting and ты / вы
entries.definition: Добры дзень is a daytime greeting. The choice between ты and вы is separate: ты addresses one person informally, whereas вы serves formal address and plural listeners. The textbook shows this distinction in paired questions and verb forms.
entries.mental_model: The relationship determines how you address the listener throughout the conversation.
entries.gotchas: Do not translate every English “you” as ты. A polite singular listener still takes the вы-pattern.
entries.notes:
https://www.livelingua.com/dli/Belarusian/textbook/Belarusian%20-%20Textbook%20Units%2001-07.pdf — Unit 1 p. 10; Unit 2 pp. 54, 81, 89–90, 95, 108; Unit 3 pp. 160, 163, 175 Search alias: Belarusian; display name retained as Belorussian.

entries.summary: Use a conventional greeting and distinguish familiar singular ты from polite or plural вы.
entries.formality: Daytime greeting: conventional; ты: informal singular; вы: formal singular or plural.

entries.title: Present identity without an overt copula
entries.definition: The source’s identity sentence directly links a name with a nationality. Both nouns are nominative. English needs “is an” in the natural translation, but the Belorussian sentence does not. A dash is often used between noun subject and noun predicate in writing.
entries.mental_model: A noun-to-noun link can be a complete present-tense statement.
entries.gotchas: Do not generalize this to every tense or every meaning of “be”: the existence/possession form ёсць appears in another starter. A dash is punctuation, not a spoken verb.

https://www.livelingua.com/dli/Belarusian/textbook/Belarusian%20-%20Textbook%20Units%2001-07.pdf — Unit 1 p. 10; Unit 2 pp. 54, 81, 89–90, 95, 108; Unit 3 pp. 160, 163, 175 Search alias: Belarusian; display name retained as Belorussian.

Name and nationality — Unit 2 p. 89, The Nominative Case, subject and predicate illustrations; p. 95 explains the present copula and dash. [Belarusian Basic Course, Textbook Units 1–7]
entries.summary: Basic present identity sentences can have a subject and noun predicate without a word for “is.”

entries.title: Location uses a case form
entries.definition: The place name is Каліфорніі, not dictionary-form Каліфорнія. Its ending marks the locative (also called prepositional) case after the location preposition. Learn the full phrase, including the written ў.
entries.mental_model: Learn a place name together with its “in that place” form.
entries.gotchas: Not all place names take this ending, and some do not change. The same preposition can participate in other constructions; this entry covers location.

entries.summary: The preposition у/ў combines with a locative form when expressing location.

entries.title: Ask where someone lives
entries.signature: Дзе ты жывеш? / Дзе вы жывеце?
entries.definition: Дзе means “where.” The familiar question uses ты жывеш; the polite or plural one uses вы жывеце. The verb changes with the address form, so replacing only the pronoun would leave a mismatched pattern.
entries.mental_model: Learn the two questions as parallel units, not as one sentence with a swappable pronoun.
entries.gotchas: These questions ask location, not destination or origin. Their English translation is identical because English leaves the address distinction unmarked.
entries.notes:
https://www.livelingua.com/dli/Belarusian/textbook/Belarusian%20-%20Textbook%20Units%2001-07.pdf — Unit 1 p. 10; Unit 2 pp. 54, 81, 89–90, 95, 108; Unit 3 pp. 160, 163, 175 Search alias: Belarusian; display name retained as Belorussian.

Example source locations:
Familiar question — Unit 2 p. 81, Formal and informal speech situations; p. 108 supplies the word-by-word English glosses. [Belarusian Basic Course, Textbook Units 1–7]
Polite or plural question — Same parallel table on p. 81 and vocabulary on p. 108. [Belarusian Basic Course, Textbook Units 1–7]
entries.summary: Дзе requests a location, with the verb matching the chosen form of address.
entries.formality: Ты question: familiar singular; вы question: polite singular or plural.

entries.title: Not having something: няма
entries.signature: У мяне няма [missing item in genitive]
entries.definition: У мяне identifies the possessor; няма expresses absence. Грошай is the genitive plural of грошы “money.”
entries.mental_model: The item is absent “with me.”
entries.gotchas: Do not use няма for every English “not.” This entry covers absence, not all verbal negation.
entries.notes:
https://www.livelingua.com/dli/Belarusian/textbook/Belarusian%20-%20Textbook%20Units%2001-07.pdf — Unit 1 p. 10; Unit 2 pp. 54, 81, 89–90, 95, 108; Unit 3 pp. 160, 163, 175; https://www.vitba.org/fofmb/fofmb.pdf — §1.8, printed pp. 5–6 (PDF pp. 5–6); §30.3, printed p. 84 (PDF p. 84); https://universaldependencies.org/be/ — Morphology, Verbal Features, Polarity; https://www.skarnik.by/rusbel/44899 — Example contrasting наконт грошай with пра грошы Search alias: Belarusian; display name retained as Belorussian.

Example source locations:
No money — Marchant §30.3, printed p. 84, complete translated example; DLI p. 175 verifies У мяне няма; Skarnik насчёт entry independently shows грошай / грошы. [Fundamentals of Modern Belarusian; насчёт — Russian–Belarusian dictionary entry; Belarusian Basic Course, Textbook Units 1–7]
entries.summary: У мяне няма expresses absence in relation to the speaker.
entries.dialect: Standard Belarusian, modern orthography; display label Belorussian.

entries.title: Preserve doubled vowels
entries.signature: аа / ээ / ии / оо / өө / уу / үү / ыы
entries.definition: The alphabet includes ң, ө and ү. Preserve these letters and doubled vowels: vowel length belongs to the word’s form.
entries.mental_model: A doubled vowel represents one long vowel.
entries.gotchas: Russian letter readings do not transfer automatically.
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan1.pdf — printed pp. 12, 14, 20–21, 187, 201; https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan6.pdf — headwords аас, экии (PDF pp. 7, 138)

Example source locations:

entries.summary: Doubled vowels mark length.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).

entries.title: A first greeting: Экии!
entries.definition: The conversation book models Экии! when greeting someone; the dictionary independently labels it a greeting.
entries.mental_model: Learn it as a complete expression.
entries.gotchas: No narrower register rank is established here.
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan3.pdf — printed pp. 7–8, 11, 14, 17; https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan6.pdf — headwords аас, экии (PDF pp. 7, 138)

Example source locations:

entries.summary: Экии! is a documented greeting.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).

entries.title: Two positions for мен
entries.definition: Initial мен is the subject; final мен marks first person. The subject can be omitted.
entries.mental_model: The final marker belongs to the predicate.
entries.gotchas: Keep the final marker even when initial мен appears.
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan1.pdf — printed pp. 12, 14, 20–21, 187, 201

Example source locations:
Attested example — §15.1, printed p. 201 (PDF p. 202), explicit example and explanation. [基礎トゥヴァ語文法 (Basic Tuvan Grammar)]
entries.summary: Final мен marks a first-person predicate.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).

entries.title: Find the predicate at the end
entries.definition: The place precedes ажылдаар мен, the predicate. English places “will work” earlier.
entries.mental_model: Read through to the predicate.
entries.gotchas: This example does not establish every use of the case ending.
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan3.pdf — printed pp. 7–8, 11, 14, 17

Example source locations:
Attested example — Printed p. 8, §5 Word order; Japanese gloss states planned work in the village; §6 gives case functions. [トゥヴァ語会話集 (Tuvan Conversation)]
entries.summary: A simple Tuvan clause places its predicate after the other material.
entries.formality: Neutral statement of intention in the source.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).
entries.related_concepts: Word order; place phrases; person markers

entries.title: Recognize the ending in ажылым
entries.definition: The source pairs ажыл “work” with ажылым “my work.” The ending identifies the possessor.
entries.mental_model: The noun itself can identify its owner.
entries.gotchas: -ым is this word’s variant, not an ending to attach unchanged everywhere.
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan3.pdf — printed pp. 7–8, 11, 14, 17

Example source locations:
Attested example — Printed p. 8, §4 possessive table and ажыл examples. [トゥヴァ語会話集 (Tuvan Conversation)]
entries.summary: A possessive ending can identify whose work is meant.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).

entries.title: Permission to speak
entries.definition: The -п form links to болур for permission; бе marks a question.
entries.mental_model: Learn the complete request.
entries.gotchas: This does not translate every use of English “can.”
entries.notes:
https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2008tuvan1.pdf — printed pp. 12, 14, 20–21, 187, 201

Example source locations:
Attested example — §14.10, printed p. 187 (PDF p. 188), болур entry with the Japanese permission gloss. [基礎トゥヴァ語文法 (Basic Tuvan Grammar)]
entries.summary: This question asks permission to speak.
entries.formality: Permission request; no extra politeness label asserted.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Tuvan of the Republic of Tuva; Cyrillic (TUFS teaching materials).

entries.title: Preserve Tatar Cyrillic letters
entries.signature: ә ө ү җ ң һ
entries.definition: These are distinct letters. Native vocabulary generally has front/back vowel harmony; unfamiliar spellings still need checking.
entries.mental_model: Copy every vowel letter.
entries.gotchas: Do not assume Russian pronunciation.
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

entries.summary: Tatar spelling distinguishes ә, ө, ү, җ, ң and һ.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: A polite greeting
entries.definition: The course contrasts this with familiar Исәнме! Син is familiar singular “you”; сез is plural or polite.
entries.mental_model: Address follows the relationship.
entries.gotchas: Син does not cover every English “you.”
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

entries.summary: Исәнмесез! is the greeting modeled for polite address.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: A simple introduction
entries.definition: Мин identifies the speaker; the name supplies the identity without a separate “am.”
entries.mental_model: The name acts as predicate.
entries.gotchas: The dash is punctuation, not a spoken word.
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

Example source locations:

entries.summary: A present identity can use a pronoun and name.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: Read through to the verb
entries.definition: Ул refers to the person; журнал names the reading material. Ул itself does not distinguish gender.
entries.mental_model: The action comes last here.
entries.gotchas: Other sentence structures are possible.
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

entries.summary: This clause puts the object before the verb.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: Plural -нар after a nasal
entries.definition: The noun’s final м selects the nasal-initial plural variant -нар here.
entries.mental_model: Separate the noun from its number ending.
entries.gotchas: Other plural variants include -лар, -ләр and -нәр.
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

entries.summary: Ханым takes plural -нар.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: A short confirmation question
entries.definition: The lesson pairs Алсу with -мы and Әминә with -ме. The particle requests confirmation.
entries.mental_model: Recognize the name before the question marker.
entries.gotchas: Preserve the attested vowel choice and joined spelling.
entries.notes:
https://ibt.org.ru/sites/default/files/files/TTR_Gram_R_web.pdf — §§10, 55, 88–90, 179, 388–392, 709, 954(j); https://dspace.kpfu.ru/xmlui/bitstream/net/22101/1/10_179_000943.pdf — pp. 5–10, 13, 39, 96, 170, 175

entries.summary: -мы and -ме attach to the questioned predicate.
entries.dialect: Standard literary Kazan Tatar; contemporary Cyrillic.

entries.title: Keep о and ө distinct
entries.definition: Learn the letter and the word together: substituting о for ө changes this example’s meaning. Kazakh Cyrillic has distinctions that are absent from the Russian alphabet.
entries.mental_model: A small written difference can identify a different word.
entries.gotchas: This pair illustrates spelling and meaning, not a complete vowel-harmony or pronunciation rule.
entries.notes:
https://slaviccenters.duke.edu/sites/slaviccenters.duke.edu/files/file-attachments/kazakh-grammar.pdf — §2.1 alphabet chart (PDF p. 6); §§3.7.2–3.7.5; §4.1

Example source locations:

entries.summary: The letters о and ө distinguish the attested words қол and көл.

entries.title: Start with Сәлеметсіз бе!
entries.definition: The beginner course models this greeting alongside polite address. It also shows familiar Сәлем! exchanges. Сен is familiar singular “you”; сіз is the polite counterpart.
entries.mental_model: Learn the greeting as a complete conversational unit.
entries.gotchas: Do not remove the space before бе or treat the greeting’s literal structure as a universal greeting rule.
entries.notes:
https://tilqural.kz/assets/books/3a5df9b9e6318277b68949ffbdb4d7ea.pdf — pp. 59–63, 88–89, 224; vocabulary section; https://tilqural.kz/books/download/25 — pp. 3–4, Meeting people; https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED402757.pdf — printed p. 15 (PDF p. 16), points 7 and 10

entries.summary: Сәлеметсіз бе! is a polite greeting.

entries.title: An identity noun can take a person ending
entries.definition: Мен identifies the speaker, while -пін marks the noun predicate as first person. The source gives other personal endings alongside this form; the English word “am” has no separate word here.
entries.mental_model: The predicate ending helps say who has the identity.
entries.gotchas: -пін is correct for this attested noun. Other nouns can require different variants.
entries.notes:
https://tilqural.kz/assets/books/74f4de591669fcb3d2da468082d04509.pdf — lessons 20–21, printed pp. 77–80 (PDF pp. 76–79)

entries.summary: In Мен студентпін, the noun carries the first-person ending.

entries.title: Put the reading action after the book
entries.definition: In this model, Мен is the subject, кітап is the reading material, and оқимын is the first-person present form. Read the whole predicate before choosing the English phrasing.
entries.mental_model: Follow “I — book — read” in this example.
entries.gotchas: The example has a bare object. Do not infer from it that Kazakh never marks objects with case endings.
entries.notes:

entries.summary: The elementary reading clause places the object before the verb.
entries.related_concepts: Word order; bare objects; present tense

entries.title: Write бе separately in this question
entries.definition: Сіз and the predicate ending -сіз agree in polite address. The final бе requests confirmation and remains a separate written word.
entries.mental_model: Keep the identity statement intact, then recognize the question particle.
entries.gotchas: Kazakh has other question-particle variants. This entry establishes бе after the attested ending, not a universal choice.
entries.notes:
https://slaviccenters.duke.edu/sites/slaviccenters.duke.edu/files/file-attachments/kazakh-grammar.pdf — §2.1 alphabet chart (PDF p. 6); §§3.7.2–3.7.5; §4.1; https://tilqural.kz/assets/books/74f4de591669fcb3d2da468082d04509.pdf — lessons 20–21, printed pp. 77–80 (PDF pp. 76–79); https://tilqural.kz/assets/books/3a5df9b9e6318277b68949ffbdb4d7ea.pdf — pp. 59–63, 88–89, 224; vocabulary section

Example source locations:

entries.summary: The particle бе makes the attested identity sentence a yes/no question.

entries.title: Distinguish noun negation from verb negation
entries.definition: With a noun predicate, емес receives the person ending. A verb such as “speak” is negated within its verbal form. Learn these as separate constructions.
entries.mental_model: First identify whether the predicate names an identity or an action.
entries.gotchas: Do not replace every English “not” with емес. Other negative constructions are outside this starter note.

entries.title: Read the parts of kula
entries.definition: The source explains that most Swahili words stress the next-to-last syllable. Short verb roots need care: kula is an infinitive, while -ku- can also appear inside conjugated short verbs for a different reason.
entries.mental_model: Keep the written syllables visible before learning a conjugation.
entries.gotchas: Do not assume every ku inside a verb is an infinitive marker, or remove it from a learned form.

https://olrc.ku.edu/sites/olrc/files/documents/projects/kiswahili/Hujambo%20Volume%201_2025%20Version%20online.pdf — Unit 1.3, printed pp. 18, 21; Unit 3.1, p. 114

entries.title: Learn the greeting and its response together
entries.definition: The question asks how the other person is; the response says the speaker is fine. Memorizing both turns makes the expression usable in an exchange.
entries.mental_model: A greeting also prepares an expected reply.
entries.gotchas: This is one taught greeting pair. It does not establish a universal greeting for every region, relationship or setting.

entries.summary: Hujambo? pairs with Sijambo! in the documented two-person exchange.
entries.formality: Conventional two-person greeting; no stronger formal/informal claim.
entries.dialect: Standard Swahili (Kiswahili Sanifu); Latin orthography; KU classroom examples.

entries.title: Use ni for a simple identity
entries.definition: The course models Mimi ni for “I am” in an identity answer. In this construction ni is a separate word, unlike the first-person prefix ni- attached to a verb.
entries.mental_model: Use word boundaries to distinguish two similar-looking forms.
entries.gotchas: This identity pattern does not cover location or every English use of “be.”

entries.title: See the subject and tense inside ninasoma
entries.definition: The independent mimi and the attached ni- both refer to the speaker, but occupy different positions. Keep the subject marker on the verb while learning the complete sentence.
entries.mental_model: A Swahili verb carries information English often puts in separate words.
entries.gotchas: This entry covers -soma. Short roots and other verb types can behave differently.

entries.title: Change the noun and its agreement together
entries.definition: The singular student takes a- on the verb; the plural students take wa-. Recognize the matching pair instead of treating a noun’s plural as an isolated vocabulary change.
entries.mental_model: The verb tracks the participant’s class and number.

entries.definition: The source’s negative counterpart uses si- for “I” plus negation, removes -na-, and changes final -a to -i. Treat the whole change as a pattern.

entries.title: Noun capitals are grammar clues
entries.definition: Write ordinary German nouns with an initial capital, even in the middle of a sentence. The article often comes just before the noun. Learning these together makes a vocabulary item easier to recognize and retains its grammatical gender. A noun's capital does not mean that it is a person's name.
entries.mental_model: Look for the capital as a signpost to a noun, then read the article with it.
entries.gotchas: Keep umlaut marks in words such as Tür; they are part of the spelling. A capital at the beginning of a sentence alone does not identify a noun. This entry does not supply a general pronunciation algorithm.
entries.notes:

entries.title: Greetings and choosing du or Sie
entries.definition: Guten Tag is a daytime greeting. In a name question, du addresses one person familiarly; Sie addresses one or more people politely. The verb changes with the choice: heißt with du, heißen with Sie. Use a consistent form of address through the exchange rather than switching the pronoun alone.
entries.mental_model: Choose who you are speaking to before choosing the verb form.
entries.gotchas: Polite Sie has a capital S. Familiar plural address is ihr, not du. Actual use varies by relationship and setting; follow the form established with your interlocutor.

entries.title: Use the matching form of sein
entries.signature: ich bin; du bist; er/sie/es ist; wir sind; ihr seid; sie/Sie sind
entries.definition: Sein means 'to be'. It links a subject to an identity, condition or location. Its present forms are irregular: the form after ich is bin, not the dictionary form sein. Keep the pronoun and verb together when learning them. A description such as müde follows the verb without an English-style extra helper.
entries.mental_model: Treat each pronoun plus verb pair as one familiar speaking unit.
entries.gotchas: Do not substitute bist for polite sind. The spelling sie can mean 'she' or 'they'; its verb and context resolve the meaning.

entries.formality: Neutral standard usage; the address pronoun supplies the familiar/polite distinction.

entries.title: The finite verb follows the first phrase
entries.definition: 'Second position' counts sentence elements, not individual words. A subject containing an article, adjective and noun can all occupy the first position together. Locate the verb that carries tense and agreement, then check what precedes it. This gives a practical reading strategy for longer sentences as well as short ones.
entries.mental_model: One phrase goes in front; the finite verb is the next structural piece.
entries.gotchas: Do not move the verb after a multiword subject just to make it the second written word. Yes/no questions can begin with the verb. Subordinate clauses introduced by words such as dass follow a different pattern.

entries.title: Learn nouns with their articles
entries.signature: Nominative: der/ein [masculine noun]; die/eine [feminine noun]; das/ein [neuter noun]
entries.definition: Start with nominative singular forms: der, die and das accompany masculine, feminine and neuter nouns. The corresponding indefinite articles are ein, eine and ein. These are grammatical classes; they are not a reliable way to infer the sex of a referent. Learn each new noun with its article rather than trying to assign gender from English.
entries.mental_model: The article is a compact label for how the noun behaves.
entries.gotchas: These are nominative forms, not a complete article table. Articles change in other cases. German has no plural form of the indefinite article ein.

entries.title: Choose kein or nicht
entries.definition: Kein negates a noun phrase that would have ein or no article. Nicht can negate a description or other sentence material. The difference follows the kind of expression being denied: kein behaves like a determiner, while nicht works as an adverb. Kein takes endings according to the noun phrase.
entries.mental_model: Choose the negative that fits the material you are denying.
entries.gotchas: Do not interchange kein and nicht just because English uses 'not' in both translations. Nicht placement depends on its scope and the sentence structure; the short phrase below is not a rule for every negative clause.

entries.formality: Neutral standard grammar; Nicht schlecht! is a conventional everyday response.

entries.title: Spelling and linking work together
entries.definition: Preserve accents in words such as êtes: they belong to the spelling. Do not assume that every written final consonant is spoken. In regular -er present forms, several different endings are silent. At some boundaries a normally silent consonant is pronounced before a vowel; this is liaison. Learn common phrases with their audio, not as isolated strings of letter names.
entries.mental_model: Listen to a word together with the word that follows it.
entries.gotchas: The source shows specific linking environments, not a rule for pronouncing every final consonant. Use audio for new phrases.

entries.title: Bonjour and tu versus vous
entries.definition: Bonjour opens a greeting. Tu addresses one person familiarly; vous can address a group or one person politely. The verb follows the chosen pronoun even when polite vous refers to only one person. A name or title in a greeting does not replace the subject pronoun in the question that follows.
entries.mental_model: French 'you' carries information about relationship as well as number.
entries.gotchas: Do not choose tu solely because English uses the same 'you' everywhere. The social setting and established relationship matter. A greeting question can retain statement word order and rely on questioning intonation.

entries.title: Être links a subject to a description
entries.signature: je suis; tu es; il/elle/on est; nous sommes; vous êtes; ils/elles sont
entries.definition: Être supplies the link in identity and description sentences. Its forms are irregular, so learn them with their subjects. A noun subject can replace a pronoun: a single named character takes est, while a plural subject takes sont. In an ordinary complete statement, retain an explicit noun or subject pronoun.
entries.mental_model: Choose the subject first, then the matching linking verb.
entries.gotchas: Do not use the infinitive être after je in an ordinary present statement. The plural form sont is different from singular est. The indefinite article in the example belongs to the identity noun phrase.

entries.title: Build a first regular -er clause
entries.definition: For a regular verb such as parler, remove -er to find parl-, then select the present ending: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez or -ent. The subject helps the listener recover who acts because several endings sound alike. Begin with a subject followed by the conjugated verb; add the information the verb needs after it.
entries.mental_model: Written endings and spoken subjects work together to mark the person.
entries.gotchas: This pattern does not make every verb ending in -er regular. Keep the subject pronoun in ordinary statements. Before a vowel sound, je can become j'; that apostrophe is part of normal spelling.

entries.title: Un, une and des introduce nouns
entries.signature: un [masculine singular noun]; une [feminine singular noun]; des [plural noun]
entries.definition: A basic French noun phrase normally needs a determiner. Use un with masculine singular nouns and une with feminine singular nouns. Des supplies the indefinite plural, which English may translate with 'some' or leave unexpressed. Learn the gender with the noun instead of choosing an article from the English translation.
entries.mental_model: The noun and its article are a useful vocabulary pair.
entries.gotchas: Des is not a plural of only masculine nouns; it works with either gender. The beginner pattern has limits: bare profession and nationality descriptions after être behave differently, and negative clauses can change indefinite articles to de.

entries.title: Ask a first question and make a negative
entries.definition: Est-ce que allows a yes/no question while keeping the following subject–verb order. To negate a simple present clause in standard writing, place ne before the verb and pas after it. Ne becomes n' before a vowel or silent h.
entries.mental_model: Keep the core clause recognizable: mark a question at the front, or place the negative around the finite verb.
entries.gotchas: Spoken French often omits ne; retain both parts in standard written practice. Non is an answer word, not the clause's negation.

entries.title: Keep the marked letters and predictable stress
entries.signature: ĉ ĝ ĥ ĵ ŝ ŭ; [word with two or more vowels] → stress its penultimate vowel
entries.definition: The marks in ĉ, ĝ, ĥ, ĵ, ŝ and ŭ identify distinct letters, not optional decorations. The five vowel letters are a, e, i, o and u. For a normal word with at least two vowels, count back to the second-to-last vowel to find the stress. J and ŭ behave as consonants for this purpose.
entries.mental_model: Keep the spelling intact, then count vowel letters to find the strong syllable.
entries.gotchas: Do not silently remove diacritics. In the uncommon poetic omission of final -o, the missing vowel still counts for stress. This entry does not supply guessed English pronunciation spellings.

entries.title: Thanks and a polite reply
entries.definition: Use Dankon to thank someone and Ne dankinde as a polite response. The first expression contains the noun ending -o and the accusative ending -n. It functions as a complete conversational formula even without an explicit subject and verb. The reply conveys that thanks are unnecessary; natural English uses 'You're welcome' or 'My pleasure'.
entries.mental_model: Learn the exchange as two complete conversational moves before analyzing every ending.
entries.gotchas: Danko is the noun 'thanks'; the conventional spoken formula is Dankon. Ne dankinde is also written as the single word nedankinde. Its normal function is a courteous reply, not a literal evaluation of someone's gratitude.

entries.title: Pronouns with the present form estas
entries.definition: Mi refers to the speaker; vi addresses one or more listeners; ni includes the speaker and others. In a simple identity sentence, estas is the present form of esti. The ending -as marks present time, not a special person. Learn the identity or description after it as information about the subject.
entries.mental_model: Estas supplies a present-time link; the pronoun tells you who it is about.
entries.gotchas: The form after estas is not a direct object and does not take -n merely because it follows a verb. Vi does not distinguish polite from familiar address or singular from plural. Do not use the infinitive esti as the finite verb in an ordinary statement.

entries.title: Recognize -o, -a and -as at a glance
entries.definition: Many Esperanto words consist of a root plus a grammatical ending. In a simple phrase, -o marks a noun and -a marks an adjective describing it. The present verb ending -as turns a clause into a statement about an action or state. Recognizing the endings lets you identify each word's job before knowing every root.
entries.mental_model: The root contributes vocabulary; the ending makes that vocabulary usable in a sentence.
entries.gotchas: Particles and pronouns need not take these endings. Nouns and adjectives may carry number or case endings after -o or -a. The phrase below needs no indefinite article.

entries.title: Use ĉu for a yes/no question
entries.definition: Put ĉu at the front of a basic yes/no question and leave the following clause in ordinary subject–verb order. The particle asks for confirmation of the whole proposition. Jes gives a positive answer and ne a negative one. An explicit answering clause is useful when a short answer might be unclear.
entries.mental_model: Ĉu turns a statement into something to confirm or deny.
entries.gotchas: Ĉu is not the word for every English question. Questions asking who, where or when use the appropriate question word. With negative questions, different yes/no conventions exist in Esperanto; state the intended meaning explicitly when necessary.

entries.title: Mark the object with -n
entries.definition: English often distinguishes a subject from an object by position. Esperanto can instead keep the object's -n ending when moving it. This makes alternative orders possible while preserving the basic participant roles. Begin with a subject–verb–object order, but read the endings when encountering other arrangements.
entries.mental_model: Follow the ending to find the object rather than assuming it is the last word.
entries.gotchas: The subject has no accusative -n merely because it comes later. Words describing the subject after esti also do not become objects. The -n ending has additional uses, including direction and some measurements; this starter covers direct objects only.

entries.title: Keep vowel length and vowel groups distinct
entries.signature: хол ≠ хоол; vowel groups: а о у / э ө ү, with и neutral
entries.definition: The extra written vowel in a pair such as хол and хоол matters to meaning. Learn the spelling and audio together. Vowel harmony also groups а, о, у separately from э, ө, ү, while и is neutral. Traditional teaching labels these groups 'masculine' and 'feminine'; those labels describe vowels, not people's gender.
entries.mental_model: Keep two checks separate: which vowel is written, and whether it is doubled.
entries.gotchas: Do not replace ө with о or ү with у. The grouping is an introduction, not enough to predict every suffix spelling. Later-syllable vowels and loanwords need further study; this entry offers no invented phonetic transcription.

entries.title: A full greeting and a familiar greeting
entries.definition: Use Сайн байна уу? when greeting someone in an ordinary first or polite encounter. It functions as 'Hello' or a greeting-style 'How are you?'. The shorter Сайн уу? is common among friends and younger people. Learn the whole greeting with its social use before trying to replace its words.

entries.title: A first identity sentence without an overt verb
entries.definition: In this attested identity pattern, Би is followed directly by the description гадаад хүн. English needs 'am' in its natural translation; this Mongolian sentence does not contain a separate word for it. Learn this specific construction as a starting point rather than translating every English linking verb word for word.
entries.mental_model: Read the noun phrase as identifying the subject.
entries.gotchas: Би means 'I'; тэр can mean 'he' or 'she'. Do not generalize this verb omission to every statement about location, existence or condition. The adjective comes before хүн in the example.

entries.title: Put the habitual verb after its object
entries.definition: Read the subject first, the thing involved next, and the action last in the beginner pattern below. The ending -даг expresses a habitual, repeated or continuing activity in this example. Its vowel has variants in other words, so keep the attested form уудаг intact while learning the construction.
entries.mental_model: The final verb completes the meaning of the preceding participants.
entries.gotchas: This is an ordinary clause pattern, not a claim that every utterance ends in a verb: question particles can follow. Do not insert English 'do' as a separate habitual marker.
entries.notes:
https://www.mongolianlanguage.mn/free-lessons/mongolian-grammar-forms — 1. Mongolian Sentence Structure; 2. Present Simple Tense; 3. Past Simple Tense; 4. Expressing action in the future.

Example source locations:

entries.summary: A basic Khalkha action clause places its object before the verb.
entries.related_concepts: subject–object–verb order; habitual aspect; vowel harmony

entries.title: A case form can mark the recipient
entries.definition: Mongolian case forms tell you a participant's role in a sentence. In the attested example, John is the giver, the book is what is given, and надад identifies the recipient. English expresses that relationship with 'to me'; Mongolian uses a case form of the pronoun.
entries.mental_model: Read the pronoun's shape as a clue to its job, not just its dictionary meaning.
entries.gotchas: Do not make надад by mechanically attaching an ending to би. Learn this pronoun pair directly. The example does not license one suffix for every noun: noun and pronoun case patterns require their own forms.
entries.notes:
https://www.mongolianlanguage.mn/free-lessons/guide-to-mongolian-cases-1 — First example: John gave a book to me; explanation of би → надад.

Example source locations:
Identify who receives the book — First example: full Mongolian sentence, English meaning, and explicit би → надад dative explanation. [Guide to Mongolian Cases: Part I]
entries.summary: The pronoun form надад identifies 'to me', rather than the subject 'I'.
entries.related_concepts: dative case; recipient; pronoun stems; verb-final clauses

entries.title: Ask about a language and say you do not know it
entries.definition: The first phrase asks about English ability; the second says that the speaker does not know Mongolian. Хэл means 'language' here. The question ends in the separate particle үү; the negative predicate is written мэдэхгүй, as one word.
entries.mental_model: Look at the end to distinguish a question from a negative statement.
entries.gotchas: Keep the verified forms мэдэх үү and мэдэхгүй intact. This pair does not establish the correct question or negative form for every verb.

entries.title: 01. Start here: values, addresses, & and .*
entries.definition: score is a u32 value. &score produces a pointer to that storage. The type *u32 means a pointer to one u32. p stores that pointer; p.* accesses the u32 it points at. Assigning to p.* changes score. Taking an address does not request a heap allocation.
entries.mental_model: Think of score as a box holding 10. p is a note telling you where that box is. & makes the note; .* follows the note. A copy of the number is a different box. A copy of the pointer still leads to the original box.
entries.gotchas: The star has different jobs: *u32 describes a TYPE; p.* accesses a VALUE through a pointer. Multiplication, such as 2 * 3, is another use. Zig dereferences with p.*, not C-style *p. The actual numeric address is rarely useful for learning this.

entries.summary: A pointer tells you where an existing value lives. Read this entry before the others.

entries.title: 02. const p versus *const T: two separate decisions
entries.signature:
const p: *u32 = &value;      // fixed pointer, writable value
var q: *const u32 = &value;  // movable pointer, read-only access
entries.definition: Read a declaration in two parts. const p means p cannot be reassigned. *u32 means p can be used to change a u32. *const u32 means this pointer cannot be used to write the u32. It does not freeze the original object against changes through a different mutable reference. A var pointer can be reassigned; its pointee still follows the permissions in its type.
entries.mental_model: There are two questions: Can I change the destination written on this note? Can I change the contents of the box by following this note? Binding const answers the first. Pointee const answers the second.
entries.gotchas: const p: *u32 allows p.* = 9 but rejects p = &other. var p: *const u32 allows p = &other but rejects p.* = 9. const p: *const u32 allows neither. var p: *u32 allows both. Taking & of a const value gives read-only access. Zig also rejects a local var that is never mutated; prefer const for a pointer whose destination stays fixed.

entries.title: 03. Functions taking pointers: change the caller’s value
entries.definition: A u32 parameter receives the number. A *u32 parameter receives a pointer value: a copy of the address still points at the caller’s same storage. The function can write that storage with count.*. The parameter binding itself cannot be reassigned. Passing the pointer does not transfer ownership or copy the entire pointee.
entries.mental_model: Sending the number is like sending a photocopy of the box contents. Sending a pointer is like sending directions to the original box. Both arguments are values; the pointer value tells the function where to act.
entries.gotchas: addJob(jobs) is wrong when addJob expects *u32; pass &jobs. A pointer-taking function is not the same thing as a function pointer: the latter stores which function to call (entry 11). Prefer a plain value when you only need a small number. *const T is read-only through this argument, not a guarantee no other alias can change the object.

entries.title: 04. Struct methods: self, *Self, and *const Self
entries.signature:
fn increment(self: *Counter) void
fn current(self: *const Counter) u32
entries.definition: self is an ordinary parameter name, not a special keyword. Inside a struct, a function whose first parameter is the instance can be called with method syntax. A pointer receiver permits mutation of the original. For a struct pointer, self.value automatically accesses the field through the pointer; self.*.value is the explicit equivalent. @This() can be named Self inside a struct if you see that style in other code.
entries.mental_model: counter.increment() hands the method a way to reach counter. The method changes the value field inside that same counter, rather than a separate Counter.
entries.gotchas: A method that needs *Counter must have mutable storage available. A const Counter cannot be passed where mutable access is required. self: Counter receives a value, while self: *Counter receives an address. Zig may optimize how aggregate value parameters are passed; do not use a pointer merely because you assume every struct value call copies all bytes.

entries.title: 05. Read the brackets: [N]T, *[N]T, []T, and [*]T
entries.signature:
[3]u8       // the array value
*[3]u8      // pointer to one whole 3-element array
[]u8        // slice: pointer plus length
[*]u8       // many-item pointer: no stored length
entries.definition: In [3]u8 and *[3]u8, 3 is part of the type. A []u8 slice has a .ptr and a .len; its length is a value and need not be known at compile time. A [*]u8 can index consecutive u8 elements, but carries no length. *[3]u8 is a single-item pointer whose one item happens to be an array. Use []T for ordinary functions handling a variable number of elements.
entries.mental_model: The array is a row of boxes. *[3]T points at a row whose size is written into the type. []T is a note with both the starting position and the number of boxes. [*]T records only where to start.
entries.gotchas: slice.ptr loses the length carried by the slice. many[i] cannot check against an allocation length it does not know. slice[i] has bounds checks with runtime safety enabled (Debug and ReleaseSafe); it is still your job to keep its storage alive. Slicing with compile-time-known bounds can infer an array pointer. An explicit []T annotation makes the desired slice type clear.

entries.title: 06. Slice parameters: writable elements, copied view
entries.signature:
fn clear(items: []u8) void
fn total(items: []const u8) u32
entries.definition: A slice parameter passes a view of existing storage. Writing items[0] changes a backing element. Returning items[1..] creates a shorter view without moving or copying the elements. The caller’s original slice length does not change unless the caller assigns the returned slice. Most APIs should take a slice by value, not a pointer to a slice.
entries.mental_model: Copying the view copies a map of which boxes to visit. It does not copy the boxes. Shortening one map does not shorten another map that was copied earlier.
entries.gotchas: const view: []u8 still permits view[0] = 0; const fixes the descriptor binding. []const u8 prevents writes through that view. *[]u8 is a pointer to the slice descriptor itself: an API could use it to replace the caller’s pointer and length, but that is a different need from editing elements. An empty slice is valid; check length before accessing index zero.

entries.title: 07. Pointer capture in for loops: |*item|
entries.definition: A normal capture |item| gives the element value. A pointer capture |*item| gives a pointer to the element so assignment through item.* changes the original. For an array, iterate over &array when you want element pointers; for a slice, iterate over the slice.
entries.mental_model: The loop hands you one note to one box at a time. * in the capture asks for the note; .* in the body follows it to update that box.
entries.gotchas: Do not confuse |*item| with multiplication or the *T type spelling. Mutable pointer capture needs writable elements. []const T does not become mutable just because the capture has a star. Do not retain element pointers after their backing storage ends or a growing container reallocates.

entries.title: 08. Optional pointers: ?*T, null, and safe unwrapping
entries.definition: An ordinary *u32 cannot represent null. ?*u32 means either a pointer to a u32 or null. if (maybe) |p| enters the branch only when a pointer is present; p is then a *u32. That is a normal capture of an already-pointer payload, so you do not need |*p| to edit the target.
entries.mental_model: An optional is an envelope. It contains either a note giving an address or nothing. Open the envelope first; then follow the note.
entries.gotchas: maybe.? asserts that the optional is non-null; it is not a safe fallback for a missing value. A present pointer can still be dangling; non-null does not establish lifetime. ?*T means optional pointer to T, while *?T means pointer to storage containing an optional T. Those are different types.

entries.title: 09. Lifetimes: a pointer does not keep storage alive
entries.definition: A borrowed pointer refers to storage managed elsewhere. Taking &, copying a pointer, returning a pointer, or adding const does not extend storage lifetime. A local variable usually ends when its function returns. A slice also borrows storage unless an API explicitly returns owned allocation. Zig has no Rust-style borrow checker to prove all of these relationships for you.
entries.mental_model: An address written on a note is useful only while the box is still there. Keeping the note does not keep the box alive. A successful compilation does not prove your lifetime reasoning correct.
entries.gotchas: UNSAFE ANTI-EXAMPLE (do not run): fn bad() *u32 { var local: u32 = 7; return &local; }. The returned pointer outlives local. Likewise, never return a slice into a local stack array. This may compile; compilation is not permission to use it. Returning a value, borrowing caller storage, or explicitly allocating with documented ownership are different valid designs. A cast cannot repair a dangling pointer. Container growth, freeing memory, and resetting an arena can invalidate outstanding views.

entries.title: 10. Allocation and ownership: create/destroy, alloc/free
entries.definition: allocator.create(T) allocates storage for one T and returns *T. allocator.alloc(T, n) allocates element storage and returns []T. Initialize allocated storage before reading it. Match create with destroy and alloc with free using the responsible allocator. Taking &existing does none of this and gives you nothing to free. Document which caller or object is responsible for releasing an allocation.
entries.mental_model: Borrowing gets you directions to an existing box. Allocation requests new storage and creates a cleanup responsibility. A pointer does not carry an automatic instruction to free anything.
entries.gotchas: Copying the pointer does not create another allocation or another owner. After destroy/free, every alias to that storage becomes unusable. Freeing twice is wrong. Do not free stack storage or string literals. defer runs at scope exit: a function that returns owned memory must not defer freeing it on its successful return. ! and try here handle allocation errors, not pointer dereferencing.

entries.title: 11. Function pointers: *const fn and callbacks
entries.definition: fn double(value: u32) u32 { ... } declares a function body. *const fn (u32) u32 is the type of a pointer to a function taking u32 and returning u32. A parameter of that type lets the caller choose behavior. Call it with ordinary parentheses: callback(value). Function body values are compile-time-only; function pointers can be stored and chosen at runtime.
entries.mental_model: A data pointer says “use this box.” A function pointer says “run this operation.” A callback is an operation supplied to another function so that function can call it at the appropriate moment.
entries.gotchas: The const in *const fn belongs to the function pointer type. var callback: Transform can still be reassigned to another matching function. All parameter types, return type, and calling convention must match. Use &double to make the address explicit; Zig can also coerce a compatible function name to the pointer type. A plain function pointer does not carry captured local state like a closure. APIs needing state commonly pass a separate context value/pointer; that context must outlive its use.

entries.title: 12. Advanced: sentinel pointers and zero-terminated strings
entries.signature:
[*:0]const u8  // many-item pointer with zero terminator contract
[:0]const u8   // slice with length and zero sentinel at .len
entries.definition: A sentinel is a marker value used to mark an end. In [*:0]const u8, 0 is the terminator, not a length. This pointer does not store .len. [:0]const u8 also carries a length and guarantees a zero at that length. Zig string literals have sentinel-terminated array storage and can coerce to either type. Ordinary []const u8 is a bounded byte view and does not promise a trailing zero.
entries.mental_model: A slice gives you a count. A sentinel pointer asks you to walk until a stop marker. The marker must really exist in valid accessible storage; spelling a type or applying a cast cannot create it.
entries.gotchas: Use regular slices for your own ordinary Zig APIs. Do not pass arbitrary slice.ptr to a zero-terminated API: it may read beyond the buffer. std.mem.span scans for the sentinel, so its input must already satisfy that contract. A sentinel pointer does not give arbitrary indexing the bounds information of a slice. [:0]T has a length; [*:0]T does not. Embedded zero bytes can make a sentinel scan end earlier than a slice’s full length.

entries.title: 13. Advanced: pointer casts do not make memory safe
entries.definition: @ptrCast converts pointer types when its requirements are met. @alignCast asserts suitable alignment; it does not move bytes to an aligned address. @constCast removes a const qualifier; it does not make truly immutable storage writable. @intFromPtr exposes an address as an integer, and @ptrFromInt constructs a pointer from an integer; neither proves that an object exists there. Most beginner pointer code needs none of these builtins.
entries.mental_model: Changing the label on a note cannot repair a missing box, make the box larger, or change who owns it. Before a cast, establish what object is really there and why its storage, size, alignment, lifetime, and permissions match the destination.
entries.gotchas: Do not reach for a cast to silence expected-*T-found-T or constness errors. Fix the argument or API design first. *anyopaque is common at interface boundaries, but the programmer must remember the actual object type. Never use a cast to revive freed memory, manufacture a missing sentinel, reinterpret too few bytes as a larger object, or write a string literal. Unrelated function signatures are not made compatible by a cast.

entries.title: 14. Troubleshooting: read the expected and found types
entries.signature:
expected *u32, found u32      -> value supplied instead of address
expected *u32, found *const u32 -> mutable access requested to const storage
const p versus p.*            -> pointer binding versus pointed-to value
entries.definition: Read the error as a request from the function or assignment. Is it asking for the value, an address, a slice, or a callable? First identify the type you actually have. Fix the mismatch with a suitable value, &, a read-only parameter, or a slice conversion. Then consider lifetime. Avoid changing several stars at random until the compiler accepts the code.
entries.mental_model: An error is often telling you that you handed over a box when it expected directions, or asked for write permission using a read-only note. It is a clue about the contract, not a reason to add a cast.
entries.gotchas: The examples in this entry are INTENTIONALLY INVALID and were verified to fail with Zig 0.16.0. Keep them separate from the passing examples. For a “local variable is never mutated” diagnostic, a fixed pointer should usually be const even if its pointee changes. Compilation still cannot establish every lifetime guarantee (entry 09).

entries.title: 01. Read a function name: module, name, and arity
entries.signature:
Book.label("Dune")
Book.label("Dune", "Frank Herbert")
# References: Book.label/1 and Book.label/2
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Sketch a Postcard module with greeting/1 and greeting/2. What is different about the two calls? Do not implement a process.

A module groups named functions. Arity is the number of arguments, so Book.label/1 and Book.label/2 are different functions. def creates a public function; defp creates a private helper callable from the same module. The final expression is the return value. Calling an ordinary function executes in the calling process; defining a module does not create a process.
entries.mental_model: Read Book.label/2 as: in module Book, call label with two inputs. The slash notation describes a function; a call uses parentheses and actual arguments.
entries.gotchas: Book is a module alias, not an instance holding fields. Arity counts function arguments, not elements inside a list or tuple passed as one argument. A default argument can generate additional arities; start with explicit definitions to make the distinction clear. Private functions cannot be called externally as Book.decorate/1.

entries.title: 02. Recognize atoms, tuples, lists, and tagged data
entries.signature:
:ready                 # atom
{:ready, "tea"}         # two-element tuple
[:ready, "tea"]         # two-element list
"ready"                # string
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Predict whether :tea equals "tea", and whether {:ok, "tea"} equals [:ok, "tea"]. Explain the tag and payload.

An atom is a named constant such as :ready. A tuple groups a fixed number of positional values, for example {:reading, "Dune", 12}. A list is a sequence written with square brackets. A leading atom in a tuple is often a tag that tells you how to interpret its remaining values. :ok, true, false, and nil are atoms; the last three do not need a leading colon.
entries.mental_model: The outer brackets tell you the container shape. A tag on a tuple is like a label on an envelope; the payload is what the envelope carries.
entries.gotchas: Atoms and strings are different values. Avoid converting arbitrary user input into new atoms; atoms are not garbage-collected. Use a fixed set of known atom labels or keep external names as strings. A tuple tag is a convention, not a special success/error mechanism.
