entries.title: 03. Match, extract, rebind, and pin
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Match {:city, "Oslo"} to extract its name. Then predict what happens if the tuple tag is :country instead.

The expression on the right of = is evaluated, then the pattern on the left must fit it. Variables in the pattern can receive values. Reusing a variable name in a later match can rebind it. Prefix an existing variable with ^ when the old value must match. _ ignores a position; it is not a value you can read later.
entries.mental_model: A pattern is a shaped template: literal parts must fit exactly, and variable-shaped holes collect the data inside.
entries.gotchas: A failed standalone = raises MatchError. It does not return false. In function heads or case clauses, a nonmatching pattern instead lets selection continue. 1 and 1.0 compare equal with ==, but a literal 1 pattern does not match 1.0. Use === when you want strict comparison in ordinary expressions.

entries.title: 04. Function clauses: specific cases before the fallback
entries.signature:
def label({:book, title}), do: title
def label(_other), do: "unknown"
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Design describe/1 for {:pet, name}, {:plant, name}, and unknown input. List the clause order before writing code.

Clauses of the same name and arity are tried from top to bottom. The first matching head whose guard succeeds runs. A broad final clause catches everything left over. Keep clauses of the same function together. Pattern matching in a function head lets you extract and choose in one step.
entries.mental_model: Imagine checking a stack of labelled trays from the top. Put narrow trays before the tray marked “anything”. Once an item fits, selection stops.
entries.gotchas: A catch-all first clause makes later clauses unreachable. There is no fall-through after a selected clause runs. Without a matching clause, calling the function raises FunctionClauseError. Different arities are different functions; a fallback label/1 does not catch a bad label/2 call.

entries.title: 05. Map patterns, key types, and immutable updates
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Extract the city from a map that also contains a country. Predict whether an atom key :city matches the string key "city".

Map patterns may require only some keys and ignore other keys. %{city: value} is shorthand for %{:city => value}; %{"city" => value} uses a different key. The update form %{map | key: value} requires the key to exist. Map.put/3 can add a key. Both create a new map value, leaving the original usable.
entries.mental_model: A map pattern is a checklist of keys you need. Updating makes a revised version; it does not erase the earlier version.
entries.gotchas: %{} in a pattern matches any map, not only an empty map. map.city is for an existing atom key and raises when missing; map[:city] normally returns nil when absent. Map.fetch/2 distinguishes a missing key (:error) from a present nil ({:ok, nil}). Matching a map does not accept nil just because the pattern mentions few keys.

entries.title: 06. Guards: refine a shape with allowed checks
entries.signature:
def zone(value) when is_number(value) and value < 0, do: :below_zero
def zone(value) when is_number(value), do: :at_or_above_zero
def zone(_value), do: :not_a_number
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Write down the cases for a temperature classifier: below zero, zero or above, and not a number. Decide which cases need guards.

A when guard runs as part of clause selection. It must evaluate to true to select that clause. Use allowed checks such as is_integer/1, is_number/1, is_binary/1, comparisons, and, or, not, byte_size/1, length/1, map_size/1, and rem/2. in is available in guards with a permitted list or range on the right. Ordinary function calls such as String.trim/1 and Enum functions do not belong in guards; call them in the body.
entries.mental_model: The pattern checks the shape at the door. The guard adds a short checklist before the clause is admitted.
entries.gotchas: Check the type as well as the comparison: Elixir defines ordering between different term types, so value < 0 alone is not a numeric type test. A guard that errors, such as a size check on the wrong type, fails that clause rather than raising from the guard. The same operation in a normal function body can raise. String.length/1 and String.trim/1 are not allowed guard calls. Allowed guards are a defined set, not all functions that happen to be pure.

entries.title: 07. Choose case, cond, or if
entries.signature:
case value do
  {:ok, payload} -> payload
  _other -> :fallback
end

cond do
  condition -> :first
  true -> :fallback
end
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Pick a construct for each: inspect a result tuple; classify a score into three bands; choose a message from one checkbox.

case evaluates one value and matches it against ordered patterns, optionally with guards. cond tries condition expressions in order and runs the first truthy one. if evaluates one condition and chooses between do and else. All three are expressions: their selected branch produces a return value. Only false and nil are falsey; 0, an empty string, and an empty list are truthy.
entries.mental_model: case asks “which shape is this?” cond asks “which statement holds first?” if asks one yes-or-no question.
entries.gotchas: case with no matching clause raises CaseClauseError. cond with no truthy condition raises CondClauseError, so use true as a final fallback where appropriate. if without else returns nil for false/nil. if does not pattern-match a tuple. A binding made inside a branch does not automatically rebind an outer variable; assign the entire expression’s result.

entries.title: 08. Result tuples: unwrap success and handle failure
entries.signature:
case result do
  {:ok, value} -> use(value)
  {:error, reason} -> explain(reason)
end
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Design the caller of a colour lookup that returns {:ok, code} or {:error, :unknown_colour}. Decide what the caller should display for each branch.

Many APIs return tagged tuples so callers can distinguish successful values from expected failures. {:ok, value} carries success; {:error, reason} carries an explanation. This is a convention: read each API’s actual contract. Map.fetch/2 uses :error by itself, while Integer.parse/1 returns {integer, remainder} or :error. A direct {:ok, value} = result asserts success; case can handle either outcome.
entries.mental_model: A result tuple is an envelope with a success or failure label. Opening it is separate from using the enclosed value.
entries.gotchas: Do not pass the whole {:ok, value} tuple into a function that expects value alone. A normal returned error and an exception are different mechanisms. Functions ending in ! often raise where their partner returns an error, but check their documentation. Pattern matching only the success shape is appropriate when failure should be treated as a violated assumption.

entries.title: 09. with: chain successful matches without hiding failures
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Describe two dependent steps for reading a setting: find its key, then parse its text. List the failure shapes before choosing an else block.

with runs expressions in sequence. For pattern <- expression, a match makes bindings available to later steps and the do block. A mismatch stops the chain. Without else the unmatched value is returned as-is. With else, that value is matched against the else clauses. An ordinary = inside with still raises on mismatch. with does not automatically catch exceptions or turn arbitrary results into {:ok, value}.
entries.mental_model: Each gate admits only the expected shape. If a gate rejects a value, that exact value reaches the exit handler.
entries.gotchas: All failed <- steps share one else, so the same :error from different APIs may lose information about which step failed. Normalize failure shapes in helper functions when that distinction matters. An else that does not match an unexpected value raises WithClauseError. Bindings created inside with are not available outside it or automatically in else.

entries.title: 10. Transform data with Enum, functions, and pipes
entries.signature:
items
|> Enum.filter(fn item -> keep?(item) end)
|> Enum.map(&convert/1)
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: From a list of word strings, plan a pipeline that keeps long words and then uppercases them. State the type of value between stages.

Enum.filter/2 selects elements, Enum.map/2 transforms them, and Enum.reduce/3 combines them into an accumulator. The pipe |> inserts the previous result as the first argument of the next call. fn item -> ... end creates a function value; &String.upcase/1 captures a named function. Call a function value with a dot, such as transform.(text). Enum operations are eager and return their results now.
entries.mental_model: A pipeline passes a finished value from one workbench to the next. Each stage gets input and produces output; it does not secretly mutate the starting collection.
entries.gotchas: A pipe is not a process, a loop variable, or automatic error handling. It inserts into the first argument, which may not be where a particular API expects the data. Enum.each/2 is for side effects and returns :ok, so do not use it when you need a transformed list. Rebinding a variable can name a new result, but does not mutate an old value held elsewhere.

entries.title: 11. Strings are UTF-8 binaries; bytes are not characters
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Predict byte_size("é") and String.length("é"). Then distinguish "cat" from ~c"cat".

Elixir strings are UTF-8 encoded binaries. byte_size/1 counts bytes, while String.length/1 counts graphemes: user-facing character units that may contain several code points. is_binary/1 only checks the binary type; it does not prove valid UTF-8. String.valid?/1 checks encoding. A charlist such as ~c"cat" is a list of integer code points, a different type often used by Erlang APIs.
entries.mental_model: A byte is a storage unit. A grapheme is a text unit someone reads. One visible character can require several storage units.
entries.gotchas: An empty string and a whitespace-only string are different values. byte_size/1 is allowed in guards; String.length/1, String.trim/1, and String.valid?/1 are not ordinary guard calls. <<255>> is a binary but not valid UTF-8. Prefer String functions for text operations rather than assuming one byte per character. <> concatenates binaries; ++ concatenates lists.

entries.title: 12. List recursion: the empty case and a smaller problem
entries.signature:
def count([]), do: 0
def count([_head | tail]), do: 1 + count(tail)
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Write down what count([]) should return. Then describe how count([head | tail]) can use the answer for tail.

A list can be matched as [] or [head | tail]. tail is another list containing the remaining items. A recursive function has a base clause and a clause that calls itself with a smaller problem. An accumulator can carry the partial result as an argument. A tail call is a call whose result is returned directly without further work. Use Enum for ordinary collection tasks unless recursion makes the algorithm clearer.
entries.mental_model: Solve one small part, then ask the same question about what is left. The empty list is where there is no work left to do.
entries.gotchas: [head | tail] does not match []. A fallback or explicit contract is needed for inputs outside the intended list domain. Recursing on the same unchanged list never reaches the base case. Repeated list ++ appends copy the left side; for building lists efficiently, prepend then reverse when appropriate. A private helper with an accumulator has a different arity from the public function.

entries.title: 13. A module is code; a process has a mailbox
entries.signature:
send(pid, {:echo, self(), reference, text})
receive do
  {:reply, ^reference, reply} -> reply
after
  1_000 -> :timeout
end
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Draw two processes and the messages between them for a single echo request. What identifies the reply if several requests are in flight?

Code always runs in a BEAM process. spawn/1 starts a new lightweight process running a function and returns its PID. self/0 gives the current process PID. send/2 sends a message and returns the message, not a reply. receive scans the current process mailbox for a matching message. Include an after timeout when waiting should be bounded. A module merely groups code; many processes can run the same module’s functions.
entries.mental_model: The module is a recipe. A process is one cook following it, with a private inbox. Starting another cook does not create a new recipe.
entries.gotchas: Unmatched messages remain in the mailbox. A successful send does not prove a live recipient handled the request. Capturing parent = self() before spawn is different from calling self() inside the spawned function. Use a unique reference to correlate replies. This one-request example exits after replying; it is not a robust service. Use OTP behaviours for long-lived services.

entries.title: 14. GenServer: client calls, callbacks, and state
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Separate an API for a shared list into client operations and server state transitions. Which operations need a reply?

A GenServer runs callbacks in its own process and carries a state value from one callback to the next. A public wrapper such as add(pid, item) runs in the caller, then GenServer.call sends a request and waits for a reply. init/1 supplies the initial state. handle_call/3 returns {:reply, reply, new_state}. handle_cast/2 handles asynchronous cast requests with no reply, and handle_info/2 handles ordinary messages.
entries.mental_model: The client wrapper is the service counter. The callback is the worker behind it. The worker finishes one callback and hands the next state value to its next turn.
entries.gotchas: A module definition or use GenServer does not itself start a process. start_link starts one. Avoid a GenServer for simple calculations that need no shared state or concurrent coordination. GenServer.call can exit on failure or timeout; it is not guaranteed to return {:error, reason}. cast returning :ok does not confirm processing. Do not write your own receive inside callbacks. State is in memory and is not automatically durable.

entries.title: 15. Supervision: restart a process, not its lost data
entries.signature:
Supervisor.start_link(children, strategy: :one_for_one)
# replacement state comes from startup, not a saved memory snapshot
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: Suppose a supervised reading queue crashes after adding a title. Predict which state returns if startup always receives an empty list.

A supervisor starts children from child specifications and applies a restart strategy. :one_for_one restarts an eligible terminated child without restarting its siblings. A replacement is a new process with a new PID, initialized from its startup arguments. Restart policy controls eligibility: permanent, transient, or temporary. In-memory changes do not survive a restart unless the child explicitly reloads or reconstructs them.
entries.mental_model: A supervisor can replace a worker using its starting instructions. It does not automatically recover the worker’s notebook. Durable records belong in storage designed to outlive the worker.
entries.gotchas: Supervision is not durable storage, a database transaction, or a guarantee of endless retries. Restart intensity limits can stop a repeatedly failing supervisor. A supervisor intentionally stopped through its management API handles lifecycle differently from a child crash. Keep process boundaries tied to runtime responsibilities, not one process per module. The demonstration below intentionally stops and restarts its own child to show state reset without a timing race; it does not simulate automatic crash recovery.

entries.title: 12b. ExUnit basics and the fallback arity trap
entries.signature:
assert actual == expected
refute condition
assert {:ok, value} = result
assert_raise FunctionClauseError, fn -> bad_call() end
entries.definition:
TRY FIRST: For an unrelated multiply/2 function, list one successful pair and three invalid input pairs. Before writing tests, count the arguments in every clause.

ExUnit tests name a behaviour and assert its observable result. A common structure is arrange the input, act by calling the function, and assert the expected result. describe groups related tests. When testing a result tuple, assert the exact tuple or match it to extract the payload and test that value. A fallback belongs to the same function only when its name AND arity match.
entries.mental_model: A test is a concrete example of your promise to the caller. If you promise that every multiply/2 call returns a product or :unsupported, a multiply/1 clause does not fulfill that promise for two-argument calls.
entries.gotchas: A test that compiles is not necessarily a test that passes. use ExUnit.Case provides test, assert, refute, and assertion helpers. assert_raise is for a function expected to raise; a returned {:error, reason} should normally be asserted as data. If an invalid /2 input raises FunctionClauseError unexpectedly, check the fallback name and argument count before changing the guard. Keep named function clauses of the same arity together. Each test has its own local bindings.

entries.title: 01. First program and the compiler feedback loop
entries.signature:
void main() { /* statements */ }
int main(string[] args) { return 0; }
entries.definition: D compiles to a native executable. main is the program entry point; imports select library declarations. A void main completes successfully unless execution fails. An int main can return a process exit status. Use small programs with assert to check your understanding, then move repeated logic into functions. The sample uses no desktop integration or external dependencies.
entries.mental_model: The compiler checks your source and produces a program; running the program is a separate step.
entries.gotchas: LDC, DMD, and GDC are different compilers with overlapping but different command-line options. A successful compilation alone does not prove runtime behaviour. auto still has a compile-time type; it is not dynamically typed. Do not use assert as the only validation of external input because build settings can disable it.
entries.notes:

Standalone example: save as lesson.d; compile with ldc2 -unittest -boundscheck=on -of=lesson lesson.d, then run ./lesson. Assertions are active in these checks.
Suggested route: 01-13 basics and text; 14-27 functions and ownership; 28-40 error handling, ranges, testing and builds; 41-52 practical boundaries. For desktop work, revisit 43, 45-47, 49, and 52 before choosing an integration library.

entries.title: 02. Modules and selective imports
entries.definition: A module is a source-level namespace, usually one .d file. A module named catalog.labels conventionally lives at catalog/labels.d under an import root. A selective import names the declarations needed; a module alias gives a short qualifier. A normal import does not re-export its imported names; public import does. Import paths find source declarations, while linking still needs the implementation.
entries.mental_model: Modules are named shelves for declarations. Imports let you choose which shelf labels to use in this file.
entries.gotchas: private in D is module-based, so other code in the same module may access private members. Avoid broad public imports unless you intend to expose a facade. A module name alone does not tell a build tool which source files to compile. DUB handles conventional source trees; a manual multi-file build must include the relevant implementations.

entries.summary: Keep namespaces and source layout understandable.

entries.title: 03. Types, auto, and default initialization
entries.definition: An explicit type states the intended representation. auto infers the concrete type of its initializer. D initializes ordinary local variables by default: integers to zero, references to null, and floating types to NaN. Type.init exposes the default initializer. size_t is an unsigned type suitable for sizes and indices whose width depends on the target.
entries.mental_model: A variable has one known type even when the compiler writes that type down for you.
entries.gotchas: double.init is NaN, not 0.0; NaN does not compare equal to itself. Character types have special .init values, not necessarily a usable blank character. = void suppresses initialization and is an advanced tool; reading such storage before writing it is a bug. An unsigned index cannot represent a negative result.

entries.title: 04. Conversions: checked to!T versus cast
entries.definition: std.conv.to converts between supported types and checks many numeric range constraints. Parsing invalid text or narrowing out-of-range values can throw ConvException. cast asks for a language-level conversion and may truncate; it is not an input validator. Numeric types include signed int and long, unsigned uint and ulong, and floating float and double.
entries.mental_model: A checked conversion asks whether the value fits. A cast tells the compiler to perform a conversion under the language rules.
entries.gotchas: Does not fit is different from failed to parse. Handle both at the input boundary. Integer division truncates; 5 / 2 is 2 when both operands are integers. Mixing signed and unsigned arithmetic can produce surprising comparisons. Use range checks or suitable checked arithmetic when overflow matters.

entries.title: 05. Enums, aliases, and distinct intent
entries.definition: A named enum defines a distinct type with named values. An alias renames an existing type or symbol without creating a new type. A manifest constant written with enum is a compile-time value and need not have addressable storage. For a genuinely different type with its own invariants, use a struct rather than assuming alias prevents mixing values.
entries.mental_model: An alias is another label on the same type. A named enum introduces a small vocabulary of values.
entries.gotchas: An explicit cast can manufacture an unnamed enum value; validate external integers before treating them as enum members. A manifest constant is not the same as an immutable variable with storage. Keep string-to-enum parsing explicit at configuration boundaries.

entries.title: 06. if, loops, switch, and early returns
entries.definition: if chooses a branch, while and for repeat work, and foreach handles collections or integer ranges. A range a .. b excludes b. switch dispatches among cases; return exits the function. final switch on an enum asks the compiler to account for all its named members, making newly added modes harder to forget.
entries.mental_model: Write the decisions plainly first. Add abstractions only when they clarify repeated decisions.
entries.gotchas: Use break or return where a switch case is finished; an empty case can share the next case body. final switch does not validate hostile integers cast into an enum. Avoid long or blocking loops on an event-loop thread. A zero-length range executes no iterations.

entries.title: 07. Strings, UTF-8, code points, and graphemes
entries.definition: D string is an alias for immutable(char)[], normally holding UTF-8. char is one code unit; wchar is a UTF-16 code unit; dchar can hold a Unicode code point. A typed foreach(dchar; text) decodes UTF-8. Code-point count still differs from grapheme count for combined marks and some emoji. Use Unicode-aware library operations when manipulating user-visible text.
entries.mental_model: Bytes store text; code points encode symbols; graphemes approximate the units a reader sees.
entries.gotchas: string.length counts bytes. Slicing arbitrary byte positions can split an encoding sequence. A char[] or string type does not prove the bytes are valid UTF-8. A D string is not guaranteed to be zero-terminated for C. For clipboard text, validate and convert at the boundary rather than treating arbitrary bytes as characters.

entries.title: 08. Static arrays: fixed length is part of the type
entries.definition: A static array stores N elements and its length is part of its type. Assignment between static arrays copies their elements. Slicing it produces a dynamic-array view into that storage. A static array declared locally usually has the lifetime of its enclosing scope; a slice does not extend that lifetime.
entries.mental_model: A static array is the row of boxes itself; a slice is directions to a portion of the row.
entries.gotchas: The syntax is int[3], not a C-style int name[3]. Do not return a slice of a local static array after its storage expires. A copy of an array of class references copies those references, not the class objects.

entries.title: 09. Slices, aliasing, dup, and idup
entries.definition: A dynamic array is a pointer-and-length view. Slicing and assignment can produce views of the same underlying elements. $ inside an index expression represents the relevant array length. .dup creates a mutable element copy; .idup creates an immutable element copy. The copy is shallow when elements themselves reference other objects.
entries.mental_model: Two maps of the same shelf still lead to the same books. dup duplicates the shelf’s element values.
entries.gotchas: Writing view[0] can change the original array. Changing one view’s length does not update other view lengths. Avoid returning views into expired stack storage. Use an explicit copy when storing a view whose owner may reuse or replace its buffer.

entries.summary: Copying a dynamic array copies its view, not its element storage.

entries.title: 10. Append, capacity, and borrowed views
entries.definition: Appending grows a dynamic array and may allocate new storage. Capacity is an implementation-managed opportunity to reuse a backing allocation, not a promise about aliasing. An existing slice does not grow when another descriptor appends. Use reserve when useful for a measured batch operation, and reacquire views after operations that may replace storage.
entries.mental_model: A list descriptor can move to a bigger shelf. Other descriptors do not automatically move with it or gain its new length.
entries.gotchas: Do not depend on whether a particular append reallocates. Old GC-managed slices may remain valid but refer to older storage; manually owned buffers have stricter lifetime constraints. Concatenating repeatedly can allocate repeatedly; consider an appender for building large output.

entries.summary: Use ~ for concatenation and ~= for appending; account for possible reallocation.

entries.title: 11. Associative arrays: lookup without assuming presence
entries.definition: An associative array stores key/value associations. Index assignment inserts or replaces a value. The in operator returns a pointer to the stored value or null, allowing one lookup to both test presence and access the value. get(key, default) reads with a fallback. remove deletes an association.
entries.mental_model: Think of a dictionary with a separate question for “does this word exist?” before reading its definition.
entries.gotchas: Reading an absent key with [] is an error; use in or get when absence is expected. Iteration order is not a stable display order. Do not retain an in pointer across removals or operations that may invalidate the underlying storage. Ordinary associative arrays are not a concurrent map.

entries.title: 12. foreach values versus ref elements
entries.signature:
foreach (int value; values) { }
foreach (ref int value; values) { value *= 2; }
entries.definition: A normal scalar foreach variable receives an element value. Adding ref aliases the element, so assigning through that variable changes the collection. With an index variable you can inspect positions as well. foreach_reverse walks in reverse order. For associative arrays, key/value iteration follows the collection’s iteration order.
entries.mental_model: A value iteration hands you a copy to examine; a ref iteration lets you edit the element in its original slot.
entries.gotchas: Do not resize or structurally alter a collection while iterating unless the operation’s contract explicitly allows it. A copied struct can still contain aliased slices or class references. Use immutable or const views when a reader should not write through its reference.

entries.title: 13. Text utilities: strip, split, format, and parse
entries.definition: std.string provides common text operations, std.format formats values, and std.conv parses or converts values. Prefer a constant format string with user data passed as arguments. Keep whitespace normalization separate from validation so the intended policy is visible. split creates tokens according to its delimiter overload; read the selected overload’s treatment of empty fields.
entries.mental_model: First decide how input text should be interpreted, then parse it; formatting is the reverse operation.
entries.gotchas: Do not use a user-provided string as a format template accidentally. Byte offsets are not grapheme positions. Parsing can throw, and a successful conversion does not prove the value is allowed by your application. Do not use string formatting to build shell commands from untrusted data.

entries.title: 14. Functions, ref, out, and argument intent
entries.definition: Ordinary scalar parameters receive values. ref binds a parameter to the caller’s variable, so assignments affect that variable. out also aliases caller storage but initializes it to its default value on function entry. Arrays passed by value copy the descriptor and can still refer to shared elements. Use const element views for read-only access.
entries.mental_model: The parameter type and storage class describe what the function may do to the caller’s data.
entries.gotchas: ref is not an ownership transfer and does not keep storage alive. out can overwrite a value before the body uses it, so do not treat it as an input. For arrays, distinguish changing elements from changing the caller’s descriptor; the latter requires ref. Prefer returning a value when it makes a simple transformation clearer.

entries.title: 15. Function pointers, delegates, and captured context
entries.signature:
int function(int) functionPointer = &doubleValue;
int delegate(int) callback = (int n) => n + offset;
entries.definition: A function pointer identifies a non-contextual callable. A delegate carries a function and a context, commonly an instance or captured variables. Nested functions and lambdas that use outer locals can create delegates. Use the declared callable type when you want the API contract to be obvious; templates can accept more general callables.
entries.mental_model: A function pointer chooses a recipe. A delegate chooses a recipe together with the ingredients it remembers.
entries.gotchas: A captured variable is not necessarily a snapshot. Closures may allocate, depending on escape and compilation needs. A delegate using stack or manually owned context must not outlive that context. A D delegate is not interchangeable with a C callback pointer; a C API often needs a separate user-data pointer.

entries.title: 16. Overloads, defaults, and typesafe variadics
entries.signature:
int total(int[] values...) { /* use values */ }
string label(string text, string suffix = "!") { return text ~ suffix; }
entries.definition: Overloads share a name but have different parameter lists. Default arguments fill omitted trailing inputs. A typesafe variadic array parameter lets a function accept a sequence of values as one typed array. Templates handle cases where each argument type must be known independently. Keep API variants focused rather than relying on subtle implicit conversions.
entries.mental_model: An overload set is a menu of signatures; defaults fill optional fields on one of those forms.
entries.gotchas: Default expressions are evaluated at the call as specified by the language, not a universal shared mutable default object. Typesafe variadics differ from C-style varargs. Avoid storing a borrowed variadic view beyond its valid lifetime. Overloads selected through numeric conversions can surprise a reader; explicit argument types help.

entries.title: 17. Structs: values with fields and methods
entries.signature: struct Point { int x; int y; int sum() const { return x + y; } }
entries.definition: A struct groups fields and methods and normally has value semantics: assigning it copies its fields. It may contain slices or class references, so the copied fields can still reference shared storage. Methods with const promise not to modify the object through this. Constructor, destructor, and copy behavior can be customized for resource-owning types.
entries.mental_model: A struct value is a labelled bundle. Copying the bundle copies the contents of its fields, including any addresses those fields contain.
entries.gotchas: Value semantics do not imply recursive deep copying. Default construction and .init follow field initialization rules; structs do not behave exactly like classes. For exclusive resource ownership, think through copying, moving, and destruction together; a raw handle in a copyable struct can be released twice.

entries.title: 18. Classes: references, inheritance, and identity
entries.definition: A class definition describes reference objects and can participate in single class inheritance. new creates an instance, commonly using GC-managed memory. Assigning a class reference aliases the same object. is tests identity; == can use the class equality behavior. A class reference defaults to null, so establish existence before invoking instance members.
entries.mental_model: Two class variables can be two name tags pointing at one object.
entries.gotchas: Copying a class reference does not clone its fields. GC finalization is not a prompt cleanup strategy for files, processes, or GUI handles. override documents and checks overriding an inherited virtual method. Keep mutable state ownership clear when references cross callbacks.

entries.summary: A class variable is a reference to an object.

entries.title: 19. Interfaces and replaceable boundaries
entries.signature:
interface TextSource { string read(); }
class FixedSource : TextSource { override string read() { return "tea"; } }
entries.definition: An interface declares a contract implemented by classes. A client using the interface can work with different implementations, useful for placing desktop or file access behind a testable boundary. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Keep the interface small and document errors, ownership, and thread requirements that method types alone cannot express.
entries.mental_model: The caller depends on a socket shape, not on a particular appliance plugged into it.
entries.gotchas: An interface declaration does not start a service or supply an implementation. D class interfaces are not automatically a C ABI or a GUI toolkit binding. A test double should model the contract’s meaningful failures as well as its success case. Avoid an interface when a simple function parameter would suffice.

entries.title: 20. Properties and operator methods
entries.signature:
@property int count() const { return value; }
int opCall(int n) const { return n * factor; }
entries.definition: Property functions expose getter/setter-style access. Operator overload methods such as opCall let a user type participate in familiar expressions. Define these only when the operation’s meaning and cost are natural for the type. A named method is often clearer for actions with I/O, side effects, or expensive work.
entries.mental_model: Syntax is part of the interface: a property should feel like reading a value, and a call operator like applying a callable.
entries.gotchas: Property enforcement and optional parentheses have historical subtleties; keep getter/setter shapes conventional. An operator overload can perform arbitrary work, so document nontrivial behavior. const methods provide read-only access through this, not a deep snapshot of mutable aliases elsewhere.

entries.title: 21. const versus immutable: access and guarantees
entries.signature:
const(int)[] view = mutableData;
immutable(int)[] frozen = mutableData.idup;
entries.definition: D’s const and immutable qualifiers are transitive through the referenced data structure. const permits read-only access to data that may be mutable elsewhere. immutable promises the underlying data will not change after initialization. Copying with idup is one way to produce immutable array data from mutable input. string has immutable character elements, while a string variable can normally be rebound.
entries.mental_model: A const view gives you reading permission. Immutable describes a lasting property of the data itself.
entries.gotchas: const(T)[] keeps the slice descriptor mutable while its elements are read-only through that view. const(T[]) also qualifies the descriptor. Casting away const is only valid under strict conditions when the actual underlying object is mutable; never use a cast to write genuinely immutable storage. shared and immutable solve different problems.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 22. shared and thread-local storage
entries.definition: Mutable module-level variables are normally thread-local in D. shared qualifies data intended to be accessible across threads and restricts operations that would hide unsafe access. It does not make a multi-step update atomic. Prefer immutable messages for simple worker communication; use a documented mutex or atomic protocol when sharing mutable state.
entries.mental_model: shared is a warning label about where data can be accessed, not a security guard controlling every access.
entries.gotchas: __gshared bypasses the normal shared type distinctions and requires manual synchronization. A shared reference does not make an arbitrary method thread-safe. Casting away shared is not a substitute for holding the required lock and proving exclusive access. Atomic operations protect individual operations, not an entire application invariant.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 23. @safe, @trusted, and @system
entries.signature: int readFirst(scope const(int)[] values) @safe { return values[0]; }
entries.definition: @safe asks the compiler to reject operations that can violate memory safety under its rules. @system permits lower-level operations requiring programmer proof. @trusted is a promise that a manually audited implementation exposes a safe interface even though its body may use system operations. Keep trusted code small and explain its invariants.
entries.mental_model: @trusted is a bridge whose builder is responsible for proving it safe; it is not an automatic repair for unsafe code.
entries.gotchas: @safe does not prevent command injection, authorization errors, logical bugs, or all data races. Do not mark a function @trusted merely to silence a compiler diagnostic. Lifetime checking depends on compiler support and settings; inspect the flags used by your build. Raw pointers and C calls deserve explicit ownership and length contracts.

Target checked 2026-11-02: LDC 1.41.0 / DMD frontend 2.111.0, Linux x86_64; DUB 1.40.0. Official online docs may describe a newer compiler.

entries.title: 24. pure, nothrow, and @nogc are independent promises
entries.signature: int square(int n) pure nothrow @safe @nogc { return n * n; }
entries.definition: pure limits access to mutable global state and impure calls; it can still permit mutation through suitable parameters. nothrow prohibits throwing Exception, but does not mean execution can never fail with an Error. @nogc disallows operations that allocate through the D garbage collector; it does not mean no allocation of any kind. @safe is a separate memory-safety promise.
entries.mental_model: Each attribute answers one question. Combining them states several promises rather than one vague “safe and fast” label.
entries.gotchas: @nogc does not make a function real-time, lock-free, or allocation-free. String concatenation and dynamic-array growth can require GC allocation. pure is not always mathematical purity independent of inputs and aliases. Overflow and other programming errors still need appropriate reasoning even with these attributes.

entries.title: 25. Pointers, scope parameters, and lifetime
entries.definition: A pointer identifies storage; & takes an address and * dereferences a pointer in D. scope parameters constrain escape of borrowed references where checked by the compiler. Return annotations can describe how a returned reference relates to an input. Begin with functions returning ordinary values; use borrowed references when the API needs them and its lifetime can be stated.
entries.mental_model: A note with an address remains a note even after the object at that address has disappeared.
entries.gotchas: D’s dereference spelling differs from Zig’s p.*. Never return a pointer or slice to a local stack object that has ended. Casting a pointer does not validate alignment, length, initialization, or lifetime. Passing a pointer to C that retains it requires a longer-lived ownership plan. Check lifetime-related compiler options rather than assuming Rust-style borrow checking.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 26. Garbage collection versus resource cleanup
entries.signature:
auto object = new Item();
// close files and handles explicitly or with scope guards
entries.definition: D commonly uses garbage collection for arrays and objects. Keeping a valid reference to GC-managed storage keeps it reachable, but collection timing is not a suitable schedule for closing files or releasing operating-system resources. scope(exit) and carefully designed struct destructors can provide deterministic cleanup at lexical boundaries.
entries.mental_model: Memory collection recovers unused storage eventually. Resource cleanup ends a specific obligation at a specific time.
entries.gotchas: Do not depend on class finalizers running promptly or in a convenient order. A struct that owns a resource needs a coherent copy/move policy; accidental copies may release it twice. Disabling the GC is not a general fix for performance problems and does not make allocation magically disappear. Measure before optimizing.

entries.title: 27. Manual allocation and ownership pairs — advanced
entries.definition: Low-level interfaces may require manually managed memory. malloc returns uninitialized storage or null; free releases a compatible allocation. Check allocation success, initialize before reading, and arrange exactly one cleanup. Keep the pointer’s lifetime visible and avoid escaping a borrowed slice of it. Prefer higher-level ownership unless an ABI or measured requirement calls for manual storage.
entries.mental_model: Manual allocation adds an obligation: one owner must eventually release the storage with the matching allocator.
entries.gotchas: Do not mix GC allocation, malloc/free, or a library-specific allocator’s release function. @nogc alone does not guarantee resource safety. A slice over freed storage dangles even if it still carries a length. Writing beyond the allocation or using the wrong alignment/type is not repaired by a cast.

entries.title: 28. Exceptions and enforce at input boundaries
entries.signature:
enforce(condition, "explanation");
try { work(); } catch (Exception error) { /* report */ }
entries.definition: Phobos commonly reports operational failures with exceptions. enforce checks a condition and throws when it fails; unlike an ordinary assert, it is intended to remain useful for runtime validation. Catch errors where the caller can add context, recover, or choose a user-facing result. D’s Throwable hierarchy distinguishes Exception from Error.
entries.mental_model: Expected external failure belongs in an explicit handling path. Broken internal assumptions deserve a different response.
entries.gotchas: Avoid catching Throwable indiscriminately and pretending a corrupted assumption is recoverable. Do not discard error context silently. Message text alone is not a stable machine-readable error category. Returning a result type is also possible; choose a consistent contract for each boundary.

entries.title: 29. scope(exit), scope(success), and scope(failure)
entries.definition: A scope guard schedules work when the current scope ends. exit runs on normal exit or exception unwinding, success runs on successful exit, and failure runs when an exception leaves the scope. Guards run in reverse order of registration. This keeps resource cleanup close to the acquisition that created the obligation.
entries.mental_model: Leave instructions at the door as you enter; the most recent instruction is performed first when leaving.
entries.gotchas: Process termination or a hard kill is not ordinary exception unwinding. Cleanup code should avoid throwing another exception. scope(success) means the scope completed without a propagating exception, not that a remote transaction was durably committed. Make ownership clear before registering a release.

entries.title: 30. unittest blocks and testable pure logic
entries.definition: D has built-in unittest blocks compiled when unit testing is enabled. Tests execute before the normal main function. A library module without main can use LDC’s -main option for a generated entry point, or DUB can supply a test runner. Assert observable behavior, boundaries, and error paths. Keep desktop APIs behind interfaces so tests can use small in-memory substitutes.
entries.mental_model: A unit test is a runnable example of a function’s contract.
entries.gotchas: Compiling without -unittest omits the test blocks. Assert settings and release modes affect checks, so run a deliberate test configuration. Avoid tests that manipulate the user’s real clipboard, open windows, or overwrite config files. A passing unit test is evidence about the tested cases, not every integration.

entries.title: 31. Contracts and assertions
entries.signature:
int successor(int n)
in (n < int.max)
out (result; result > n)
{ return n + 1; }
entries.definition: Function contracts express preconditions and postconditions. in states what a caller must satisfy; out can inspect the result. assert checks a local invariant, and static assert checks a compile-time condition. These are useful for programmer-facing correctness guarantees, while enforce or ordinary error handling should handle expected invalid external input.
entries.mental_model: A precondition is a promise from the caller; a postcondition is a promise from the function.
entries.gotchas: Contracts and ordinary asserts may be disabled by release settings. Never hide required side effects in them. An out contract cannot repair a bad computation. For arithmetic, include representable-range assumptions rather than silently relying on overflow behavior.

entries.summary: State caller obligations and result guarantees, but validate untrusted input separately.

entries.title: 32. Nullable and SumType: model absence and alternatives
entries.definition: std.typecons.Nullable holds a value that may be absent. Check isNull before accessing get. std.sumtype.SumType stores one of a declared set of alternatives and supports type-directed matching. These are useful when absence or multiple result shapes are normal and should be represented directly rather than encoded with a magic number.
entries.mental_model: Nullable asks whether the box is filled. SumType states which kind of box you have.
entries.gotchas: Nullable is not a pointer lifetime checker. Accessing an absent value is an error. A string alternative alone may not distinguish all failure categories you need; use named structs or enums for domain-specific states. Decide how exceptions and result values interact instead of mixing conventions accidentally.

entries.title: 33. Ranges: empty, front, popFront, and save
entries.definition: An input range supplies empty, front, and popFront. Forward ranges additionally support save to obtain an independent iteration position. Other range categories add reverse traversal, indexing, or known length. Algorithms ask for the capabilities they need. Arrays work as ranges, but generated ranges such as iota can represent values without storing them all.
entries.mental_model: A range is a cursor that can describe how to produce the next item.
entries.gotchas: Do not read front when empty. Not every range can be restarted or copied as an independent traversal. A range can borrow backing storage and inherit its lifetime. Input ranges may have side effects when advanced, so avoid assuming repeated iteration is free or equivalent.
entries.notes:

entries.summary: A range is an iteration protocol; it need not be an allocated collection.

entries.title: 34. Lazy map/filter and deliberate materialization
entries.signature:
auto selected = values.filter!(n => n > 0).map!(n => n * 2);
int[] stored = selected.array;
entries.definition: Phobos range algorithms such as map and filter often return lazy adapters rather than arrays. The computation happens as the resulting range is consumed. std.array.array materializes a range into an array when you need stored results. Be explicit about this boundary when passing data to a UI or retaining it beyond the original input’s lifetime.
entries.mental_model: A lazy chain is a recipe for visiting values. array cooks that recipe into stored results.
entries.gotchas: Lazy does not mean cached, asynchronous, or parallel. Captured variables and borrowed inputs must remain valid during traversal. Avoid side effects in lazy transformations unless evaluation order and count are intentional. Materializing costs memory; repeatedly traversing a lazy range can repeat work.

entries.summary: Algorithms can describe work now and perform it during iteration.

entries.title: 35. UFCS: free functions with method-like syntax
entries.signature:
string shout(string text) { return text ~ "!"; }
assert("tea".shout() == shout("tea"));
entries.definition: Uniform Function Call Syntax lets eligible free functions be called with the first argument before the dot. It enables readable chains without adding methods to the data type. The function still has its ordinary signature and must be visible to lookup. Many Phobos examples combine UFCS with template arguments.
entries.mental_model: The dot can be another way to feed the first argument, rather than proof that a method belongs to the object.
entries.gotchas: UFCS does not mutate the receiver automatically or change ownership. Member lookup and overload resolution matter, so avoid choosing names that obscure which function is called. A long chain can hide intermediate types; assign a named local when it helps explain the pipeline.

entries.title: 36. Templates and constraints
entries.signature: T twice(T)(T value) if (isIntegral!T) { return value + value; }
entries.definition: A function template has compile-time parameters before its runtime parameters. D can often infer type parameters from arguments; explicit instantiation uses !. A template constraint limits viable instantiations and improves intent. std.traits provides reusable type predicates. Keep arithmetic and ownership contracts meaningful for every admitted type.
entries.mental_model: A template is a typed recipe whose ingredients are chosen during compilation.
entries.gotchas: Accepting a type with a constraint does not prove every value avoids overflow. More generic is not automatically clearer. Instantiation errors can be lengthy; reduce them to a small example and check the constraint first. String mixins are not needed for most ordinary generic functions.
entries.notes:

Official references: https://dlang.org/spec/template.html ; https://dlang.org/phobos/std_traits.html

entries.title: 37. static if and version: compile-time selection
entries.signature:
static if (is(T == int)) { /* type-specific code */ }
version (Windows) { /* Windows branch */ } else { /* other branch */ }
entries.definition: static if selects declarations or statements using a compile-time condition. version selects code according to predefined or user-supplied version identifiers. This differs from a runtime if: excluded code is not semantically checked in the same way as selected code. Use a platform boundary to keep OS-specific behavior out of portable logic.
entries.mental_model: Runtime if chooses a route while travelling. Compile-time selection chooses which roads are built into this executable.
entries.gotchas: Compiling on Linux does not validate the Windows branch. A custom version flag needs a documented build configuration. Do not use version(Posix) as a claim that every Unix desktop offers the same clipboard or screenshot API. Cross-platform code needs builds and tests on each supported target.

entries.summary: Separate type-dependent code from platform-dependent code.

entries.title: 38. CTFE, template mixins, and string mixins
entries.definition: Compile-Time Function Evaluation runs suitable ordinary D functions when a compile-time result is required. A template mixin inserts reusable declarations. A string mixin parses a compile-time string as D source. These are different tools: computation, declaration reuse, and code generation. Start with the least powerful mechanism that expresses the task.
entries.mental_model: CTFE computes an answer; a mixin contributes declarations to the surrounding scope.
entries.gotchas: CTFE cannot perform arbitrary runtime I/O. String mixins can make diagnostics and name interactions harder to understand. Never feed untrusted configuration text into generated source. A constant enum result is a compile-time value; an ordinary call to the same function can execute at runtime.
entries.notes:
Target checked 2026-11-02: LDC 1.41.0 / DMD frontend 2.111.0, Linux x86_64; DUB 1.40.0. Official online docs may describe a newer compiler.
Standalone example: save as lesson.d; compile with ldc2 -unittest -boundscheck=on -of=lesson lesson.d, then run ./lesson. Assertions are active in these checks.

Official references: https://dlang.org/spec/function.html#interpretation ; https://dlang.org/spec/template-mixin.html ; https://dlang.org/spec/expression.html#mixin_expressions
entries.summary: Prefer ordinary compile-time functions before generating source text.

entries.title: 39. DUB recipes and conventional project layout
entries.signature:
dub.json
source/app.d
# optional dub.selections.json records resolved dependencies
entries.definition: DUB reads dub.json or dub.sdl and builds D packages. A conventional executable project has a recipe at its root and source/app.d with main. The name identifies the package; targetType chooses an executable or library form. Dependencies belong in the recipe and resolved versions can be recorded in dub.selections.json. The example uses no dependencies.
entries.mental_model: The recipe is the project’s build description; it is not the application’s runtime configuration.
entries.gotchas: Do not confuse a DUB package name with a D module name. Adding dependencies may fetch code and introduce build hooks, native libraries, or licenses to review. Pin reproducible selections for applications as appropriate. Compiler flags differ across toolchains; prefer DUB’s portable build settings where available.

This JSON is a build recipe, not D source. Validated with an isolated dependency-free project; no M5 files or dependencies were created.
Official references: https://dub.pm/dub-guide/recipe/ ; https://dub.pm/dub-reference/recipe/
entries.summary: A recipe describes how to build a package and its dependencies.

entries.title: 40. Build, run, test, and inspect release assumptions
entries.signature:
dub build --compiler=ldc2
dub run --compiler=ldc2
dub test --compiler=ldc2
entries.definition: dub build produces the target, dub run builds and executes it, and dub test runs enabled unit tests. Select the compiler explicitly when more than one is installed. Debug and release build types make different optimization and checking choices. Inspect the effective flags when an assertion or bounds check is important to your reasoning.
entries.mental_model: Build checks whether the program can be made; tests and runs check selected behavior of the resulting program.
entries.gotchas: Never infer correctness from an optimized build alone. LDC -release can disable ordinary asserts/contracts and alter bounds checking. Keep input validation outside removable checks. Do not use release-nobounds casually. DUB executable test configurations may exclude the main source file; keep core tests in imported modules and inspect the test output. Offline flags do not supply missing dependencies; this fixture is dependency-free.
entries.notes:
Target checked 2026-11-02: LDC 1.41.0 / DMD frontend 2.111.0, Linux x86_64; DUB 1.40.0. Official online docs may describe a newer compiler.

Official references: https://dub.pm/dub-guide/building/ ; https://dub.pm/dub-guide/tests/ ; https://github.com/ldc-developers/ldc

entries.title: 41. Paths and working directories
entries.signature:
string path = buildPath(base, "settings.json");
string name = baseName(path);
entries.definition: std.path manipulates path syntax; std.file operates on the filesystem. buildPath combines components using platform conventions. A desktop launcher may start with a working directory different from your source tree. Decide where configuration and cache files belong, pass explicit paths to helpers, and avoid changing the process working directory as an implicit dependency.
entries.mental_model: A relative path is a direction that needs a starting point. Make that starting point explicit.
entries.gotchas: Path normalization is not proof that a path is authorized or confined to a directory. Symlinks, absolute components, and parent traversal need a policy at trust boundaries. A path existing during a check does not guarantee a later operation will succeed. Report actual I/O errors, not just preflight guesses.

entries.title: 42. File I/O with isolated fixtures and cleanup
entries.definition: std.file.read and readText read a whole file; write writes its supplied content to a path. Whole-file operations are simple for small configuration files. For large data, consider std.stdio.File and streaming APIs. Handle filesystem exceptions at the boundary. Tests should create their own unique directory, register cleanup, and avoid real user files.
entries.mental_model: A file operation is an external effect; make the target and cleanup obligations explicit.
entries.gotchas: write can replace existing content, so choose the path intentionally. Do not claim write is an atomic or crash-durable update. A production config update may need a temporary file, rename, permission handling, and appropriate durability requirements. Avoid readText for arbitrary binary data. Cleanup must only remove paths this operation owns.

entries.title: 43. JSON configuration: parse, check types, then apply
entries.signature:
JSONValue document = parseJSON(text);
if (document.type == JSONType.object) { /* inspect keys */ }
entries.definition: std.json parses JSON into JSONValue. Check the root kind, required keys, field types, and allowed ranges before converting the document into application settings. Missing keys and wrong types are separate failures. Construct a complete candidate configuration first; apply it only after validation succeeds so a bad field cannot leave partial live settings.
entries.mental_model: Parsing confirms the envelope is JSON. Schema and domain checks confirm it means what your application expects.
entries.gotchas: JSON object access can throw on absent keys or mismatched types. JSON integers and floating numbers have distinct kinds. Decide whether unknown keys are errors or forward-compatible extensions. Do not execute configuration values as shell source or source-code mixins. File size and nesting limits matter for untrusted documents.

entries.title: 44. Command-line parsing with std.getopt
entries.definition: std.getopt parses a mutable argument array into option variables and removes processed options. main(string[] args) receives command-line arguments, usually with the executable name first. Define flags and options explicitly, validate their values afterward, and pass a structured request to the rest of the program. Keep help and parse errors separate from side effects.
entries.mental_model: The command line is input data to parse, not a script to evaluate.
entries.gotchas: Parsing an integer does not establish its allowed range. Unknown options and malformed values need a useful error path. Do not execute work while half the arguments are still unvalidated. A -- separator can matter when passing arguments onward to another program; understand both parsers.
entries.notes:
Target checked 2026-11-02: LDC 1.41.0 / DMD frontend 2.111.0, Linux x86_64; DUB 1.40.0. Official online docs may describe a newer compiler.
Standalone example: save as lesson.d; compile with ldc2 -unittest -boundscheck=on -of=lesson lesson.d, then run ./lesson. Assertions are active in these checks.

entries.summary: Separate option parsing from command execution.

entries.title: 45. Subprocesses: argument vectors instead of shell text
entries.signature:
auto result = execute([program, argument1, argument2]);
if (result.status != 0) { /* handle failure */ }
entries.definition: std.process.execute accepts an argument array, runs a program, waits for completion, and captures output. An argument vector keeps argument boundaries separate from shell syntax. executeShell intentionally invokes a command interpreter and needs a different threat model. A launch exception and a nonzero child exit status are different failure modes.
entries.mental_model: An argument vector is a list of labelled parcels. A shell string is source code another interpreter will parse.
entries.gotchas: No shell does not mean arbitrary commands are safe: choose the executable, validate options, and consider option injection in the child parser. Use a trusted executable path where appropriate. execute blocks and can collect substantial output; it belongs off a responsive UI thread. Do not log sensitive clipboard contents casually.

Standalone example: save as lesson.d; compile with ldc2 -unittest -boundscheck=on -of=lesson lesson.d, then run ./lesson. Assertions are active in these checks.

entries.title: 46. Process lifecycles: spawnProcess, tryWait, and wait
entries.definition: spawnProcess starts a child and returns a handle without waiting for completion. tryWait probes without blocking; wait waits and obtains the exit status. Design who owns the child handle, how cancellation works, and where completion is delivered. A desktop event loop should integrate a nonblocking notification or delegate blocking waits to a worker.
entries.mental_model: A child handle is an outstanding job with a lifecycle, not its final result.
entries.gotchas: Do not busy-spin on tryWait in a GUI loop. Waiting while leaving redirected pipes unread can deadlock when buffers fill; use an appropriate drain strategy. A timeout should lead to a deliberate cancellation/cleanup policy. APIs such as waitTimeout can be platform-specific; do not assume their availability from their names.
entries.notes:

Official references: https://dlang.org/phobos/std_process.html#spawnProcess ; https://dlang.org/phobos/std_process.html#tryWait

entries.title: 47. Message passing with std.concurrency
entries.definition: std.concurrency provides thread-based message passing with Tid identifiers and typed messages. spawn starts a worker function; send delivers a message; receive and receiveTimeout dispatch to matching handlers. Pass values or suitably immutable data rather than casually sharing mutable references. Keep request identifiers when results may complete out of order.
entries.mental_model: Each worker has a mailbox. Send work and results instead of giving every worker write access to the same notebook.
entries.gotchas: D threads are not Elixir’s lightweight BEAM processes. A reply timeout is not automatic worker cancellation. Mailbox growth, ownership, shutdown, and failure reporting need a design. A blocking receive on a GUI thread can freeze it. A worker reply must be marshalled through the chosen toolkit’s documented UI dispatch mechanism.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 48. Threads and mutex-protected state
entries.signature:
auto mutex = new Mutex();
synchronized (mutex) { /* access protected state */ }
entries.definition: core.thread provides explicit threads, and core.sync.mutex provides mutual exclusion. When multiple threads access mutable state, define one lock discipline for every access that needs protection. Hold locks briefly and release them before calling unknown callbacks or waiting on external work. Join worker threads when their completion is required before their context can expire.
entries.mental_model: A mutex gives one thread the key to a protected region at a time. Every participant must use the same key.
entries.gotchas: The compiler does not prove this manually shared closure state is race-free. Do not read the protected variable outside the lock while workers can write it. Avoid inconsistent lock ordering and joining a worker while holding a lock it needs. A shared qualifier alone does not perform synchronization.

entries.summary: Protect the whole invariant, not just one convenient assignment.

entries.title: 49. Event-loop ownership and queued callbacks
entries.definition: A GUI event loop receives events and dispatches callbacks. Most UI toolkits require widget access on a designated thread. Keep pure state changes separate from slow I/O; send completed worker results back through the toolkit’s official mechanism. The example is only a small in-memory callback queue demonstrating delayed execution, not a GUI framework API.
entries.mental_model: The UI thread is the owner of a desk. Workers deliver messages to the desk rather than moving its objects themselves.
entries.gotchas: Phobos does not provide a universal GUI event loop. A captured stack reference must remain alive until a queued callback runs. Do not call unknown callbacks while holding an unrelated mutex. Reentrancy, nested event loops, and cancellation can change state between events. Never assume that an invented dispatch function exists in a chosen binding.

entries.title: 50. Deadlines, cancellation, and stale replies
entries.signature:
MonoTime deadline = MonoTime.currTime + msecs(250);
if (reply.generation == currentGeneration) { /* apply */ }
entries.definition: core.time provides Duration and MonoTime for elapsed-time reasoning. A monotonic deadline avoids wall-clock adjustments changing the meaning of an elapsed timeout. A generation or request token distinguishes a still-relevant response from an older one. Ignoring a stale reply is different from cancelling the underlying operation; cancellation needs its own cooperative or process-lifecycle protocol.
entries.mental_model: A deadline asks whether work is late. A request token asks whether the answer is still wanted.
entries.gotchas: Do not sleep on the UI thread to implement a timer. Use the selected event loop’s timer API, whose exact calls depend on the external toolkit. Incrementing a generation does not stop CPU work or a child process. Decide how shutdown drains or discards replies and frees their resources.

entries.title: 51. C interop: ABI, zero termination, and borrowed pointers
entries.signature:
extern(C) int foreignFunction(int value);
const(char)* cText = toStringz(text);
entries.definition: extern(C) selects the C calling/linkage convention for a declaration. Existing core.stdc and core.sys bindings provide many standard and platform declarations. A C string is a zero-terminated pointer; a D string is a length-bearing slice, so use a suitable conversion such as toStringz. Keep the backing storage alive for the entire period the C side may read it.
entries.mental_model: Crossing the ABI boundary requires agreement about representation, lifetime, and who releases each resource.
entries.gotchas: D’s int, long, size_t, and C types do not map identically on every platform; use the binding’s declared types. Embedded NUL bytes truncate a C string’s apparent content. A callback pointer and a D delegate have different representations. Do not let a D exception unwind across a C boundary without an explicit compatible contract. Libraries that retain pointers need more than a temporary conversion.

entries.title: 52. Desktop adapters: OS capabilities and external bindings
entries.signature:
enum Availability { available, unsupported, denied }
// a backend reports capability before the application acts
entries.definition: D’s standard library does not supply a universal clipboard, screenshot, colour-picker, or desktop launcher API. A real application chooses an OS service, desktop protocol, external binding, or carefully invoked helper. Linux Wayland and X11 sessions can expose different capabilities and permission flows. The XDG Screenshot portal is an asynchronous request interface; callers must handle its response and cancellation. Keep portable parsing/state logic separate from that backend.
entries.mental_model: The language supplies building blocks. The desktop supplies capabilities whose availability and permission must be negotiated.
entries.gotchas: Do not assume a Wayland session permits arbitrary X11-style screen access. A portal method returning a request handle is not the completed screenshot. Clipboard behavior can depend on selection ownership, formats, and an active event loop. External D bindings must be checked for maintenance, supported library version, threading rules, and native dependencies. No GUI binding API is implied by this entry.

entries.title: 01. AI, machine learning, features, and targets
entries.signature:
X = features available at prediction time
y = target values for supervised training
entries.definition: AI is a broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data, and deep learning uses neural networks with multiple learned stages. In supervised learning, each row has inputs (features) and a desired answer (target). Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number. Unsupervised methods explore structure without supplied target labels. Generative models produce new sequences or other content. Start a project with a concrete task, a simple baseline, and a way to evaluate unseen cases.
entries.mental_model: Features are the clues available when making a prediction. The target is the answer you are trying to estimate.
entries.gotchas: A row identifier is not automatically a useful feature. Do not include answers or information that arrives after the prediction. A high score on a few invented rows is not evidence of useful real-world performance. These entries teach mechanics using small synthetic data, not production models.
entries.notes:
Checked 2026-11-03. Version target: Python 3.14.4, NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.3.3. These are separate packages; np and pd are import aliases.
Executed with assertions on Python 3.14.4; NumPy 2.3.5 and pandas 2.3.3 where imported.
Suggested route: 01-06 data, 07-12 splitting/training, 13-18 evaluation, then 19-24 neural networks and inference.
Official references: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/getting_started.html
entries.summary: Start by defining what one example means and what the model should predict.

entries.title: 02. NumPy shapes, dtypes, and matrix operations
entries.signature:
X.shape == (n_samples, n_features)
y.shape == (n_samples,)
prediction = X @ weights + bias
entries.definition: NumPy arrays hold numeric values with a shape and dtype. A typical table has one sample per row and one feature per column. @ performs matrix multiplication; * multiplies corresponding elements with broadcasting. Reducing axis=0 aggregates across rows, leaving one value per feature. A single sample usually still needs a two-dimensional shape: (1, n_features).
entries.mental_model: Shape is the contract that says which numbers belong to which sample and feature.
entries.gotchas: An array shaped (n,) differs from (n, 1). Subtracting those shapes can accidentally create an (n, n) result by broadcasting. Integer arrays cannot represent fractional values without conversion. Use floating arrays for these examples and check finite values before fitting.
entries.notes:

Executed with assertions on Python 3.14.4; NumPy 2.3.5 and pandas 2.3.3 where imported.

entries.title: 03. pandas data inspection and explicit cleaning
entries.definition: A pandas DataFrame keeps column names and row indexes. Inspect the meaning, units, range, and missingness of each column. to_numeric with errors="coerce" converts invalid text to missing values; that is a decision to record, not a silent repair. Duplicate IDs may indicate repeated exports, multiple measurements, or an incorrect unit of analysis. Resolve their meaning before splitting data.
entries.mental_model: Data inspection checks the labels on your ingredients before you cook with them.
entries.gotchas: Never drop every duplicate-looking row automatically: repeated observations may be legitimate. Missing does not mean zero. pandas aligns by index, so independently filtering X and y can misalign rows. Learned cleaning statistics belong to the training partition; initial schema checks can use rules defined independently of the dataset.

entries.title: 04. Missing values: fit an imputer on training data
entries.signature:
medians = np.nanmedian(X_train, axis=0)
filled = np.where(np.isnan(X), medians, X)
entries.definition: Imputation replaces missing input values using an explicit policy. Median imputation learns one number per numeric feature. Learn it from training rows, then reuse it unchanged on validation, test, and inference rows. scikit-learn provides SimpleImputer for a pipeline; this NumPy example exposes the arithmetic.
entries.mental_model: Training writes the replacement-value lookup table. Later inputs only read that table.
entries.gotchas: Fitting imputation on test rows leaks their distribution. An entirely missing training column has no finite median; choose a domain rule or remove that feature explicitly. Missing targets are a separate supervision problem. np.isnan detects NaN, not infinity, so validate infinities too.
entries.notes:
Checked 2026-11-03. Version target: Python 3.14.4, NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.3.3. These are separate packages; np and pd are import aliases.
Executed with assertions on Python 3.14.4; NumPy 2.3.5 and pandas 2.3.3 where imported.

Official references: https://numpy.org/doc/2.3/reference/generated/numpy.nanmedian.html ; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer.html

entries.title: 05. Scaling: learn once and transform consistently
entries.signature:
mean = X_train.mean(axis=0)
scale = X_train.std(axis=0)
z = (X - mean) / scale
entries.definition: Standardization expresses each numeric feature relative to its training mean and standard deviation. It helps many distance-based and gradient-based methods when feature units differ. StandardScaler packages this operation in scikit-learn. Tree models often do not need this scaling. Scaling does not make a distribution normal and does not repair outliers.
entries.mental_model: A fitted scaler is a ruler calibrated on training data. Keep that ruler for every later measurement.
entries.gotchas: Do not standardize each test batch using its own statistics. Constant training features need a safe scale rather than division by zero. This example uses population standard deviation (ddof=0); pandas std defaults differ. Impute or otherwise handle missing inputs before applying this simple formula.
entries.notes:

entries.summary: Use training means and scales for later data.

entries.title: 06. Categorical features and a stable column schema
entries.definition: Unordered categories such as tea varieties should not automatically become arbitrary numbers like 1, 2, 3: those imply an order or distance to some models. One-hot encoding creates indicator columns. Learn the vocabulary from training data and keep it fixed. For full workflows, OneHotEncoder inside ColumnTransformer is preferable; see entry 09.
entries.mental_model: Each known category gets a named switch. The model expects those switches in a fixed order.
entries.gotchas: Encoding train and test independently can produce different columns. An unseen category requires an explicit policy; here it becomes all zeros, which is not a learned unknown-category embedding. Missing values also need a policy. High-cardinality columns can create very large matrices.
entries.notes:
Checked 2026-11-03. Version target: Python 3.14.4, NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.3.3. These are separate packages; np and pd are import aliases.
Executed with assertions on Python 3.14.4; NumPy 2.3.5 and pandas 2.3.3 where imported.

entries.summary: Keep encoded columns in the same order at training and inference.

entries.title: 07. Train, validation, and test partitions
entries.signature:
train_ids, validation_ids, test_ids = ...
X_train, y_train = X[train_ids], y[train_ids]
entries.definition: Training rows fit model parameters. Validation rows guide choices such as model family or learning rate. The final test set estimates performance after those choices are fixed. Cross-validation can replace a single validation partition within the development data. Split X and y using the same row indexes, before learning preprocessing statistics.
entries.mental_model: Practice material, feedback material, and a final exam serve different purposes.
entries.gotchas: A random split assumes rows can be treated as independent and the future resembles that sampling process. It can fail for repeated users, duplicate documents, or time series. Stratification can preserve class proportions, but it cannot fix group or temporal leakage. A seed makes a particular procedure repeatable; it does not make a split representative.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 08. Group and time splits: match the future use case
entries.definition: If multiple rows come from one device, person, document, or session, holding out rows may still expose the same source during training. Hold out entire groups when evaluating generalization to new groups. For future prediction, respect chronological order; rolling evaluation can use TimeSeriesSplit. The right split depends on what new means for the application.
entries.mental_model: A new photograph of the same object is a different challenge from a photograph of an object never seen before.
entries.gotchas: Group separation does not automatically prevent time leakage, and a time boundary does not automatically separate groups. Features derived from future events leak even if row dates are ordered. Some tasks need both constraints or a time gap. The example demonstrates two independent audits, not one universal splitting algorithm.

entries.title: 09. scikit-learn pipelines for mixed columns
entries.definition: Pipeline chains transformers and a final estimator. ColumnTransformer sends selected columns through different transformations. fit learns preprocessing and model parameters from training inputs; predict applies those saved transformations. Putting this whole object inside cross-validation fits preprocessing separately within each training fold.
entries.mental_model: The pipeline carries the preparation recipe and the predictor together.
entries.gotchas: A pipeline cannot remove leakage already present in your features or split. Keep column names and units consistent. handle_unknown="ignore" produces zeros for unseen categories. sparse_output is the current OneHotEncoder option (introduced in scikit-learn 1.2); older examples may use sparse instead. This example only illustrates fitting and prediction, not evaluation.
