entries.title: 10. Fit a linear model and compare a simple baseline
entries.signature:
weights, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y_train, rcond=None)
prediction = new_design @ weights
entries.definition: Linear regression predicts a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. Least squares chooses coefficients that minimize squared training residuals. A column of ones represents the intercept in this manual design matrix. A mean-target baseline predicts the training target mean for every future row; an improvement over it is a useful first comparison.
entries.mental_model: Training adjusts a line to the practice examples. Prediction plugs new inputs into the fitted line.
entries.gotchas: Use a library solver rather than manually inverting X.T @ X. Collinear inputs can make coefficients unstable. This tiny exact dataset checks arithmetic, not real predictive quality. Baseline statistics must come from training targets, not test targets. A good training fit says little by itself about unseen data.

entries.title: 11. A complete scikit-learn classification workflow
entries.signature:
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
labels = model.predict(X_test)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)
entries.definition: LogisticRegression is a classifier despite its name. It learns a decision rule and can estimate class probabilities. Its classes_ attribute identifies the order of probability columns. This example uses a locally generated dataset, a stratified holdout, and scaling learned inside the pipeline. A DummyClassifier supplies a majority-class baseline.
entries.mental_model: fit studies labelled examples. predict applies the learned rule without receiving the new answers.
entries.gotchas: Do not choose hyperparameters repeatedly by the test score. Accuracy may conceal poor minority-class performance. Estimated probability is not a guarantee, and calibration needs separate evaluation. The synthetic score here would not establish usefulness on real data; no runtime score is claimed because scikit-learn is unavailable locally.

entries.title: 12. Loss, gradients, and a training loop in NumPy
entries.signature:
prediction = X @ weights
loss = np.mean((prediction - y)**2)
weights -= learning_rate * gradient
entries.definition: A loss reduces prediction errors to a number that training tries to minimize. A gradient measures how the loss changes with each parameter. For mean squared error in this linear example, the gradient is 2 * X.T @ (X @ weights - y) / n. Gradient descent repeatedly moves parameters against that gradient. An epoch is a pass through the training data; this example uses the entire dataset each step.
entries.mental_model: The loss is a height on a landscape; the gradient tells you the uphill direction at your current location.
entries.gotchas: Too large a learning rate can make loss diverge; too small can make progress slow. A lower training loss does not prove better generalization. Neural-network libraries calculate gradients automatically, but you still choose the training loop and evaluation plan. This manual linear example is for understanding, not a general optimizer implementation.

entries.title: 13. Regression evaluation: MAE, RMSE, and residuals
entries.signature:
error = prediction - truth
mae = np.mean(np.abs(error))
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(error**2))
entries.definition: Mean absolute error (MAE) averages error magnitudes. Root mean squared error (RMSE) puts extra weight on large errors; both have the target units. Residuals reveal direction and patterns hidden by one average. Compare with a baseline and inspect meaningful subgroups or time periods. R-squared is a relative fit score and can be negative on held-out data; it is not an accuracy percentage.
entries.mental_model: An average tells you the typical bill; the residuals tell you where the bill came from.
entries.gotchas: Check shapes before subtraction to avoid accidental broadcasting. A few huge errors can dominate RMSE. Metrics from different target scales are not directly comparable. Report sample size and evaluation split; a handful of examples gives a noisy estimate. Do not silently discard hard cases from scoring.
entries.notes:
Checked 2026-11-03. Version target: Python 3.14.4, NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.3.3. These are separate packages; np and pd are import aliases.
Executed with assertions on Python 3.14.4; NumPy 2.3.5 and pandas 2.3.3 where imported.

entries.summary: Measure error in units that make sense for the task.

entries.title: 14. Classification: confusion counts, precision, recall, F1
entries.signature:
precision = TP / (TP + FP)
recall = TP / (TP + FN)
F1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
entries.definition: For a chosen positive class, true positives are correct positive predictions, false positives are false alarms, and false negatives are missed positives. Precision asks how often positive predictions are right; recall asks how many actual positives were found. F1 balances precision and recall with a harmonic mean. A confusion matrix shows counts by actual and predicted class.
entries.mental_model: Precision asks whether the alarms deserve attention. Recall asks whether important cases escaped the alarms.
entries.gotchas: State which label is positive. Accuracy can look high when a rare positive class is always missed. Precision or recall can have a zero denominator; choose and report a convention instead of hiding it. Macro averages weight classes equally, while weighted averages use class support and can hide weak minority performance.
entries.notes:

entries.title: 15. Probabilities, thresholds, and calibration
entries.definition: A classifier can return a score or estimated probability before a threshold turns it into a class decision. Lowering the threshold usually produces more positive predictions, trading false alarms against missed positives. Choose thresholds using validation data and the real cost of mistakes. Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies across many cases.
entries.mental_model: The model supplies a score; the application chooses what action that score triggers.
entries.gotchas: A value of 0.9 is not a promise of correctness for this one case. Not every score is a probability. In scikit-learn, locate the positive class through classes_ rather than assuming column 1 always means your label. Do not tune thresholds on the final test set. Calibrate on data separated appropriately from fitting.

entries.title: 16. Cross-validation, overfitting, and hyperparameter search
entries.signature:
search = GridSearchCV(pipeline, parameter_grid, cv=splitter)
search.fit(X_development, y_development)
entries.definition: Overfitting occurs when a model learns details that do not generalize. Cross-validation rotates held-out folds within development data to compare choices. Hyperparameters, such as regularization strength, configure training; parameters are learned during fitting. GridSearchCV tries specified combinations and, with refit=True, refits the selected configuration on all data supplied to fit.
entries.mental_model: Cross-validation provides several practice exams before you open the final test set.
entries.gotchas: The best cross-validation score is influenced by the search and is not an untouched final estimate. Put preprocessing inside the pipeline. Use group/time-aware folds when required. A large training-validation gap suggests overfitting; poor scores on both may suggest weak features or underfitting. For negative loss scorers, larger is better because scikit-learn negates the loss.

entries.title: 17. Data leakage: audit features and split boundaries
entries.definition: Leakage can enter through a target copied into inputs, statistics fitted before splitting, duplicate source material across partitions, or features recorded after the predicted event. A pipeline helps with fitted transformations but cannot discover the true timing or meaning of a column. Write down the prediction moment and source of each feature.
entries.mental_model: Ask whether the model was allowed to see tomorrow’s answer sheet today.
entries.gotchas: Suspiciously good results deserve investigation. Removing an obvious target column is not enough if another column encodes its consequence. Feature selection and vocabulary learning also belong inside the training procedure. ID-overlap checks detect one kind of leakage only; content duplicates and related groups need domain-specific checks.

entries.title: 18. Reproducibility and an experiment record
entries.definition: A seed initializes a random generator, which then advances as you use it. Repeating the same sequence of calls in the same environment can reproduce a split or initialization. A useful experiment record also identifies dataset revision, preprocessing, feature order, package versions, code revision, and metrics. Repeated runs can reveal sensitivity to the split or initialization.
entries.mental_model: A seed is one line in the recipe, not the whole recipe.
entries.gotchas: Changing call order changes later random values. NumPy, Python random, and PyTorch have separate generators. Exact results are not guaranteed across package versions, devices, or nondeterministic operations. Reproducible bad evaluation is still bad evaluation. Never search many seeds and report only the most flattering test score.

entries.title: 19. Neural networks: layers and a forward pass
entries.signature:
hidden = np.maximum(0, X @ W1 + b1)
logits = hidden @ W2 + b2
entries.definition: A dense layer combines inputs with learned weights and biases. An activation such as ReLU introduces nonlinearity. A forward pass computes outputs from current parameters; training changes those parameters. Multiple linear layers without intervening nonlinear operations still collapse into a linear transformation. Logits are raw class scores; softmax converts them to normalized scores.
entries.mental_model: Each layer builds a new representation and passes it to the next layer.
entries.gotchas: A forward pass is not training. Hand-written weights below only demonstrate shapes. Subtract the largest logit before exponentiating to improve softmax stability. Normalized scores need not be well-calibrated probabilities. In PyTorch classification training, CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits, so do not apply softmax first.

entries.title: 20. PyTorch tensors, autograd, and accumulated gradients
entries.signature:
parameter = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
loss.backward()
gradient = parameter.grad
entries.definition: A PyTorch tensor has shape, dtype, and device. Operations involving tensors that require gradients can build a computation graph. Calling backward on a scalar loss accumulates derivatives into leaf tensors’ grad fields. This is automatic differentiation through executed operations, not symbolic algebra or numerical finite differences.
entries.mental_model: Autograd records the route from parameters to loss, then follows that route backward to measure each parameter’s influence.
entries.gotchas: Gradients accumulate until cleared. backward alone does not update parameters. Ordinary training should clear gradients each step and rebuild the forward graph; do not retain graphs unnecessarily. Integer class labels do not require gradients. NumPy conversions or detach can break gradient tracking when used in the wrong place.

entries.title: 21. PyTorch training, mini-batches, and inference mode
entries.signature:
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode(): ...
entries.definition: TensorDataset pairs inputs and targets; DataLoader forms mini-batches. A training step clears old gradients, computes logits and loss, backpropagates, and updates parameters. model.train() enables training behavior in layers such as dropout. model.eval() changes those layer behaviors for evaluation. inference_mode disables gradient-related bookkeeping for prediction; it does not call eval for you.
entries.mental_model: Training adjusts the instrument. Evaluation puts it in measurement mode and reads it without adjusting it.
entries.gotchas: CrossEntropyLoss here expects float logits shaped (batch, classes) and long integer targets shaped (batch,) with class IDs 0..C-1. Keep model and data on compatible devices. Evaluate generalization on held-out data separately; the tiny example below only demonstrates the loop and an inference call. No GPU, download, or pretrained model is required by the snippet.

entries.title: 22. Inference contracts: shape, order, units, and finite inputs
entries.signature:
raw = [record[name] for name in feature_names]
prepared = (raw - saved_mean) / saved_scale
output = prepared @ saved_weights + saved_bias
entries.definition: Inference applies fitted transformations and parameters to new inputs. Preserve the trained feature order, units, missing-value policy, and class mapping. Validate inputs at the boundary, then use the saved preprocessing state. A batch contains multiple independent samples; batching can improve throughput, while latency and memory requirements still matter.
entries.mental_model: A model is a function with a data contract, not just a file full of weights.
entries.gotchas: Two columns in the wrong order may produce plausible but wrong predictions. Do not fit a scaler on incoming requests. Reject or explicitly handle missing and non-finite values. Real services should bound batch sizes, monitor input drift and performance, and evaluate delayed ground-truth labels when available.

entries.title: 23. Save the model contract and load only trusted artifacts
entries.definition: A usable saved model includes feature schema, preprocessing state, learned parameters, label mapping where relevant, and environment metadata. The small example uses JSON for an explicit linear-model format; it is not a general serializer for scikit-learn or PyTorch. Library-specific persistence formats require version compatibility and a deliberate loading policy.
entries.mental_model: Save the measuring instrument together with its calibration and instructions.
entries.gotchas: Unpickling an untrusted pickle or joblib artifact can execute code. Do not load arbitrary downloaded model files as though they were harmless data. JSON still needs size, schema, type, and finite-value validation. A valid hash verifies bytes only when the expected hash comes from a trusted source. Test predictions after a round trip.

entries.title: 24. Embeddings, cosine similarity, and retrieval basics
entries.definition: An embedding represents an item as a numeric vector produced by a model or feature process. Cosine similarity compares directions after normalization. Retrieval ranks stored item vectors against a query vector. Semantic text embeddings require a suitable trained encoder; the hand-made vectors below demonstrate the arithmetic only. Retrieval can supply context to a generative system, but retrieval itself does not generate an answer.
entries.mental_model: Vectors provide coordinates for comparison; retrieval finds nearby coordinates under the chosen measure.
entries.gotchas: Use compatible encoders, versions, and preprocessing for stored and query vectors. Zero vectors have undefined cosine direction. Similarity is not a probability, truth score, or proof that a document answers the question. Evaluate retrieval relevance on representative queries. A language model can still make errors even when retrieved context is provided.

import java.security.{SecureRandom, MessageDigest}

import java.util.Base64

val random: SecureRandom = new SecureRandom()
random.nextBytes(bytes)

val randomText: String = encoder.encodeToString(bytes)

examples.title: A local handler and explicit lifecycle
examples.code:
import com.sun.net.httpserver.{HttpServer, HttpExchange}
import java.net.{InetSocketAddress, URI}
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
import java.io.OutputStream
def demonstrateServer(): Unit =
  val server: HttpServer = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 8080), 0)
  server.createContext("/hello", (exchange: HttpExchange) =>
    val method: String = exchange.getRequestMethod()
    val uri: URI = exchange.getRequestURI()
    val path: String = uri.getPath()
    val rawQuery: String = uri.getRawQuery()
    val body: Array[Byte] = "Hello".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
    exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=UTF-8")
    exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length.toLong)
    val output: OutputStream = exchange.getResponseBody()
    try
      output.write(body)
    finally
      output.close()
  )
  server.start()
  server.stop(0)
examples.explanation: This lifecycle demonstration stops immediately after starting. It is compiled only; validation does not bind a port or call the function.

examples.title: Complete once and inspect waiting failures
examples.code:
import java.util.concurrent.{CompletableFuture, TimeUnit, ExecutionException, TimeoutException}
val future: CompletableFuture[String] = new CompletableFuture[String]()
val accepted: Boolean = future.complete("value")
val acceptedAgain: Boolean = future.complete("replacement")
val result: String = future.get(2, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
println(accepted)
println(acceptedAgain)
println(result)
val failed: CompletableFuture[String] = new CompletableFuture[String]()
failed.completeExceptionally(new IllegalStateException("example failure"))
try
  failed.get(2, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
catch
  case e: ExecutionException =>
    val message: String = Option(e.getCause).map(_.getMessage).getOrElse("unknown")
    println(message)
  case _: TimeoutException => println("Timed out")
  case _: InterruptedException => Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
examples.explanation: Both futures are already completed before get, so this local example does not wait for a network callback.

.thumb
.text

.type demo,%function
.thumb_func

    blt .Lless
    movs r0, #0
    bx lr
    .Lless:
    movs r0, #1
    bx lr
.size demo, .-demo

examples.output: R0=-1,R1=1 -> result 1. R0=1,R1=1 -> result 0; strict less-than excludes equality.

examples.title: Four distinct alphabet entries
examples.code: к · ку · кӀ · кӀу
examples.explanation: The group boundaries are к | ку | кӀ | кӀу; Ӏ belongs inside the last two groups.

examples.title: Good day
examples.code: Уи махуэ фӀыуэ.
examples.explanation: уи = your (singular); махуэ = day; фӀыуэ supplies the good-day wish. The English is the conventional greeting equivalent.

examples.title: Four pronouns
examples.code: сэ · уэ · дэ · фэ
examples.explanation: Four whole pronoun forms, not segmented affixes.

examples.title: Timur introduces himself
examples.code: Сэ си цӀэр Тимурщ.
examples.explanation: сэ = I; си = my; цӀэр = name in the subject phrase; Тимурщ = Timur with the affirmative predicate marker щ.

examples.title: Waiting
examples.code: сожьэ
examples.explanation: First-person singular + present + wait (source analysis s-aw-źa).
examples.output: I wait for him or them.

examples.title: Not going
examples.code: сыкӀуэркъым
examples.explanation: сы-кӀуэ-р-къым: first-person singular + go + present + negative.

examples.title: Spelling contrasts
examples.code: к · кӀ; а · аь; у · уь
examples.explanation: Compare each pair as a unit; neither Ӏ nor ь is optional decoration.

examples.title: Thanks
examples.code: Баркалла.
examples.explanation: Whole lexical expression; no internal segmentation asserted.

examples.title: Speaker and listener
examples.code: со · хьо
examples.explanation: Independent pronouns; no affix segmentation.

examples.title: Two first-person plurals
examples.code: тхо / вай
examples.explanation: Two whole pronouns distinguish exclusion from inclusion of the addressee.
examples.output: We without you / we including you.

examples.title: Naming
examples.code: Сан цӀе Иван ю.
examples.explanation: In order: my; name; Ivan; present copula (name-class agreement).

examples.title: Bread
examples.code: Ас бепиг дина.
examples.explanation: In order: I (ergative); bread (absolutive); made (bread-class agreement).

examples.title: School
examples.code: Со школе ца воьду.
examples.explanation: In order: I; to school; not; go (male-class agreement).

examples.title: One n versus two
examples.code: illunut / illunnut
examples.explanation: Both contain ll; only the second contains nn. Whole-word meanings are supplied without inventing a new inflection.
examples.output: Toward some houses / to my house.

examples.title: Thanks
examples.code: Qujanaq.
examples.explanation: Whole courtesy formula; no internal segmentation asserted.

examples.title: Ask
examples.code: Qanoq ateqarpit?
examples.explanation: qanoq = how; ateqar- = have a name; -pit is the second-person interrogative ending here.

examples.title: Answer
examples.code: Tikamik ateqarpunga.
examples.explanation: Tikamik identifies the name in the instrumental case; ateqar- = have a name; -punga marks a first-person statement.

examples.title: Person contrast
examples.code: Sulivunga. / Sulivoq.
examples.explanation: suli- = work; -vunga = first-person singular indicative; -voq = third-person singular indicative.
examples.output: I work. / He or she works.

examples.title: Location phrase
examples.code: Nuummi
examples.explanation: Nuuk + locative -mi yields Nuummi; k+m assimilates to mm.

examples.title: Not bad
examples.code: Ajunngilanga.
examples.explanation: Underlying ajor- = be bad; -NNGIT = negation; the first-person ending appears as -langa. The resulting surface form is ajunngilanga.

examples.title: Two blocks
examples.code: 레몬
examples.explanation: 레 = ㄹ + ㅔ; 몬 = ㅁ + ㅗ + ㄴ. These are letter divisions, not morphemes.

examples.title: Everyday polite greeting
examples.code: 안녕하세요?
examples.explanation: A conventional greeting, presented as one expression; no speculative internal gloss is needed.

examples.title: Formal greeting
examples.code: 안녕하십니까?
examples.explanation: The formal greeting is a different complete ending choice, not a different person form.

examples.title: A name ending in a consonant
examples.code: 저는 김민준이에요.
examples.explanation: 저 = I (humble); 는 = topic; 김민준 = the name; 이에요 = polite noun-predicate ending after a consonant.

examples.title: Going to a bookshop
examples.code: 폴은 서점에 가요.
examples.explanation: 폴 + 은 = Paul as topic; 서점 + 에 = bookshop as destination; 가요 = goes/is going, polite. English supplies an article that Korean does not require here.

examples.title: An indicated thing
examples.code: 그거 뭐예요?
examples.explanation: 그거 = that thing; 뭐 = what; 예요 = polite copular ending. The question mark marks the written question.

examples.title: Correcting ownership
examples.code: 이거 제 책 아니에요.
examples.explanation: 이거 = this thing; 제 = my (humble); 책 = book; 아니에요 = is not. This is a word-level gloss of the attested conversational sentence.

examples.title: One character, two readings
examples.code: 日曜日
examples.explanation: The source gives にちようび: 日 is read にち at the beginning and び at the end. This is a reading analysis, not a word-by-word English translation.

examples.title: Polite morning greeting
examples.code: おはようございます。
examples.explanation: One conventional greeting; ございます distinguishes the polite expression in this contrast.

examples.title: Casual alternative
examples.code: おはよう。
examples.explanation: The shorter complete greeting is the casual member of the pair.

examples.title: Self-introduction
examples.code: 私はマルシアです。
examples.explanation: 私 = I; は = topic; マルシア = Márcia; です = polite noun-predicate ending.

examples.title: A breakfast habit
examples.code: シリアルを食べます。
examples.explanation: シリアル = cereal; を = object marker; 食べ + ます = eat, polite nonpast. “I” is understood in the breakfast discussion.

examples.title: Checking a relationship
examples.code: みなさんは、友だちですか？
examples.explanation: みなさん = everyone/all of you; は = topic; 友だち = friends; です = polite predicate; か = question marker.

examples.title: Correcting an assumed origin
examples.code: ベトナムじゃないです。
examples.explanation: ベトナム = Vietnam; じゃないです = is not. “I” and “from” come from the dialogue about the speaker’s origin.

examples.title: Two distinct letters
examples.code: თ / ტ
examples.explanation: These are two separate alphabet letters, not variants of a single letter. No English sound equivalent is asserted.
examples.output: aspirated consonant letter / ejective consonant letter

examples.title: Greeting
examples.code: გამარჯობა!
examples.explanation: One conventional greeting, learned as a complete word.

examples.title: Respectful or plural inquiry
examples.code: როგორ ხართ?
examples.explanation: როგორ = how; ხართ = you are, plural or respectful singular. The translation does not display the Georgian number distinction.

examples.title: First person
examples.code: მე ვარ
examples.explanation: მე = I; ვარ = first-person singular present copula.

examples.title: Second person
examples.code: შენ ხარ
examples.explanation: შენ = you, singular; ხარ = second-person singular present copula.

examples.title: Copula before location
examples.code: მე ვარ თბილისში.
examples.explanation: მე = I; ვარ = am; თბილისში = in Tbilisi, with the locative postposition -ში.

examples.title: Copula after location
examples.code: მე თბილისში ვარ.
examples.explanation: The same words appear with the location before ვარ. The source assigns the same basic translation.

examples.title: Room and in the room
examples.code: ოთახი → ოთახში
examples.explanation: ოთახ- is the shared stem; -ი marks the nominative citation form; -ში supplies the location relation in this example.

examples.title: An identification question
examples.code: რა არის ეს?
examples.explanation: რა = what; არის = is, third-person singular; ეს = this.

examples.title: A word with x
examples.code: xoxa
examples.explanation: x is the lateral-click letter; xoxa is the verb stem supplied in the pronunciation list. It is not split into invented meaningful pieces.

examples.title: One person
examples.code: Molo!
examples.explanation: A complete singular greeting; no internal derivation is assumed.

examples.title: More than one person
examples.code: Molweni!
examples.explanation: The plural greeting is learned as its attested form, not built by an invented general suffix rule.

examples.title: Emphasizing the speaker
examples.code: Mna, ndiyahamba ngoku.
examples.explanation: Mna = emphatic I/me; ndi- marks first-person singular; -ya- marks the long positive present form; -hamba = go; ngoku = now.
examples.output: As for me, I am going now.

examples.title: First-person singular
examples.code: Ndiyafunda.
examples.explanation: ndi- = first-person singular; -ya- = long affirmative present marker; -funda = learn/read. The source chooses “learning” in this paradigm.

examples.title: First-person plural
examples.code: Siyafunda.
examples.explanation: si- changes the subject to “we”; -ya-funda remains the same.

examples.title: A person and people
examples.code: umntu / abantu
examples.explanation: um- + -ntu is class 1; aba- + -ntu is class 2. The teaching table associates these with subject concords u- and ba-.

examples.title: Lacking the information
examples.code: Andazi.
examples.explanation: The entire word is a first-person negative predicate, as translated by the source. No unverified internal segmentation is supplied.

examples.title: Lacking understanding
examples.code: Andiqondi.
examples.explanation: A separate complete negative predicate. It is not a different spelling of Andazi.

examples.title: One extra consonant
examples.code: muta / mutta
examples.explanation: These are different words: the second has a long consonant written tt.

examples.title: The same suffix in two forms
examples.code: baarissa / työssä
examples.explanation: baari + ssa and työ + ssä show the back/front alternation. The plus signs explain structure; the actual words are written together.

examples.title: Relaxed hello
examples.code: Moi!
examples.explanation: A complete informal greeting; no verb is needed.

examples.title: More formal daytime greeting
examples.code: Hyvää päivää!
examples.explanation: The two words form the conventional greeting; use this complete form.

examples.title: Give your name
examples.code: Minä olen Anna.
examples.explanation: Minä supplies the subject I; olen is the first-person singular present of olla; Anna supplies the name.

examples.title: One speaker
examples.code: Minä istun.
examples.explanation: istu-n: the stem expresses sitting and -n marks first-person singular.

examples.title: A group including the speaker
examples.code: Me istumme.
examples.explanation: istu-mme: -mme marks first-person plural; me is we.

examples.title: Question about the statement
examples.code: Rakastatko sinä minua?
examples.explanation: rakasta-t-ko combines the love stem, second-person singular -t and question -ko. Sinä is the subject you; minua expresses the object me.

examples.title: Negative with I
examples.code: Minä en puhu.
examples.explanation: Minä = I; en is first-person singular negation; puhu supplies speak.

examples.title: Negative with we
examples.code: Me emme puhu.
examples.explanation: The subject and negative verb change to plural; puhu keeps the same form.

examples.title: One spelling change alters the syllable
examples.code: koma / komma
examples.explanation: The source gives a long first vowel in koma and a short one in komma. These are different dictionary words, not inflected forms of one word.

examples.title: Greeting
examples.code: Hæ!
examples.explanation: A complete greeting.

examples.title: Gratitude
examples.code: Takk!
examples.explanation: A complete expression of gratitude.

examples.title: Singular and plural openings
examples.code: ég er / við erum
examples.explanation: Singular ég takes er; plural við takes erum.

examples.title: Put the person talked about first
examples.code: Maríu þekki ég mjög vel.
examples.explanation: Maríu is the accusative object; þekki means know; ég is the subject I; mjög vel means very well. The natural English order differs from the Icelandic verb-before-subject sequence.

examples.title: An accusative object
examples.code: Ég borða fisk.
examples.explanation: Ég is I; borða is eat; fisk is the accusative object. English supplies a.

examples.title: Ask about location
examples.code: Er ég hér?
examples.explanation: Er precedes ég; hér means here.

examples.title: Deny the location
examples.code: Ég er ekki hér.
examples.explanation: Ekki negates the location claim.

examples.title: A written consonant contrast
examples.code: bada / badda
examples.explanation: Bada has a long stressed vowel; badda has a short one followed by a long consonant.

examples.title: Greeting and gratitude
examples.code: Hej! / Tack!
examples.explanation: The first expression greets; the second thanks. Each is a complete short turn.

examples.title: A short evaluation
examples.code: Det är bra.
examples.explanation: Det supplies that/it, är links it to the description, and bra means good. The source translates the whole phrase naturally as That's good.

examples.title: Begin with the time
examples.code: Nu går jag.
examples.explanation: Nu = now; går = present go; jag = I. The subject follows the verb.

examples.title: Common gender
examples.code: en flaska → flaskan
examples.explanation: En marks common gender; flaska + n yields the displayed definite form.

examples.title: Neuter gender
examples.code: ett brev → brevet
examples.explanation: Ett marks neuter gender; brev + et yields the displayed definite form. Letter means a piece of mail.

examples.title: Ask whether someone is coming
examples.code: Kommer Peter imorgon?
examples.explanation: Kommer is the present verb; Peter is the subject; imorgon means tomorrow.

examples.title: Say you do not understand
examples.code: Jag förstår inte.
examples.explanation: Jag = I; förstår = understand; inte = not.

examples.title: Keep the first letter intact
examples.code: æble
examples.explanation: The word begins with the single Danish letter æ. This example teaches spelling and meaning, not a sound approximation.

examples.title: Say hello
examples.code: Hej!
examples.explanation: A complete greeting, with no subject or verb required.

examples.title: Recognize the irregular present
examples.code: jeg er
examples.explanation: Jeg is the subject; er is the present form of være. This is a paradigm fragment, not a complete self-introduction.

examples.title: Start with now
examples.code: Nu spiser jeg.
examples.explanation: Nu = now; spiser = present eat; jeg = I. English can use am eating for this Danish present.

examples.title: Common gender
examples.code: en stol → stolen
examples.explanation: En identifies the gender; stol + en makes this definite form.

examples.title: Neuter gender
examples.code: et hus → huset
examples.explanation: Et identifies the gender; hus + et makes this definite form.

examples.title: Ask about English
examples.code: Taler du engelsk?
examples.explanation: Taler means speak and comes before du, the subject you; engelsk is English.

examples.title: Say you do not speak Danish
examples.code: Jeg taler ikke dansk.
examples.explanation: Jeg means I; taler is the present verb; ikke negates it; dansk names Danish.

examples.title: Soft sign contrast
examples.code: угол — уголь
examples.explanation: These are two separate nouns. Final л is hard in угол and soft in уголь; ь does not add a vowel.

examples.title: Vowel-letter contrast
examples.code: лук — люк
examples.explanation: The initial л differs in softness. The spelling pair у/ю signals that difference here.

examples.title: Broadly usable greeting
examples.code: Здравствуйте!
examples.explanation: A conventional greeting; learn the whole form as a unit.

examples.title: Informal greeting
examples.code: Привет!
examples.explanation: An informal greeting used among friends and other familiar people.

examples.title: Masculine role noun
examples.code: Он журналист.
examples.explanation: Он means “he”; журналист is the nominative noun “journalist.” English supplies “is a.”

examples.title: Feminine role noun
examples.code: Она студентка.
examples.explanation: Она means “she”; студентка is the feminine noun for a student. The source contrasts it with masculine студент.

examples.title: A book as direct object
examples.code: Я читаю книгу.
examples.explanation: Я = I; читаю = I read/am reading; книг-у = book in the accusative singular. English chooses “a” from context.

examples.title: Yes/no question
examples.code: У них есть дом?
examples.explanation: У них identifies the possessors (“at them” in a literal analysis); есть expresses existence; дом is the house possessed. The question uses no auxiliary “do.”

examples.title: Ask what something is
examples.code: Что это?
examples.explanation: Что = what; это = this. English inserts “is” in the translation.

examples.title: Missing textbook
examples.code: У меня нет учебника.
examples.explanation: У меня = with/at me; нет = there is no; учебник-а = textbook, genitive singular.
examples.output: I do not have the textbook.

examples.title: The vowel letter ъ
examples.code: България
examples.explanation: This country name contains ъ as a vowel letter. The example is a word, not a sentence.

examples.title: One familiar person
examples.code: Здравей!
examples.explanation: The source labels this greeting singular and informal.

examples.title: Polite or plural greeting
examples.code: Здравейте!
examples.explanation: The -те form is used for plural or formal address.

examples.title: Introduce your origin
examples.code: Аз съм от Америка.
examples.explanation: Аз = I; съм = am; от = from; Америка = America.

examples.title: Identify a building
examples.code: Това е хотел.
examples.explanation: Това = this; е = is; хотел = hotel. English supplies “a” in the natural translation.

examples.title: Subject stated
examples.code: Аз работя тука.
examples.explanation: Аз = I; работя = I work; тука = here.

examples.title: Subject understood
examples.code: Не знам.
examples.explanation: Не negates знам, the first-person singular “I know”; аз is unstated.

examples.title: Article on the noun
examples.code: книга — книгата
examples.explanation: Книга is indefinite/bare; книга-та adds the feminine singular definite article.

examples.title: Article on the adjective
examples.code: нова книга — новата книга
examples.explanation: Нова = new, feminine singular; нова-та carries the article before книга.
examples.output: a new book — the new book

examples.title: A useful question
examples.code: Разбирате ли?
examples.explanation: Разбирате is the second-person plural/polite form; ли makes the yes/no question.

examples.title: A negative reply
examples.code: Не разбирам.
examples.explanation: Не = not; разбирам = I understand. No English-style auxiliary “do” is added.

examples.title: Two vowel spellings
examples.code: mână — înger
examples.explanation: Mână has internal â; înger has initial î. Both letters represent the same vowel in these different words.

examples.title: Daytime greeting
examples.code: Bună ziua!
examples.explanation: The source places this conventional phrase in its formal greeting set. Learn it as a unit.

examples.title: Polite question
examples.code: Ce mai faceți?
examples.explanation: The conventional formal question uses faceți; the informal counterpart uses faci. Learn the greeting as a whole expression.

examples.title: Identify yourself
examples.code: Eu sunt din România.
examples.explanation: Eu = I; sunt = am; din = from; România = Romania.

examples.title: Identify a profession
examples.code: Eu sunt profesoară.
examples.explanation: Eu = I; sunt = am; profesoară is a feminine profession noun. English supplies “a.”

examples.title: Origin without an overt pronoun
examples.code: Sunt din America.
examples.explanation: Sunt = am here; din America = from America. The dialogue identifies the speaker.

examples.title: Masculine example
examples.code: un student — studentul
examples.explanation: Un is separate; student-ul attaches the definite article to the masculine singular noun.

examples.title: Find a room
examples.code: Unde este baia?
examples.explanation: Unde = where; este = is; baia = the bathroom, from baie plus the definite article.

examples.title: Request understanding through a negative reply
examples.code: Nu înțeleg.
examples.explanation: Nu = not; înțeleg = I understand here. There is no overt eu and no equivalent of English auxiliary “do.”

examples.title: A noun and its location form
examples.code: хлеў — у хляве
examples.explanation: Хлеў names a shed. У хляве is the attested prepositional phrase “in the shed”; its stem has в before the ending.

examples.title: Daytime greeting
examples.code: Добры дзень!
examples.explanation: Добры = good; дзень = day. The whole expression functions as the conventional greeting given in the source.

examples.title: Name and nationality
examples.code: Майкл — амерыканец.
examples.explanation: Майкл is the subject; амерыканец is the predicate noun. Both use the nominative; English adds the linking verb and article.

examples.title: Say where you live
examples.code: Я жыву ў Каліфорніі.
examples.explanation: Я = I; жыву = I live; ў = in; Каліфорніі is the locative form of Каліфорнія.

examples.title: Familiar question
examples.code: Дзе ты жывеш?
examples.explanation: Дзе = where; ты = familiar singular you; жывеш = you live.

examples.title: Polite or plural question
examples.code: Дзе вы жывеце?
examples.explanation: Дзе = where; вы = polite/plural you; жывеце = the corresponding verb form.

examples.title: No money
examples.code: У мяне няма грошай.
examples.explanation: У мяне = with/at me; няма = there is none; грошай = money, genitive plural of грошы. The natural translation uses English “have.”
examples.output: I do not have any money.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: аас
examples.explanation: A single dictionary headword; аа is the long vowel, not a suffix.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Экии!
examples.explanation: A fixed greeting; no productive morpheme segmentation is asserted.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен студент мен.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; студент = student; final мен = first-person predicate marker.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен суурга ажылдаар мен.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; суур-га = village + case ending, here work location; ажылдаар = will work; final мен = first-person marker.
examples.output: I plan to work in the village.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: ажылым
examples.explanation: ажыл = work; -ым = first-person singular possessive ending.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Чугаалап болур бе?
examples.explanation: Чугаала-п = speak + linking converb ending; болур supplies permission here; бе marks the question.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: күз
examples.explanation: A single noun; ү belongs to the root.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Исәнмесез!
examples.explanation: A conventional greeting, learned here as a whole.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мин — Алсу.
examples.explanation: Мин = I; Алсу = the speaker’s name.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Ул журнал укый.
examples.explanation: Ул = he in the source’s male referent; журнал = magazine; укый = reads/is reading.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: ханымнар
examples.explanation: ханым = lady; -нар = plural.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Алсумы?
examples.explanation: Алсу = a name; -мы = question particle. English supplies the context-dependent “is it.”

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: қол / көл
examples.explanation: Each is a single root; о and ө are different letters.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Сәлеметсіз бе!
examples.explanation: A fixed greeting. The final бе is written separately; no further productive segmentation is required here.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен студентпін.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; студент = student; -пін = first-person singular predicate ending.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен кітап оқимын.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; кітап = book; оқимын = I read. This is a word-by-word analysis, not a proposed letter-by-letter suffix split.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Сіз есепшісіз бе?
examples.explanation: Сіз = polite you; есепші-сіз = accountant + polite second-person ending; бе = question particle.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен есепші емеспін.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; есепші = accountant; емес-пін = negative nominal predicate + first-person ending.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Мен қазақша сөйлемеймін.
examples.explanation: Мен = I; қазақша = in Kazakh; сөйлемеймін = first-person negative “speak.” The whole verbal form is given without inventing a new conjugation.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: kula
examples.explanation: ku- = infinitive marker; -la = eat. The two written syllables are ku-la.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Hujambo? — Sijambo!
examples.explanation: The lesson connects jambo with an issue or trouble. The complete forms function here as greeting and response; no new forms are generated.
examples.output: How are you? — I am fine!

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Ndiyo, mimi ni mwanafunzi.
examples.explanation: Ndiyo = yes; mimi = I; ni links the identity; mwanafunzi = student. English supplies “a.”

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Mimi ninasoma Kiswahili.
examples.explanation: Mimi = I; ni- = first-person subject; -na- = present; -soma = study/read; Kiswahili = Swahili.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Mwanafunzi anasoma.
examples.explanation: Mwanafunzi = student; a- = singular human subject agreement; -na- = present; -soma = read.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Wanafunzi wanasoma.
examples.explanation: Wanafunzi = students; wa- = plural human subject agreement; -na-soma retains the present reading predicate.

examples.title: Attested example
examples.code: Sisomi Kiswahili.
examples.explanation: si- = negative first-person subject; -som- = study/read; -i = present-negative final vowel; Kiswahili = Swahili.

examples.title: Keep both the capital and the umlaut
examples.code: die Tür
examples.explanation: die is the feminine nominative singular article here; Tür is the noun. Learn the two-word unit.

examples.title: Daytime greeting
examples.code: Guten Tag!
examples.explanation: A conventional greeting; learn it as a phrase. Tag is the noun meaning 'day'.

examples.title: Ask a name politely
examples.code: Wie heißen Sie?
examples.explanation: Wie asks 'how'; heißen means 'be called'; Sie is polite 'you'. The natural English question asks for a name.

examples.title: Describe your condition
examples.code: Ich bin müde.
examples.explanation: Ich identifies the speaker; bin is first-person singular sein; müde gives the condition.

examples.title: Two written words fill the first position
examples.code: Die Zwerge lieben die junge Prinzessin.
examples.explanation: Die Zwerge is the subject phrase; lieben is the finite plural verb. die junge Prinzessin is the object phrase. The verb is the third written word but the second sentence element.
examples.output: The dwarves love the young princess.

examples.title: A feminine noun phrase
examples.code: die Prinzessin / eine Prinzessin
examples.explanation: die marks the definite phrase; eine introduces an indefinite feminine singular phrase. The noun keeps its capital in both.

examples.title: A neuter noun phrase
examples.code: das Märchen / ein Märchen
examples.explanation: das and ein are the nominative neuter singular articles here; Märchen is the noun.
examples.output: the fairy tale / a fairy tale

examples.title: A short negative assessment
examples.code: Nicht schlecht!
examples.explanation: nicht negates the adjective schlecht. There is no noun phrase requiring kein.

examples.title: Negating an indefinite noun
examples.code: kein Kind
examples.explanation: kein is the negative determiner; Kind is a neuter noun. The source's paradigm shows this form in both nominative and accusative.

examples.title: A common liaison
examples.code: vous êtes
examples.explanation: vous is 'you'; êtes is its present form of être. The final s of vous links to the following vowel with a /z/ sound, explicitly described by the source.

examples.title: Polite greeting question
examples.code: Bonjour, Paw-Paw. Vous allez bien?
examples.explanation: Bonjour is the greeting; vous is polite address here; allez is the vous form of aller; bien means 'well'. This is an everyday wellbeing formula.
examples.output: Hello, Paw-Paw. Are you doing well?

examples.title: Identify a character
examples.code: Tex est un tatou.
examples.explanation: Tex is the subject; est is third-person singular être; un introduces the masculine singular noun tatou.

examples.title: Say which language you speak
examples.code: Je parle français.
examples.explanation: Je is 'I'; parl-e is the regular first-person singular present form of parler; français names the language here. The clause is excerpted from the source's longer sentence.

examples.title: A singular feminine noun
examples.code: une université
examples.explanation: une is feminine singular; université is the noun. The source's sentence UT est une université supplies this complete noun phrase and its meaning.

examples.title: An indefinite plural
examples.code: des universités
examples.explanation: des introduces an indefinite plural; université takes the written plural ending -s.

examples.title: A question without inversion
examples.code: Est-ce que tu connais Yoda?
examples.explanation: Est-ce que marks a yes/no question; tu is the subject; connais is the tu form of connaître; Yoda is the person asked about.

examples.title: A complete negative clause
examples.code: Je ne vais pas bien.
examples.explanation: Je is the speaker; ne…pas surrounds vais; bien means 'well'. The natural translation describes wellbeing, rather than movement.

examples.title: Two vowels give an easy stress pattern
examples.code: tablo
examples.explanation: The vowels are a and o, so a carries the stress. The source marks this as tAblo for instruction; ordinary spelling remains tablo.

examples.title: Thank someone
examples.code: Dankon!
examples.explanation: dank-o is the noun 'thanks'; -n is its accusative ending. The dictionary explicitly records this standalone formula.

examples.title: Reply to thanks
examples.code: Ne dankinde!
examples.explanation: ne supplies negation; dank-ind-e combines thanking with -ind- ('worth doing') and the adverb ending -e. Its practical meaning is the conventional polite reply.

examples.title: Identify your occupation
examples.code: Mi estas advokato.
examples.explanation: Mi is 'I'; est-as is the present form of 'be'; advokat-o names the profession. The noun is a subject description, not an object.

examples.title: Description plus noun
examples.code: granda domo
examples.explanation: grand-a describes size; dom-o names the house. The phrase has no Esperanto word corresponding to English 'a'.

examples.title: Turn the description into a clause
examples.code: La domo estas granda.
examples.explanation: La marks the definite noun phrase; dom-o is its noun; est-as is the present verb; grand-a describes the subject.

examples.title: Check understanding
examples.code: Ĉu vi komprenas min?
examples.explanation: Ĉu marks the question; vi is the listener; kompren-as is present 'understand'; mi-n is the object form 'me'. The verb remains after the subject.

examples.title: Ordinary order
examples.code: Mi amas vin.
examples.explanation: Mi is the subject; am-as is present 'love'; vi-n marks the listener as the object.

examples.title: Same roles, different order
examples.code: Vin mi amas.
examples.explanation: Vin is still vi plus object -n even in first position; mi remains the subject. The basic meaning is unchanged, though the order can emphasize the object.

examples.title: One written vowel versus two
examples.code: хол / хоол
examples.explanation: хол contains one о; хоол contains оо. These are separate vocabulary items, not one word with a grammatical ending added.

examples.title: General greeting
examples.code: Сайн байна уу?
examples.explanation: сайн = good/well; байна = be; уу = question particle. The natural translation expresses its greeting function.

examples.title: Familiar greeting
examples.code: Сайн уу?
examples.explanation: The shorter formula keeps сайн and the question particle уу. The source labels it informal and suitable with friends.

examples.title: Describe yourself
examples.code: Би гадаад хүн.
examples.explanation: Би = I; гадаад = foreign; хүн = person. Literally the sequence is 'I — foreign person'; 'am' appears in the English translation only.

examples.title: A habitual activity
examples.code: Би кофе уудаг.
examples.explanation: Би = I; кофе = coffee; уу-даг = drink with the habitual ending -даг. The word order is literally 'I coffee drink'.

examples.title: Identify who receives the book
examples.code: Жонн надад ном өгсөн.
examples.explanation: Жонн = John, using the source's spelling; надад = to me; ном = book; өгсөн = gave. The recipient precedes the book and final verb.
examples.output: John gave a book to me.

examples.title: Ask about English
examples.code: Та англи хэл мэдэх үү?
examples.explanation: Та = respectful you; англи хэл = English language; мэдэх concerns knowing; үү marks the question. The natural translation asks about language ability.

examples.title: State a limitation
examples.code: Би монгол хэл мэдэхгүй.
examples.explanation: Би = I; монгол хэл = Mongolian language; мэдэхгүй = do not know. The negative meaning belongs to the final predicate.

examples.title: One value, one copy, one pointer
examples.explanation: Predict the three values before running: score is 15, snapshot is 10, and p.* is 15. There is no allocator here. Next: 02 explains why const p still permits p.* += 5.

examples.title: Fixed pointer, mutable pointee, read-only alias
examples.explanation: writer never points anywhere else, so its binding is const. reader observes the same box, but cannot write through its own pointer.

examples.title: A pointer variable that changes destination
examples.explanation: chosen is var because it is reassigned. The *const u32 type permits reading either number, but not modifying either through chosen.

examples.title: Return a new number or mutate the existing number
examples.explanation: nextCount produces a new value. addJob returns void and changes jobs. inspect borrows an address for reading. All three functions finish while jobs is still alive.

examples.title: Both spellings of the same method call
examples.explanation: The two calls each increment counter once. self.value means the value field of the pointed-to Counter. The read method accepts a pointer with read-only access.

examples.title: Four types sharing three bytes
examples.explanation: whole, view, and many all refer to data; none allocates or copies its bytes. Only access many[2] because the original storage establishes that index is valid. Do not access many[3].

examples.title: Change an element, then return a smaller view
examples.explanation: clearFirst edits data. tail returns a borrowed view into the same array. view still has length 3, while rest has length 2. Both must stop being used when data expires.

examples.title: Increment the caller’s array elements
examples.explanation: Both loops operate on the original counts storage. In the helper, items is already a slice. In the test, &counts provides an addressable array for pointer capture.

examples.title: Find the first element, or return null
examples.explanation: The result of first borrows values; it is only valid while that array is alive. On an empty slice the function returns null before trying index zero.

examples.title: Return a value, letting the caller own its storage
examples.explanation: initialCount returns a number. count belongs to the caller’s test scope. p is used only within that scope.

examples.title: Return a view into the caller’s longer-lived buffer
examples.explanation: writeTag does not return its own local storage. It fills the caller’s buffer and returns a view of that buffer. tag must not outlive buffer.

examples.title: Explicit allocation with test-checked cleanup
examples.explanation: std.testing.allocator belongs in tests and reports leaked allocations. Both defers run after the assertions. Neither pointer nor slice is used after cleanup.

examples.title: Choose behavior and call it through a pointer
examples.explanation: Transform is a type alias. apply receives a number and a function pointer. Reassigning callback changes the chosen operation; it does not modify either function’s code.

examples.title: Literal to sentinel pointer to bounded slice
examples.explanation: The stored bytes include W, y, n, and a zero terminator. span finds the zero and constructs a length-bearing view. Its length is 3, excluding the sentinel. This is reference material to revisit when an API requires it.

examples.title: A known object makes this opaque round trip valid
examples.explanation: This works because count really is an aligned, live u32 and remains alive throughout. The casts do not discover that history for you. The destination annotation supplies *u32 to the builtins; no old two-argument @ptrCast syntax is needed.

examples.title: INVALID: value passed where a pointer is required
examples.explanation: Fix: declare var count: u32 = 1 and call setCount(&count), because this function intends to write the caller’s count. Alternatively redesign the function to accept a value and return a new value. Both the storage and argument need to match your intent.
examples.output: EXPECTED COMPILE ERROR: expected type '*u32', found 'u32'

examples.title: INVALID: trying to write through *const u32
examples.explanation: If mutation is intended, use var count and const p: *u32 = &count. If count should stay immutable, remove the write. Do not use @constCast on genuinely const storage.
examples.output: EXPECTED COMPILE ERROR: cannot assign to constant

examples.title: INVALID: reassigning a const pointer binding
examples.explanation: Fix only the binding: var p: *const u32 = &first. Keep *const u32 because this example reads the numbers. If the goal were changing the pointed-to number, reassigning p would be the wrong operation.
examples.output: EXPECTED COMPILE ERROR: cannot assign to constant

examples.title: two arities and a private helper
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule Book do
  def label(title), do: decorate(title)
  def label(title, author), do: decorate(title) <> " by " <> author
  defp decorate(title), do: "[" <> title <> "]"
end

defmodule WynReference01Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "two arities and a private helper" do
    assert Book.label("Dune") == "[Dune]"
    assert Book.label("Dune", "Frank Herbert") == "[Dune] by Frank Herbert"
    assert is_atom(Book) # a module name is represented by an atom
  end
end
examples.explanation: Both public functions return strings. decorate/1 is a shared private helper. Nothing starts a server or creates persistent state.

examples.title: container shape and tag
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference02Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "container shape and tag" do
    result = {:reading, "Dune", 12}
    {:reading, title, page} = result
    assert title == "Dune"
    assert page == 12
    assert tuple_size(result) == 3
    refute :tea == "tea"
    refute {:ok, "tea"} == [:ok, "tea"]
    assert is_atom(nil)
  end
end
examples.explanation: The match extracts the second and third tuple elements. The atom :reading also checks that the tuple has the expected meaning.

examples.title: extract values and pin an expectation
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference03Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "extract values and pin an expectation" do
    {:book, title, _page} = {:book, "Dune", 12}
    assert title == "Dune"
    title = "Foundation" # rebind the name; no string is mutated
    assert title == "Foundation"
    expected = "Dune"
    assert {:book, ^expected, page} = {:book, "Dune", 12}
    assert page == 12
    assert_raise MatchError, fn ->
      {:book, ^expected, _} = {:book, "Foundation", 8}
    end
  end
end
examples.explanation: The first match extracts data; the pinned match checks an existing expectation. assert_raise tests the intentionally failing match without failing the whole test.

examples.title: INVALID AT RUNTIME: mismatched tuple tag
examples.code:
{:city, name} = {:country, "Norway"}
IO.puts(name)
examples.explanation: This script intentionally raises MatchError before IO.puts runs. To handle both shapes, use case with separate clauses instead of asserting the wrong shape.

examples.title: ordered clauses select a shape
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule Shelf do
  def label({:book, title}), do: "Book: " <> title
  def label({:magazine, title}), do: "Magazine: " <> title
  def label(_other), do: "Unknown item"
end

defmodule WynReference05Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "ordered clauses select a shape" do
    assert Shelf.label({:book, "Dune"}) == "Book: Dune"
    assert Shelf.label({:magazine, "Orbit"}) == "Magazine: Orbit"
    assert Shelf.label(nil) == "Unknown item"
    assert Shelf.label({:book, "Dune", 12}) == "Unknown item"
  end
end
examples.explanation: The final assertion fails the two-element tuple shape and reaches the fallback. It does not partially match the longer tuple.

examples.title: partial map matches and new versions
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference06Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "partial map matches and new versions" do
    original = %{city: "Oslo", country: "Norway"}
    %{city: city} = original
    revised = %{original | city: "Bergen"}
    expanded = Map.put(revised, :population_note, "example")
    assert city == "Oslo"
    assert original.city == "Oslo"
    assert revised.city == "Bergen"
    assert Map.has_key?(expanded, :population_note)
    refute Map.has_key?(original, :population_note)
    assert Map.fetch(%{nickname: nil}, :nickname) == {:ok, nil}
    assert Map.fetch(%{}, :nickname) == :error
    refute match?(%{city: _}, %{"city" => "Oslo"})
  end
end
examples.explanation: The old and revised maps coexist. The final assertion demonstrates why JSON-style string keys and internal atom keys need deliberate handling.

examples.title: classify numbers with guards
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule Climate do
  def zone(value) when is_number(value) and value < 0, do: :below_zero
  def zone(value) when is_number(value), do: :at_or_above_zero
  def zone(_value), do: :not_a_number
end

defmodule WynReference07Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "classify numbers with guards" do
    assert Climate.zone(-2.5) == :below_zero
    assert Climate.zone(0) == :at_or_above_zero
    assert Climate.zone(8) == :at_or_above_zero
    assert Climate.zone("cold") == :not_a_number
    assert Climate.zone(nil) == :not_a_number
  end
end
examples.explanation: The first clause is the narrower numeric case. The second covers remaining numbers; the last covers other types. The fallback handles arbitrary non-numeric input.

examples.title: INVALID AT COMPILE TIME: ordinary call in a guard
examples.code:
defmodule BadGuard do
  def blank?(text) when String.trim(text) == "", do: true
  def blank?(_text), do: false
end
examples.explanation: This intentionally does not compile. Move trimming into a normal function body after establishing that the input is a binary. Do not assume every String function is allowed in when.
examples.output: EXPECTED FAILURE: cannot invoke remote function String.trim/1 inside a guard

examples.title: three branching expressions
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference09Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "three branching expressions" do
    value = {:colour, :blue}
    label = case value do
      {:colour, colour} -> Atom.to_string(colour)
      _ -> "unknown"
    end
    score = 72
    band = cond do
      score >= 90 -> :high
      score >= 60 -> :middle
      true -> :low
    end
    assert label == "blue"
    assert band == :middle
    assert if(0, do: :truthy, else: :falsey) == :truthy
    assert if(nil, do: :truthy, else: :falsey) == :falsey
  end
end
examples.explanation: label and band receive the chosen branch values. The two if assertions highlight Elixir truthiness, which differs from languages that treat zero as false.

examples.title: caller handles both lookup outcomes
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule Palette do
  def lookup(:ocean), do: {:ok, "#005577"}
  def lookup(:sun), do: {:ok, "#FFCC00"}
  def lookup(_), do: {:error, :unknown_colour}
  def display(name) do
    case lookup(name) do
      {:ok, code} -> "Colour " <> code
      {:error, :unknown_colour} -> "Choose another colour"
    end
  end
end

defmodule WynReference10Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "caller handles both lookup outcomes" do
    assert Palette.display(:ocean) == "Colour #005577"
    assert Palette.display(:forest) == "Choose another colour"
    assert {:ok, code} = Palette.lookup(:sun)
    assert code == "#FFCC00"
    assert Palette.lookup(:forest) == {:error, :unknown_colour}
  end
end
examples.explanation: The lookup produces data. display/1 decides what to do with it. The tests separately check the full return contract and the unwrapped successful value.

examples.title: lookup and parse a complete integer
examples.explanation: The guard on the first <- prevents calling Integer.parse/1 on non-text. Matching an empty remainder ensures the whole text was parsed. The missing-key and unparseable cases intentionally share one error here.

examples.title: new collection and unchanged input
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference12Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "new collection and unchanged input" do
    prices = [2, 7, 4]
    original = prices
    discounted = prices
      |> Enum.filter(fn price -> price >= 4 end)
      |> Enum.map(fn price -> price - 1 end)
    total = Enum.reduce(discounted, 0, fn price, sum -> price + sum end)
    upper = &String.upcase/1
    assert discounted == [6, 3]
    assert total == 9
    assert prices == [2, 7, 4]
    assert original == prices
    assert upper.("tea") == "TEA"
  end
end
examples.explanation: filter produces [7, 4]; map produces [6, 3]; reduce produces 9. The named prices binding and original still refer to the unchanged input list.

examples.code:

defmodule WynReference15Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "a correlated request and reply" do
    parent = self()
    worker = spawn(fn ->
      receive do
        {:echo, from, ref, text} -> send(from, {:reply, ref, String.upcase(text)})
      after
        1_000 -> :idle_timeout
      end
    end)
    ref = make_ref()
    try do
      send(worker, {:echo, parent, ref, "tea"})
      reply = receive do
        {:reply, ^ref, text} -> text
      after
        1_000 -> :reply_timeout

      refute worker == parent
    after
      Process.exit(worker, :kill) # cleanup only this example's worker
    end
  end
end

examples.title: replacement uses its startup state
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule WynReference17Test do
  use ExUnit.Case, async: false

  test "replacement uses its startup state" do
    child = %{id: :scratch_note, start: {Agent, :start_link, [fn -> [] end]}}
    {:ok, supervisor} = Supervisor.start_link([child], strategy: :one_for_one)
    try do
      [{:scratch_note, first, :worker, _}] = Supervisor.which_children(supervisor)
      Agent.update(first, fn _ -> ["remember this"] end)
      assert Agent.get(first, & &1) == ["remember this"]
      :ok = Supervisor.terminate_child(supervisor, :scratch_note)
      {:ok, replacement} = Supervisor.restart_child(supervisor, :scratch_note)
      refute replacement == first
      assert Agent.get(replacement, & &1) == []
    after
      Supervisor.stop(supervisor)
    end
  end
end
examples.explanation: Only this example’s child is stopped. Its replacement runs the original fn -> [] end initializer, so the changed list is gone. Explicit lifecycle calls make the demonstration deterministic and do not claim to test crash restart timing.

examples.title: Group success and fallback cases with describe
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule Scale do
  def multiply(value, factor) when is_number(value) and is_number(factor) do
    value * factor
  end
  def multiply(_value, _factor), do: :unsupported
end

defmodule ScaleTest do
  use ExUnit.Case

  describe "multiply/2" do
    test "returns the product" do
      value = 3                       # arrange: choose the input
      result = Scale.multiply(value, 4) # act: call the function
      assert result == 12              # assert: check its contract
      refute result == 11
    end

    test "handles other numeric values" do
      assert Scale.multiply(-2, 3) == -6
      assert Scale.multiply(3.5, 2) == 7.0
      assert Scale.multiply(0, 8) == 0
    end

    test "fallback handles invalid argument combinations" do
      for {value, factor} <- [{nil, 2}, {2, :many}, {"3", 4}] do
        assert Scale.multiply(value, factor) == :unsupported
      end
    end
  end
end
examples.explanation: The tests check the public contract using exact results. describe groups related cases. Each {value, factor} pair calls multiply/2, and its fallback also takes two arguments. The tested numeric policy deliberately permits negative numbers, zero, and floats.

examples.title: Intentional arity mistake, safely tested
examples.code:
ExUnit.start()

defmodule BrokenScale do
  def multiply(value, factor) when is_number(value) and is_number(factor) do
    value * factor
  end
  def multiply(_value), do: :unsupported # WRONG fallback arity for /2
end

defmodule BrokenScaleTest do
  use ExUnit.Case

  test "a /1 fallback cannot handle a /2 call" do
    assert BrokenScale.multiply(:many) == :unsupported
    assert BrokenScale.multiply(3, 4) == 12
    assert_raise FunctionClauseError, fn ->
      BrokenScale.multiply(3, :many)
    end
  end
end
examples.explanation: This intentionally flawed API compiles because multiply/1 and multiply/2 are separate functions. A two-argument call never tries the one-argument clause. assert_raise checks that failure as part of a passing test. Correcting the fallback to def multiply(_value, _factor), do: :unsupported restores the /2 contract shown in the first example.

examples.title: Loss, gradients, and a training loop in NumPy — example

import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-1., 1., 20)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
y = 1.0 + 2.0*x
weights = np.zeros(2)
before = np.mean((X @ weights-y)**2)
for step in range(300):
    error = X @ weights-y
    gradient = (2 / len(y)) * X.T @ error
    weights -= 0.1 * gradient
after = np.mean((X @ weights-y)**2)
assert np.isfinite(after) and after < before
assert np.allclose(weights, [1., 2.], atol=1e-6)
examples.explanation: Only weights are updated. The assertion verifies the known solution for this synthetic linear problem.

fp = int(((truth == 0) & (predicted == 1)).sum())

recall = tp / (tp+fn) if tp+fn else 0.0

assert np.isclose(f1, 2/3)

examples.title: PyTorch training, mini-batches, and inference mode — example
examples.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

torch.manual_seed(5)
X = torch.tensor([[-2.], [-1.], [-0.5], [0.5], [1.], [2.]], dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.tensor([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=torch.long)
batches = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X, y), batch_size=3, shuffle=True, num_workers=0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 2))
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
model.train()
for epoch in range(10):
    for features, targets in batches:
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        logits = model(features)
        loss = loss_fn(logits, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    logits = model(torch.tensor([[0.75]], dtype=torch.float32))
    predicted_class = logits.argmax(dim=1)
assert predicted_class.shape == (1,) and not logits.requires_grad

            "mean": [2.0], "scale": [1.0],

import numpy as np
names = ["item-a", "item-b", "item-c"]
documents = np.array([[1., 0., 0.], [0.8, 0.2, 0.], [0., 1., 0.]])
query = np.array([1., 0., 0.])
