The + form tests presence without requiring a nonempty stored value. The - fallback is used only for an unset element, whereas :- also uses the fallback for an empty element. This distinction is useful for configuration maps. Associative-array iteration order is not a sorting guarantee. Keys in this example are fixed nonempty strings.

Validated 2026-11-04: Bash 5.3.9 on Linux. Run with bash example.sh, not sh. Assertions use [[ ... ]] followed by an explicit exit on failure.

Official references: https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Arrays.html ; https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Shell-Parameter-Expansion.html

examples.title: Create an empty vector with an explicit element type
examples.explanation: Both spellings state the element type. String is owned by the vector after push. The capacity check uses a non-zero-sized element type.

examples.title: Reserve room without creating elements
examples.explanation: The four pushes fit the reserved storage. Use len to decide which elements exist. This is a constructor call, Vec::with_capacity(4), not batch.with_capacity(4).

examples.title: Move an owned value into the end of a vector
examples.explanation: The old label variable is not used after the move. The vector owns both strings and drops them when it is dropped. Append a whole iterable with extend; append one element with push.

examples.title: Take the final owned value and handle an empty vector
examples.explanation: The first expect is justified by the immediately constructed nonempty vector. The final assertions explicitly handle the empty case. pop leaves allocated vector capacity available for later pushes.

examples.title: Count existing elements rather than reserved space
examples.explanation: A capacity of eight permits three existing elements and five or more spare slots. get(len) returns None because len is past the final element.

examples.title: Check emptiness before choosing a result
examples.explanation: clear removes the element but keeps the vector allocation. is_empty follows the element count through those changes.

examples.title: Observe available storage without relying on a growth formula
examples.explanation: The example checks guarantees rather than assuming the allocator returned exactly five slots. Existing elements, not spare capacity, may be indexed.

examples.title: Reserve additional room relative to the current length
examples.explanation: reserve itself creates no values. Six later pushes fit the guaranteed additional room. Oversized capacity requests can panic, and ordinary allocation failure is not reported as a Result by this method.

examples.title: Borrow an element or range without an out-of-bounds panic
examples.explanation: The single-index result is a reference to one value. The range result is a borrowed slice. Neither operation changes ownership of the vector.

examples.title: Change an existing element only when its index is valid
examples.explanation: The mutable borrow ends before the vector is inspected again. The range form borrows a slice and fill edits its existing elements.

examples.title: Insert at a position while preserving the surrounding order
examples.explanation: The position check demonstrates how to reject an invalid insertion without invoking a panic. Insertion at length is valid, unlike removal at length.

examples.title: Remove by index and preserve the remaining order
examples.explanation: The returned String is owned by removed. The explicit index guard handles a possible invalid index; remove itself returns T, not Option<T>.

examples.title: Remove in constant time when element order is unimportant
examples.explanation: west moves into south’s former slot. Removing the final element is also valid and needs no replacement move.

examples.title: Drop all elements while keeping storage for reuse
examples.explanation: The old String is dropped, while the Vec keeps its element-buffer allocation. Reusing the container does not mean the original String allocation is preserved.

examples.title: Keep a prefix without accidentally growing the vector
examples.explanation: The tests cover shrinking, an oversized requested length, and truncating to zero. Use resize if you intend to grow and supply new values.

examples.title: Filter owned values in place while preserving their order
examples.explanation: The mutable closure capture counts visits. No extra vector is collected, and the two retained Strings stay in their original relative order.

examples.title: Grow with cloned values or shrink to a new length
examples.explanation: String cloning makes the new values independently editable. The fill argument is evaluated even when shrinking; truncate avoids supplying an unnecessary fill value.

examples.title: Append every item produced by an iterable
examples.explanation: The two calls make the ownership difference visible. The shown signature is Extend<T>; Vec also supports some extension forms from references. This example explicitly clones owned Strings where preservation is intended.

examples.title: Read elements without consuming their vector
examples.explanation: collect drives the mapped iterator to produce a new vector of lengths. The original Strings remain owned by names. for name in &names is another common shared-borrowing form.

examples.title: Mutate each existing element through an exclusive iterator
examples.explanation: The dereference *count writes into the vector. Each loop iteration receives a distinct mutable element reference. for count in &mut counts is the concise equivalent.

examples.title: Pass a borrowed sequence to a helper without exposing Vec ownership
examples.explanation: The helper needs a sequence, not a particular owning container. It could also receive an array slice. These small values fit u32; the helper does not implement general overflow handling.

examples.title: Sort existing elements in place using their total order
examples.explanation: Duplicates remain present: sorting is not deduplication. The empty case is valid. sort_unstable is an alternative when preserving equal-element order is unnecessary.

examples.title: Check for an equal value without removing it
examples.explanation: The numeric lookup borrows the target value. The String variant uses a predicate to compare against str, illustrating the difference between contains(&T) and arbitrary comparisons.

examples.title: Consume an owned vector and move its elements into an iterator
examples.explanation: next returns Option<String> because this is the owned implementation. The extracted string can be modified independently. Use iter when the original vector must stay available.

examples.title: Start an empty set and let equality define uniqueness
examples.explanation: insert returns whether the set gained a new member. The second equal String is not a second member.

examples.title: Reserve set storage before inserting a batch
examples.explanation: The four distinct values fit the requested room without a resize. No exact bucket count is assumed.

examples.title: Use the boolean result to detect the first occurrence
examples.explanation: The Vec preserves discovery order; the HashSet only answers whether a name was already seen.

examples.title: Replace an equal stored value and recover the old one
examples.explanation: This custom type defines identity by id alone. replace updates the label even though the two records compare equal.

examples.title: Look up owned Strings using a borrowed str
examples.explanation: No temporary String is needed for the lookup. Membership is exact and case-sensitive for these Strings.

examples.title: Borrow the actual value stored in the set
examples.explanation: get returns the stored String by reference, rather than just a boolean or an owned copy.

examples.title: Remove a member and distinguish missing input
examples.explanation: The second removal is a normal absent result, not a panic.

examples.title: Move a stored member out of the set
examples.explanation: Removing before changing the value avoids altering a stored key’s hash or equality.

examples.title: Count distinct members, including after duplicate insertion
examples.explanation: The set discarded the duplicate 3 during construction.

examples.title: Check whether any members remain
examples.explanation: clear changes membership without discarding the reserved set storage.

examples.title: Separate storage capacity from the number of members
examples.explanation: Capacity is measured in elements, not bytes; it is not an index range.

examples.title: Reserve room for additional distinct members
examples.explanation: Reservation does not insert placeholder values. Use try_reserve when errors must be returned.

examples.title: Handle a reservation error as a Result
examples.explanation: The impossible capacity request is rejected without allocating enormous memory or discarding the member.

examples.title: Release excess capacity without requiring an exact size
examples.explanation: Only bounds guaranteed by the operation are asserted; the exact capacity is implementation-dependent.

examples.title: Drop all members while retaining storage for reuse
examples.explanation: The old String is dropped, but the table allocation is available for another batch.

examples.title: Keep only members matching a predicate
examples.explanation: The test checks the retained set, not callback order.

examples.title: Borrow members and sort a separate view for display
examples.explanation: The Vec supplies a deterministic display order. The HashSet is still unordered.

examples.title: Consume the set and take ownership of its members
examples.explanation: The collected Strings are independently owned by the Vec; words cannot be used after the move.

examples.title: Move members out while keeping the empty set allocation
examples.explanation: Unlike into_iter, drain leaves the set variable available for reuse after the iterator is finished or dropped.

examples.title: Combine all distinct values from two sets
examples.explanation: The signature shows the default RandomState hasher. The iterator borrows both inputs; collecting copied values creates an independent result. Both input sets remain usable.

examples.title: Find members present in both sets
examples.explanation: The signature shows the default RandomState hasher. The iterator borrows both inputs; collecting copied values creates an independent result. Both input sets remain usable.

examples.title: Find values in the left set but not the right
examples.explanation: The signature shows the default RandomState hasher. The iterator borrows both inputs; collecting copied values creates an independent result. Both input sets remain usable.

examples.title: Find members present in exactly one set
examples.explanation: The signature shows the default RandomState hasher. The iterator borrows both inputs; collecting copied values creates an independent result. Both input sets remain usable.

examples.title: Check whether every required value is available
examples.explanation: This models a set relationship only; real authorization also needs trusted inputs and application rules.

examples.title: Read the inverse of a subset relationship
examples.explanation: The two spellings express the same relationship from opposite sides.

examples.title: Test whether two sets have no overlap
examples.explanation: Use this boolean query instead of allocating an intersection merely to test emptiness.

examples.title: Insert every value from an iterable and collapse duplicates
examples.explanation: The first batch is moved; the second batch is cloned explicitly. Extend is a trait method, not a HashSet constructor.

examples.title: Collect transformed data into a set
examples.explanation: Normalization is an explicit application policy here. A HashSet itself does not trim or ignore letter case.

examples.title: Derive equality and hashing consistently for a custom key
examples.explanation: Both fields participate in identity. Use a map keyed by an ID when the associated payload should change independently of identity.

examples.title: Choose deterministic presentation and understand set operators
examples.explanation: The operator result owns cloned Strings, while both inputs remain available. Prefer BTreeSet if sorted iteration is a continuing requirement.
